Verify Now Blog > Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips by: Mila Sep 30,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout analog vs digital circuits analog and digital circuits analog circuits digital circuits mixed signal PCB design We often say that the world of chips consists of only 0s and 1s. But more accurately, digital circuits use defined voltage ranges to represent discrete logic states, while the real world is clearly not like that. Human voices have different volumes, light has different levels of brightness, temperature changes continuously, and radio waves do not simply jump between 0 V and 1 V. So here is the question: If CPUs mainly process digital data, how can a smartphone hear sound, capture photos, connect to a cellular network, and charge its battery? The answer lies in three types of chips: digital chips, analog chips, and mixed-signal chips. Understanding the differences between them is also important for PCB layout , because digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits have different requirements for signal integrity, grounding, power, and noise control. （class B analog audio amplifier） Analog vs Digital Circuits: What Is the Difference? The key difference between analog vs digital circuits is how they represent and process signals. Digital signals focus on discrete states. In a typical digital circuit, voltage is divided into high and low ranges, which are interpreted as 1 and 0. As long as the signal remains within the specified range, small amounts of noise usually do not change the logic result. Analog signals, on the other hand, preserve continuous changes. The small voltage generated by a microphone, the radio-frequency signal received by an antenna, changes in temperature detected by a sensor, and the voltage and current during battery charging and discharging can all vary continuously over time and amplitude. A simple way to understand analog and digital circuits is: A digital signal is like written text. It mainly cares about which character is being represented. An analog signal is like speech. It contains not only information, but also volume, tone, speed, and many subtle changes. In other words, digital circuits are good at processing discrete information, while analog circuits directly interact with continuously changing signals from the real world. （Analog vs Digital Signals） Digital Chips: Computing, Control, and Memory Digital chips are best suited to problems that can be clearly defined and represented as discrete data. Common digital chips include: CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs; MCUs and various controllers; DRAM, SRAM, and NAND Flash; FPGAs; Digital interface and network processing chips. Digital circuits are built from large numbers of logic gates, flip-flops, registers, and memory cells. Driven by a clock, data flows and is processed according to defined rules. Their biggest advantage is their high level of abstraction. Engineers can move from transistors to logic gates, then to adders, processors, instructions, and software. This allows complex systems to be designed, verified, and optimized at different levels of abstraction. Digital chips are particularly suitable for: Executing programs; Storing data; Implementing complex control functions; Performing large-scale logic and mathematical operations; Precisely coordinating different functions within a system. However, digital circuits themselves cannot directly process continuously changing analog signals. A CPU cannot simply take the tiny analog voltage generated by a microphone and process it as digital data. Nor can it directly turn a string of binary data into the continuous analog signal needed to drive a speaker. This is where analog circuits and mixed-signal circuits come in. Analog Chips: Connecting Electronics to the Real World Analog chips process continuously changing voltages and currents. They do not necessarily focus on extremely large amounts of digital logic, but they often determine whether a device can hear clearly, measure accurately, transmit effectively, and charge efficiently. Typical analog and analog-intensive chips include: Operational amplifiers and comparators; Voltage references and analog front ends; Power management chips such as LDOs and DC-DC converters; Audio amplifiers; Analog circuits used in RF front ends. The problems that analog circuits need to solve are very much connected to the real world: How do you amplify a weak signal? How do you filter out unwanted noise? How do you keep an output voltage stable? How do you maintain performance when temperature and supply voltage change? Analog design is challenging because many real-world details cannot simply be abstracted away. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Digital circuits mainly need to determine whether a signal should be recognized as 1 or 0, so many small variations can be tolerated. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. For example, for an analog amplifier, whether the output is 0.999 V or 1.001 V may affect the final measurement or control result. Mixed-Signal Chips: Bridging the Analog and Digital Worlds Real-world electronic devices need both analog and digital processing. That is why mixed-signal chips exist. They integrate analog and digital circuits into the same chip or system so that the two types of circuits can work together. The most typical bridge is: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Converts analog signals into digital data; DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter): Converts digital data back into analog signals. The process can be simplified as: Real world → Analog signal → ADC → Digital data → Digital processing → DAC → Analog signal → Real world For example, during audio recording and playback, a microphone first converts sound into an analog electrical signal. The analog front end processes the signal, and an ADC converts it into digital data. After the digital processor stores and processes the data, a DAC converts it back into an analog signal, which is then amplified and reproduced by a speaker. A mixed-signal chip is not simply a combination of an ADC and a DAC. It may also contain: ADCs and DACs; PLLs and clock circuits; High-speed SerDes interfaces; Analog front ends; Digital calibration and control logic. These circuits need to work together within the same system, which is one reason mixed-signal design can be challenging. How Do Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Work Together in a Smartphone? A smartphone is a typical example of a system that combines all three types of chips. It needs to process digital data while constantly interacting with the analog signals of the real world. When You Take a Photo The image sensor converts light into electrical signals; The analog front end amplifies and processes the weak signals; The ADC converts the analog signals into digital data; The ISP performs noise reduction, white balance, and color processing; The CPU, GPU, NPU, and other digital processing units continue with computation, compression, display, and AI recognition. The overall process is essentially: Light → Analog electrical signal → Digital image data → Digital processing When You Connect to a Cellular Network The antenna receives radio-frequency signals; The RF front end amplifies, filters, and converts the signals; An ADC and related circuits convert the analog signal into digital samples; The baseband processor performs demodulation, error correction, and protocol processing. The signal path can be simplified as: Radio waves → Analog RF signal → Digital data → Baseband processing When You Charge Your Smartphone Power management and charging circuits convert and regulate the input voltage and current; The system monitors battery voltage, temperature, and charging status; Power devices handle the main energy conversion; Digital control logic adjusts the charging strategy according to system conditions. So, a smartphone is not purely a “digital device.” Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Compared These three types do not simply replace one another. In real electronic systems, they usually need to work together. Why Are Analog Chips Difficult to Replace? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. Why Do These Differences Matter in PCB Design? The differences between analog and digital circuits inside a chip also extend to PCB design. Digital circuits typically require careful consideration of signal integrity, crosstalk, clocks, and return paths, while analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, grounding, power stability, and sensitive signal integrity. For mixed signal PCB design, these issues often exist at the same time. For example, an ADC or DAC may connect to analog signals on one side and digital processing circuitry on the other. If the layout, power distribution, grounding, or return paths are not properly designed, noise generated by digital circuits can couple into sensitive analog signals. Therefore, mixed-signal PCB design often requires careful consideration of: Analog and digital circuit placement; Power and ground design; Return paths for high-speed digital signals; Noise control around ADCs and DACs; Decoupling capacitors and power integrity; Isolation between sensitive analog signals and high-speed digital signals. This is why understanding the differences between analog and digital circuits is important not only for chip designers, but also for PCB designers. Conclusion Digital chips have not replaced analog chips, and analog chips are not a “lower-end” version of digital chips. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Digital circuits mainly need to determine whether a signal should be recognized as 1 or 0, so many small variations can be tolerated. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. For example, for an analog amplifier, whether the output is 0.999 V or 1.001 V may affect the final measurement or control result. Mixed-Signal Chips: Bridging the Analog and Digital Worlds Real-world electronic devices need both analog and digital processing. That is why mixed-signal chips exist. They integrate analog and digital circuits into the same chip or system so that the two types of circuits can work together. The most typical bridge is: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Converts analog signals into digital data; DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter): Converts digital data back into analog signals. After the digital processor stores and processes the data, a DAC converts it back into an analog signal, which is then amplified and reproduced by a speaker. It may also contain: ADCs and DACs; PLLs and clock circuits; High-speed SerDes interfaces; Analog front ends; Digital calibration and control logic. These circuits need to work together within the same system, which is one reason mixed-signal design can be challenging. How Do Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Work Together in a Smartphone? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Are More PCB Decoupling Capacitors Always Better? by: Mila Oct 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor PCB decoupling capacitor decoupling capacitor placement PCB power integrity If you have ever designed a PCB schematic , you have probably placed a familiar trio of capacitors near a chip’s power pins: 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF.It seems like a safe bet. Different capacitance values, neatly arranged, ready to keep the power supply stable and suppress noise. But is this tried-and-tested combination always the best choice? When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Design: Three Key Principles It comes down to three key principles. 1. Start with the requirements, not guesswork. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Can AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly in ADC PCB layout? by: Mila Sep 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout agnd vs dgnd mixed-signal PCB design ADC PCB layout When designing an ADC or DAC, one of the most common questions in PCB layout is how to handle the AGND and DGND pins. If a device has separate analog and digital ground pins, should they be connected directly, separated into different ground planes, or joined at a single point? This question is especially important in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design, where fast digital switching currents can potentially interfere with sensitive analog circuits. To understand the right approach to AGND vs DGND, the key is not simply whether the two grounds are connected, but how the return currents flow through the PCB. (schematic with AGND & GND) Why Do ADCs and DACs Have Separate AGND and DGND Pins? An ADC can be roughly understood as having two different domains. One side contains the sampling circuit, op amp, reference, comparator, PGA, DAC core, and analog bias circuits. These belong to the analog domain. The other side contains the SPI/I²C interface, digital logic, registers, clock, state machine, and other digital circuits. These belong to the digital domain. One of the biggest characteristics of digital circuits is that their current can change very quickly. For example, when an SPI interface operates at tens of MHz, every clock transition can generate transient current. These currents need to form a complete return path through the power and ground network. This is where the problem begins. Assume the digital return current is: ID = 50 mA and it flows through a PCB trace with only: R = 20 mΩ The resulting ground voltage variation is: V = IR = 50 mA × 20 mΩ = 1 mV. 1 mV may look very small, but it is not necessarily negligible for a high-resolution ADC. For example, consider a 16-bit ADC with a 2.5 V full-scale range: 1 LSB ≈ 2.5 V / 65536 ≈ 38.1 μV Therefore, a 1 mV ground voltage variation corresponds to approximately: 1 mV / 38.1 μV ≈ 26 LSB Of course, the actual ADC conversion error depends on how this ground disturbance couples into the analog input, reference, and internal circuits. However, this example illustrates an important point: For a high-precision ADC, the key concern is not simply how low the ground resistance is, but where the digital return current flows. This is one of the fundamental considerations in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly? In many designs, AGND and DGND ultimately connect to the same ground reference. However, there is an important condition: this does not mean that AGND and DGND can simply be connected with two arbitrary traces and left at that. If the ADC or DAC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND should be connected close to the device, follow the manufacturer's recommended layout. For many high-precision ADCs and DACs, the recommended PCB layout is designed to maintain a low-impedance, low-inductance connection between AGND and DGND while preventing digital return currents from flowing through sensitive analog areas. Therefore, AGND and DGND do not necessarily need to be electrically isolated. What matters more is controlling the return-current path. (return-current path) Why Ground Plane Splitting Can Cause More Problems In traditional PCB layout, it is common to see analog and digital areas separated into AGND and DGND regions, with the two planes connected at a single point. It may look like a professional solution, but there is an important question: What happens to the return current when a digital signal crosses from the digital area into the analog area? For high-speed digital signals, return current tends to follow the lowest-impedance path in the reference plane and is concentrated near the area directly underneath the signal trace. If the ground plane is split, the return current can no longer follow a short path underneath the signal. Instead, it may have to travel around the split. As the return path becomes longer, the loop area increases and parasitic inductance can also increase. This may result in more EMI and crosstalk rather than less. Therefore, splitting the ground plane does not automatically reduce noise. In some cases, it can actually make signal integrity and EMI problems worse. This is especially important when a high-speed signal crosses a ground-plane split. The return current is forced to take a longer path, which can increase the loop area and introduce additional noise. For this reason, a good mixed-signal PCB design does not simply focus on physically separating analog and digital grounds. It focuses on keeping the return-current paths controlled and predictable. (AGND plane & DGND plane) Four Critical Return Paths in ADC PCB Layout For an ADC, the most important consideration is not simply whether the analog and digital grounds are physically separated. Instead, different types of return current should follow appropriate paths and avoid sensitive circuits whenever possible. 1. Analog Input Return The reference ground for the analog input should be located as close as practical to the ADC's AGND. Avoid allowing the analog input return current to travel through the MCU area or other high-noise digital regions. 2. ADC Power Return The return path from the AVDD decoupling capacitor should be kept short and should return to the analog ground near the ADC. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor depends not only on whether the capacitor is present, but also on the loop formed by the power pin, capacitor, and ground connection. Keeping this loop small is an important part of good ADC PCB layout . 3. Digital Interface Return High-speed transitions on SPI signals such as SCLK, MOSI, MISO, and CS can generate high-frequency transient currents. These return currents should form a compact loop near the digital interface whenever possible, rather than flowing through sensitive analog ground regions. 4. AGND/DGND Connection Inside the PCB Layout Regardless of how the PCB is partitioned, AGND and DGND ultimately need to return to the same system reference ground. Whether the connection should use a single-point connection, a local connection, or a continuous ground plane depends on the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. So, what you really want to achieve is: Keep different types of return current on controlled paths rather than simply separating the two ground planes. Should You Use a Ferrite Bead Between AGND and DGND? This is one area where I would strongly recommend against blindly applying a common rule. A design like this is sometimes seen: AGND ─── Ferrite Bead ─── DGND The idea is that the ferrite bead can block digital noise from reaching the analog ground. In certain power-filtering applications, ferrite beads can indeed provide frequency-dependent impedance and help suppress high-frequency noise. However, ground is not simply a noise path. It is an important system reference and also provides return-current paths for signals. Once a frequency-dependent component is inserted between AGND and DGND, a voltage difference between the two ground domains can develop depending on the current and frequency. For high-precision ADCs and DACs, this ground potential difference can itself become a source of error or noise. Therefore, unless the device manufacturer specifically recommends it, do not add a ferrite bead between AGND and DGND simply because you have heard that analog and digital grounds should be isolated. Can AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly in ADC PCB layout? by: Mila Sep 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout agnd vs dgnd mixed-signal PCB design ADC PCB layout When designing an ADC or DAC, one of the most common questions in PCB layout is how to handle the AGND and DGND pins. If a device has separate analog and digital ground pins, should they be connected directly, separated into different ground planes, or joined at a single point? This question is especially important in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design, where fast digital switching currents can potentially interfere with sensitive analog circuits. To understand the right approach to AGND vs DGND, the key is not simply whether the two grounds are connected, but how the return currents flow through the PCB. (schematic with AGND & GND) Why Do ADCs and DACs Have Separate AGND and DGND Pins? An ADC can be roughly understood as having two different domains. One side contains the sampling circuit, op amp, reference, comparator, PGA, DAC core, and analog bias circuits. These belong to the analog domain. The other side contains the SPI/I²C interface, digital logic, registers, clock, state machine, and other digital circuits. These belong to the digital domain. One of the biggest characteristics of digital circuits is that their current can change very quickly. For example, when an SPI interface operates at tens of MHz, every clock transition can generate transient current. These currents need to form a complete return path through the power and ground network. This is where the problem begins. Assume the digital return current is: ID = 50 mA and it flows through a PCB trace with only: R = 20 mΩ The resulting ground voltage variation is: V = IR = 50 mA × 20 mΩ = 1 mV. 1 mV may look very small, but it is not necessarily negligible for a high-resolution ADC. For example, consider a 16-bit ADC with a 2.5 V full-scale range: 1 LSB ≈ 2.5 V / 65536 ≈ 38.1 μV Therefore, a 1 mV ground voltage variation corresponds to approximately: 1 mV / 38.1 μV ≈ 26 LSB Of course, the actual ADC conversion error depends on how this ground disturbance couples into the analog input, reference, and internal circuits. However, this example illustrates an important point: For a high-precision ADC, the key concern is not simply how low the ground resistance is, but where the digital return current flows. This is one of the fundamental considerations in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly? In many designs, AGND and DGND ultimately connect to the same ground reference. However, there is an important condition: this does not mean that AGND and DGND can simply be connected with two arbitrary traces and left at that. If the ADC or DAC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND should be connected close to the device, follow the manufacturer's recommended layout. For many high-precision ADCs and DACs, the recommended PCB layout is designed to maintain a low-impedance, low-inductance connection between AGND and DGND while preventing digital return currents from flowing through sensitive analog areas. Therefore, AGND and DGND do not necessarily need to be electrically isolated. What matters more is controlling the return-current path. (return-current path) Why Ground Plane Splitting Can Cause More Problems In traditional PCB layout, it is common to see analog and digital areas separated into AGND and DGND regions, with the two planes connected at a single point. It may look like a professional solution, but there is an important question: What happens to the return current when a digital signal crosses from the digital area into the analog area? For high-speed digital signals, return current tends to follow the lowest-impedance path in the reference plane and is concentrated near the area directly underneath the signal trace. If the ground plane is split, the return current can no longer follow a short path underneath the signal. Instead, it may have to travel around the split. As the return path becomes longer, the loop area increases and parasitic inductance can also increase. This may result in more EMI and crosstalk rather than less. Therefore, splitting the ground plane does not automatically reduce noise. In some cases, it can actually make signal integrity and EMI problems worse. This is especially important when a high-speed signal crosses a ground-plane split. The return current is forced to take a longer path, which can increase the loop area and introduce additional noise. For this reason, a good mixed-signal PCB design does not simply focus on physically separating analog and digital grounds. It focuses on keeping the return-current paths controlled and predictable. (AGND plane & DGND plane) Four Critical Return Paths in ADC PCB Layout For an ADC, the most important consideration is not simply whether the analog and digital grounds are physically separated. Instead, different types of return current should follow appropriate paths and avoid sensitive circuits whenever possible. 1. Analog Input Return The reference ground for the analog input should be located as close as practical to the ADC's AGND. Avoid allowing the analog input return current to travel through the MCU area or other high-noise digital regions. 2. ADC Power Return The return path from the AVDD decoupling capacitor should be kept short and should return to the analog ground near the ADC. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor depends not only on whether the capacitor is present, but also on the loop formed by the power pin, capacitor, and ground connection. Keeping this loop small is an important part of good ADC PCB layout . 3. Digital Interface Return High-speed transitions on SPI signals such as SCLK, MOSI, MISO, and CS can generate high-frequency transient currents. These return currents should form a compact loop near the digital interface whenever possible, rather than flowing through sensitive analog ground regions. 4. AGND/DGND Connection Inside the PCB Layout Regardless of how the PCB is partitioned, AGND and DGND ultimately need to return to the same system reference ground. Whether the connection should use a single-point connection, a local connection, or a continuous ground plane depends on the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. So, what you really want to achieve is: Keep different types of return current on controlled paths rather than simply separating the two ground planes. Should You Use a Ferrite Bead Between AGND and DGND? This is one area where I would strongly recommend against blindly applying a common rule. A design like this is sometimes seen: AGND ─── Ferrite Bead ─── DGND The idea is that the ferrite bead can block digital noise from reaching the analog ground. In certain power-filtering applications, ferrite beads can indeed provide frequency-dependent impedance and help suppress high-frequency noise. However, ground is not simply a noise path. It is an important system reference and also provides return-current paths for signals. Once a frequency-dependent component is inserted between AGND and DGND, a voltage difference between the two ground domains can develop depending on the current and frequency. For high-precision ADCs and DACs, this ground potential difference can itself become a source of error or noise. Therefore, unless the device manufacturer specifically recommends it, do not add a ferrite bead between AGND and DGND simply because you have heard that analog and digital grounds should be isolated. Instead, different types of return current should follow appropriate paths and avoid sensitive circuits whenever possible. 1. Analog Input Return The reference ground for the analog input should be located as close as practical to the ADC's AGND. Avoid allowing the analog input return current to travel through the MCU area or other high-noise digital regions. 2. ADC Power Return The return path from the AVDD decoupling capacitor should be kept short and should return to the analog ground near the ADC. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor depends not only on whether the capacitor is present, but also on the loop formed by the power pin, capacitor, and ground connection. Keeping this loop small is an important part of good ADC PCB layout . 3. Digital Interface Return High-speed transitions on SPI signals such as SCLK, MOSI, MISO, and CS can generate high-frequency transient currents. These return currents should form a compact loop near the digital interface whenever possible, rather than flowing through sensitive analog ground regions. 4. AGND/DGND Connection Inside the PCB Layout Regardless of how the PCB is partitioned, AGND and DGND ultimately need to return to the same system reference ground. Whether the connection should use a single-point connection, a local connection, or a continuous ground plane depends on the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. So, what you really want to achieve is: Keep different types of return current on controlled paths rather than simply separating the two ground planes. Should You Use a Ferrite Bead Between AGND and DGND? This is one area where I would strongly recommend against blindly applying a common rule. A design like this is sometimes seen: AGND ─── Ferrite Bead ─── DGND The idea is that the ferrite bead can block digital noise from reaching the analog ground. In certain power-filtering applications, ferrite beads can indeed provide frequency-dependent impedance and help suppress high-frequency noise. However, ground is not simply a noise path. It is an important system reference and also provides return-current paths for signals. Once a frequency-dependent component is inserted between AGND and DGND, a voltage difference between the two ground domains can develop depending on the current and frequency. For high-precision ADCs and DACs, this ground potential difference can itself become a source of error or noise. Therefore, unless the device manufacturer specifically recommends it, do not add a ferrite bead between AGND and DGND simply because you have heard that analog and digital grounds should be isolated. Key AGND vs DGND Considerations for Mixed-Signal PCB Design In summary, AGND and DGND can often share the same ground reference, but the exact connection method should always follow the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. When designing the board, pay particular attention to: Whether digital return current flows through sensitive analog areas Whether the analog input return path is short and well controlled Whether the ADC power-decoupling loop is compact Whether high-speed digital signals cross a ground-plane split Whether unnecessary impedance exists between AGND and DGND So, instead of simply thinking: "Analog ground must always be separated from digital ground." A more accurate way to think about AGND vs DGND is: The grounds can be shared, but the return currents should be controlled. The ground plane can remain continuous, but the paths taken by noise currents must be carefully managed. For ADCs, DACs, and other mixed-signal devices, good mixed-signal PCB design is not simply about physically isolating analog and digital ground. It is about using proper PCB layout, routing, decoupling, and return-path control to prevent digital noise from coupling into sensitive analog circuits. Verify Now Blog > How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity high-speed PCB design via stub Anyone involved in high-speed PCB design has probably heard this rule of thumb: minimize vias in high-speed routing whenever possible. But many engineers know they should do this without fully understanding why. Some consider a via simply a “wire” and assume a few extra vias will not matter. Others believe that as long as the impedance is controlled, everything will be fine. It is often only after the board comes back for testing—with a collapsed eye diagram, increased bit errors, or EMC test failures—that they realize those seemingly insignificant vias may be part of the problem. A PCB via is one of the structures in a high-speed link that can introduce impedance discontinuities and parasitic effects. It introduces parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, via stubs, and changes in the return-current path. As signal edges become faster, these effects become increasingly important to signal integrity. 1. What Parasitic Parameters Does a PCB Via Introduce? Many engineers think of a via as simply a “vertical wire.” At high frequencies, however, a PCB via is actually a three-dimensional interconnect structure with parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, and transmission-line effects. Parasitic Capacitance (C_via) Parasitic capacitance forms between the via pad and the surrounding reference plane, such as a ground or power plane. Its value depends on factors including the via pad, anti-pad, distance to the reference plane, and dielectric material. T: Length of the via passing through the reference plane D₁: Via pad diameter D₂: Anti-pad diameter εr: Relative dielectric constant In typical structures, via parasitic capacitance is usually on the order of several hundred femtofarads (fF). Parasitic capacitance lowers the local impedance around the via and, together with other parasitic parameters, creates an impedance discontinuity that can cause signal reflections. Parasitic Inductance (L_via) The copper barrel and the vertical current path of a via also introduce parasitic inductance. h: Via length in the vertical direction d: Via diameter For a typical 1.6 mm PCB with common via dimensions, the parasitic inductance can be around the 1 nH range. Parasitic inductance increases the local impedance around the via and interacts with parasitic capacitance to affect high-speed signals. If the return path is not properly controlled during layer transitions, the additional loop inductance can also increase EMI radiation. Combined Effects of Capacitance and Inductance The actual electrical behavior of a via is not determined by capacitance or inductance alone. Multiple parasitic effects work together. By properly optimizing via dimensions, pads, and anti-pads, the impedance discontinuity can be reduced to some extent. However, when a relatively long via stub is present, the frequency response of the via structure can still exhibit significant resonance. 2. Why Is Via Stub a Major Concern? （Through Via and Via Stub） This is one of the easily overlooked issues in high-speed PCB design. When a signal travels through a through-hole via from the top layer to an inner layer, such as from the Top Layer to L3, the unused portion of the plated hole extending from L3 to the bottom layer L10 becomes a via stub. The Physical Nature of a Via Stub A via stub is essentially an open-ended transmission-line section. At certain frequencies, it can produce a significant resonance. The resonant frequency can be approximately expressed as: c: Speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s) L_stub: Via stub length εr: Relative dielectric constant When the via stub's resonant frequency enters the main frequency range of the signal, it can cause a pronounced notch in insertion loss. This can result in signal attenuation and waveform distortion and, in severe cases, lead to eye-diagram closure. Therefore, for high-speed signals, via stub length can be more important than considering the parasitic capacitance and inductance of the via alone. 3. Why Does a PCB Via Cause Impedance Discontinuity? （Via Impedance Discontinuities and Reflections） The impedance of a via, Z_via, is usually not exactly the same as the characteristic impedance of the transmission line, Z₀. For example, a common target impedance for a high-speed single-ended signal is 50 Ω. When a signal transitions from a transmission line into a via structure with a different impedance, part of the signal is reflected. The reflection coefficient can be expressed as: Γ = (Z_via - Z₀) / (Z_via + Z₀) If Z_via = 40 Ω and Z₀ = 50 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.11. If Z_via = 30 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.25. This shows that a larger impedance mismatch between the via and transmission line generally results in stronger local reflections. For this reason, via optimization in high-speed PCB design is not simply about avoiding vias. The goal is to minimize the impedance discontinuity between the via structure and the transmission line. 4. Why Should You Consider the Return Path During Layer Transitions? （Layer Transition and Return Current Path） A via can affect not only the signal itself but also its return-current path. When a signal changes layers, its reference plane may also change. For example, a signal may transition between routing layers associated with different reference planes. If there is no suitable return path near the layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer route, creating a larger current loop. This can lead to: Increased loop inductance Increased EMI radiation Degraded signal integrity Increased crosstalk Therefore, high-speed via design needs to consider not only how the signal travels, but also how its return current flows back. 5. When Do Vias Significantly Affect High-Speed Signals? Many engineers have the same question: if the parasitic parameters of a via are so small, can a via really affect a high-speed signal? When evaluating the impact of a PCB via, data rate alone is not enough. Signal rise time, via propagation delay, and via stub resonance also need to be considered. Rise Time vs. Via Propagation Delay The propagation delay of a via can be approximately expressed as: For a typical via with L = 1.2 nH and C = 0.4 pF: This time scale is usually relatively small. Therefore, for many common high-speed digital signals, the impact of the via's lumped L/C parameters alone may not be as significant as the resonance caused by a long via stub. However, as signal edges become faster, via geometry, impedance discontinuity, and return-path design become increasingly important to signal integrity. Via Stub Resonance vs. Signal Spectrum Instead of using data rate alone as the criterion, it is more important to consider whether the via stub resonance falls within the main frequency range of the signal. When these frequencies become close, the via stub can create a significant notch in the frequency response, affecting insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, there is no single data-rate threshold that determines whether a via will cause problems. The actual design should consider data rate, rise time, via stub length, Nyquist frequency, and channel loss together. 6. Why Is a Via a Weak Point in a High-Speed Link? A PCB trace can be designed as a relatively continuous transmission structure by controlling parameters such as trace width, dielectric thickness, and copper thickness. A via, however, has to perform a three-dimensional transition over a very short distance. As a result, a single PCB via may introduce: Parasitic capacitance Parasitic inductance Impedance discontinuity Via stub resonance Return-path discontinuity The trace is like a “highway,” while the via is more like a combination of a “toll station + sharp turn + dead-end road.” A single via may not cause a significant problem by itself. However, when multiple discontinuities appear along the same high-speed link, their effects can accumulate and eventually appear as increased insertion loss, return loss, or eye-diagram degradation. 7. How Can You Reduce the Impact of Vias? Minimize Unnecessary Vias High-speed signals should avoid unnecessary layer transitions and multiple vias within a short routing distance. During BGA fanout, optimize the component placement and routing-layer strategy to minimize the number of layer transitions for critical high-speed signals. Use Back Drilling For high-speed SerDes links and other applications with demanding signal integrity requirements, if the via stub enters the effective frequency range of the signal, back drilling can be used to remove most of the unused plated barrel. The primary purpose of back drilling is to shorten the via stub and reduce the impact of via stub resonance on high-speed signals. The required back-drilling depth and remaining stub length should be determined based on the PCB stackup, signal characteristics, and manufacturing capabilities rather than a fixed data-rate threshold. Optimize Via Anti-Pads The anti-pad affects the parasitic capacitance between the via and the reference plane. Anti-pad too small: Higher parasitic capacitance, which may reduce the local impedance. Anti-pad too large: Although it can reduce some parasitic capacitance, it may also create a larger opening in the reference plane and affect the return path. Therefore, via anti-pad dimensions should be optimized based on via size, stackup, reference-plane spacing, and target impedance, rather than using a fixed dimension. Add Ground Return Vias During a high-speed layer transition, ground vias can be placed near the signal via to provide a shorter, lower-inductance return-current path. For differential signals, the ground vias should also be arranged as symmetrically as practical to avoid significant differences in the return environment of the two traces. Optimize Via Dimensions Within the limits of manufacturing capability, via diameter, pad size, and via length can be optimized to reduce parasitic effects. For example: A smaller drill diameter can reduce some parasitic effects. A smaller pad can reduce coupling to the reference plane. A shorter via can reduce parasitic inductance and via stub length. However, smaller is not always better. Very small vias can increase PCB manufacturing difficulty and cost. Choose an Appropriate Stackup High-speed signal layers should be placed close to continuous reference planes to maintain strong coupling between the signal and its return path. For high-density, high-speed designs, blind vias, buried vias, and HDI structures can also be used to shorten the via length and reduce the impact of through-hole via stubs. Conclusion A via is not simply a “vertical wire.” In high-speed PCB design , it is a complex three-dimensional interconnect structure involving parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, impedance discontinuity, via stub resonance, and return-path changes. In many cases, the lumped parasitic parameters of a single via are not the dominant source of signal degradation. However, when a via creates a significant impedance discontinuity or its via stub resonance enters the effective frequency range of the signal, it can have a noticeable impact on insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, the key question in high-speed PCB design is not simply whether a via can be used, but: Will this via structure introduce an unacceptable discontinuity within the effective frequency range of the target signal? Minimizing unnecessary vias, controlling via stub length, using back drilling or HDI structures when appropriate, and maintaining a continuous return path are all effective ways to improve signal integrity in high-speed links. Verify Now Blog > How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity high-speed PCB design via stub Anyone involved in high-speed PCB design has probably heard this rule of thumb: minimize vias in high-speed routing whenever possible. But many engineers know they should do this without fully understanding why. Some consider a via simply a “wire” and assume a few extra vias will not matter. Others believe that as long as the impedance is controlled, everything will be fine. It is often only after the board comes back for testing—with a collapsed eye diagram, increased bit errors, or EMC test failures—that they realize those seemingly insignificant vias may be part of the problem. A PCB via is one of the structures in a high-speed link that can introduce impedance discontinuities and parasitic effects. It introduces parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, via stubs, and changes in the return-current path. As signal edges become faster, these effects become increasingly important to signal integrity. 1. What Parasitic Parameters Does a PCB Via Introduce? Many engineers think of a via as simply a “vertical wire.” At high frequencies, however, a PCB via is actually a three-dimensional interconnect structure with parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, and transmission-line effects. Parasitic Capacitance (C_via) Parasitic capacitance forms between the via pad and the surrounding reference plane, such as a ground or power plane. Its value depends on factors including the via pad, anti-pad, distance to the reference plane, and dielectric material. T: Length of the via passing through the reference plane D₁: Via pad diameter D₂: Anti-pad diameter εr: Relative dielectric constant In typical structures, via parasitic capacitance is usually on the order of several hundred femtofarads (fF). Parasitic capacitance lowers the local impedance around the via and, together with other parasitic parameters, creates an impedance discontinuity that can cause signal reflections. Parasitic Inductance (L_via) The copper barrel and the vertical current path of a via also introduce parasitic inductance. h: Via length in the vertical direction d: Via diameter For a typical 1.6 mm PCB with common via dimensions, the parasitic inductance can be around the 1 nH range. Parasitic inductance increases the local impedance around the via and interacts with parasitic capacitance to affect high-speed signals. If the return path is not properly controlled during layer transitions, the additional loop inductance can also increase EMI radiation. Combined Effects of Capacitance and Inductance The actual electrical behavior of a via is not determined by capacitance or inductance alone. Multiple parasitic effects work together. By properly optimizing via dimensions, pads, and anti-pads, the impedance discontinuity can be reduced to some extent. However, when a relatively long via stub is present, the frequency response of the via structure can still exhibit significant resonance. 2. Why Is Via Stub a Major Concern? （Through Via and Via Stub） This is one of the easily overlooked issues in high-speed PCB design. When a signal travels through a through-hole via from the top layer to an inner layer, such as from the Top Layer to L3, the unused portion of the plated hole extending from L3 to the bottom layer L10 becomes a via stub. The Physical Nature of a Via Stub A via stub is essentially an open-ended transmission-line section. At certain frequencies, it can produce a significant resonance. The resonant frequency can be approximately expressed as: c: Speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s) L_stub: Via stub length εr: Relative dielectric constant When the via stub's resonant frequency enters the main frequency range of the signal, it can cause a pronounced notch in insertion loss. This can result in signal attenuation and waveform distortion and, in severe cases, lead to eye-diagram closure. Therefore, for high-speed signals, via stub length can be more important than considering the parasitic capacitance and inductance of the via alone. 3. Why Does a PCB Via Cause Impedance Discontinuity? （Via Impedance Discontinuities and Reflections） The impedance of a via, Z_via, is usually not exactly the same as the characteristic impedance of the transmission line, Z₀. For example, a common target impedance for a high-speed single-ended signal is 50 Ω. When a signal transitions from a transmission line into a via structure with a different impedance, part of the signal is reflected. The reflection coefficient can be expressed as: Γ = (Z_via - Z₀) / (Z_via + Z₀) If Z_via = 40 Ω and Z₀ = 50 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.11. If Z_via = 30 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.25. This shows that a larger impedance mismatch between the via and transmission line generally results in stronger local reflections. For this reason, via optimization in high-speed PCB design is not simply about avoiding vias. The goal is to minimize the impedance discontinuity between the via structure and the transmission line. 4. Why Should You Consider the Return Path During Layer Transitions? （Layer Transition and Return Current Path） A via can affect not only the signal itself but also its return-current path. When a signal changes layers, its reference plane may also change. For example, a signal may transition between routing layers associated with different reference planes. If there is no suitable return path near the layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer route, creating a larger current loop. This can lead to: Increased loop inductance Increased EMI radiation Degraded signal integrity Increased crosstalk Therefore, high-speed via design needs to consider not only how the signal travels, but also how its return current flows back. 5. When Do Vias Significantly Affect High-Speed Signals? Many engineers have the same question: if the parasitic parameters of a via are so small, can a via really affect a high-speed signal? When evaluating the impact of a PCB via, data rate alone is not enough. Signal rise time, via propagation delay, and via stub resonance also need to be considered. Rise Time vs. Via Propagation Delay The propagation delay of a via can be approximately expressed as: For a typical via with L = 1.2 nH and C = 0.4 pF: This time scale is usually relatively small. Therefore, for many common high-speed digital signals, the impact of the via's lumped L/C parameters alone may not be as significant as the resonance caused by a long via stub. However, as signal edges become faster, via geometry, impedance discontinuity, and return-path design become increasingly important to signal integrity. Via Stub Resonance vs. Signal Spectrum Instead of using data rate alone as the criterion, it is more important to consider whether the via stub resonance falls within the main frequency range of the signal. When these frequencies become close, the via stub can create a significant notch in the frequency response, affecting insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, there is no single data-rate threshold that determines whether a via will cause problems. The actual design should consider data rate, rise time, via stub length, Nyquist frequency, and channel loss together. 6. Why Is a Via a Weak Point in a High-Speed Link? A PCB trace can be designed as a relatively continuous transmission structure by controlling parameters such as trace width, dielectric thickness, and copper thickness. A via, however, has to perform a three-dimensional transition over a very short distance. As a result, a single PCB via may introduce: Parasitic capacitance Parasitic inductance Impedance discontinuity Via stub resonance Return-path discontinuity The trace is like a “highway,” while the via is more like a combination of a “toll station + sharp turn + dead-end road.” A single via may not cause a significant problem by itself. However, when multiple discontinuities appear along the same high-speed link, their effects can accumulate and eventually appear as increased insertion loss, return loss, or eye-diagram degradation. 7. How Can You Reduce the Impact of Vias? Minimize Unnecessary Vias High-speed signals should avoid unnecessary layer transitions and multiple vias within a short routing distance. During BGA fanout, optimize the component placement and routing-layer strategy to minimize the number of layer transitions for critical high-speed signals. Use Back Drilling For high-speed SerDes links and other applications with demanding signal integrity requirements, if the via stub enters the effective frequency range of the signal, back drilling can be used to remove most of the unused plated barrel. The primary purpose of back drilling is to shorten the via stub and reduce the impact of via stub resonance on high-speed signals. The required back-drilling depth and remaining stub length should be determined based on the PCB stackup, signal characteristics, and manufacturing capabilities rather than a fixed data-rate threshold. Optimize Via Anti-Pads The anti-pad affects the parasitic capacitance between the via and the reference plane. Anti-pad too small: Higher parasitic capacitance, which may reduce the local impedance. Anti-pad too large: Although it can reduce some parasitic capacitance, it may also create a larger opening in the reference plane and affect the return path. Therefore, via anti-pad dimensions should be optimized based on via size, stackup, reference-plane spacing, and target impedance, rather than using a fixed dimension. Add Ground Return Vias During a high-speed layer transition, ground vias can be placed near the signal via to provide a shorter, lower-inductance return-current path. For differential signals, the ground vias should also be arranged as symmetrically as practical to avoid significant differences in the return environment of the two traces. Optimize Via Dimensions Within the limits of manufacturing capability, via diameter, pad size, and via length can be optimized to reduce parasitic effects. For example: A smaller drill diameter can reduce some parasitic effects. A smaller pad can reduce coupling to the reference plane. A shorter via can reduce parasitic inductance and via stub length. However, smaller is not always better. Very small vias can increase PCB manufacturing difficulty and cost. Choose an Appropriate Stackup High-speed signal layers should be placed close to continuous reference planes to maintain strong coupling between the signal and its return path. For high-density, high-speed designs, blind vias, buried vias, and HDI structures can also be used to shorten the via length and reduce the impact of through-hole via stubs. Conclusion A via is not simply a “vertical wire.” In high-speed PCB design , it is a complex three-dimensional interconnect structure involving parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, impedance discontinuity, via stub resonance, and return-path changes. In many cases, the lumped parasitic parameters of a single via are not the dominant source of signal degradation. However, when a via creates a significant impedance discontinuity or its via stub resonance enters the effective frequency range of the signal, it can have a noticeable impact on insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, the key question in high-speed PCB design is not simply whether a via can be used, but: Will this via structure introduce an unacceptable discontinuity within the effective frequency range of the target signal? Minimizing unnecessary vias, controlling via stub length, using back drilling or HDI structures when appropriate, and maintaining a continuous return path are all effective ways to improve signal integrity in high-speed links.
