Verify Now Blog > How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity high-speed PCB design via stub Anyone involved in high-speed PCB design has probably heard this rule of thumb: minimize vias in high-speed routing whenever possible. But many engineers know they should do this without fully understanding why. Some consider a via simply a “wire” and assume a few extra vias will not matter. Others believe that as long as the impedance is controlled, everything will be fine. It is often only after the board comes back for testing—with a collapsed eye diagram, increased bit errors, or EMC test failures—that they realize those seemingly insignificant vias may be part of the problem. A PCB via is one of the structures in a high-speed link that can introduce impedance discontinuities and parasitic effects. It introduces parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, via stubs, and changes in the return-current path. As signal edges become faster, these effects become increasingly important to signal integrity. 1. What Parasitic Parameters Does a PCB Via Introduce? Many engineers think of a via as simply a “vertical wire.” At high frequencies, however, a PCB via is actually a three-dimensional interconnect structure with parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, and transmission-line effects. Parasitic Capacitance (C_via) Parasitic capacitance forms between the via pad and the surrounding reference plane, such as a ground or power plane. Its value depends on factors including the via pad, anti-pad, distance to the reference plane, and dielectric material. T: Length of the via passing through the reference plane D₁: Via pad diameter D₂: Anti-pad diameter εr: Relative dielectric constant In typical structures, via parasitic capacitance is usually on the order of several hundred femtofarads (fF). Parasitic capacitance lowers the local impedance around the via and, together with other parasitic parameters, creates an impedance discontinuity that can cause signal reflections. Parasitic Inductance (L_via) The copper barrel and the vertical current path of a via also introduce parasitic inductance. h: Via length in the vertical direction d: Via diameter For a typical 1.6 mm PCB with common via dimensions, the parasitic inductance can be around the 1 nH range. Parasitic inductance increases the local impedance around the via and interacts with parasitic capacitance to affect high-speed signals. If the return path is not properly controlled during layer transitions, the additional loop inductance can also increase EMI radiation. Combined Effects of Capacitance and Inductance The actual electrical behavior of a via is not determined by capacitance or inductance alone. Multiple parasitic effects work together. By properly optimizing via dimensions, pads, and anti-pads, the impedance discontinuity can be reduced to some extent. However, when a relatively long via stub is present, the frequency response of the via structure can still exhibit significant resonance. 2. Why Is Via Stub a Major Concern? （Through Via and Via Stub） This is one of the easily overlooked issues in high-speed PCB design. When a signal travels through a through-hole via from the top layer to an inner layer, such as from the Top Layer to L3, the unused portion of the plated hole extending from L3 to the bottom layer L10 becomes a via stub. The Physical Nature of a Via Stub A via stub is essentially an open-ended transmission-line section. At certain frequencies, it can produce a significant resonance. The resonant frequency can be approximately expressed as: c: Speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s) L_stub: Via stub length εr: Relative dielectric constant When the via stub's resonant frequency enters the main frequency range of the signal, it can cause a pronounced notch in insertion loss. This can result in signal attenuation and waveform distortion and, in severe cases, lead to eye-diagram closure. Therefore, for high-speed signals, via stub length can be more important than considering the parasitic capacitance and inductance of the via alone. 3. Why Does a PCB Via Cause Impedance Discontinuity? （Via Impedance Discontinuities and Reflections） The impedance of a via, Z_via, is usually not exactly the same as the characteristic impedance of the transmission line, Z₀. For example, a common target impedance for a high-speed single-ended signal is 50 Ω. When a signal transitions from a transmission line into a via structure with a different impedance, part of the signal is reflected. The reflection coefficient can be expressed as: Γ = (Z_via - Z₀) / (Z_via + Z₀) If Z_via = 40 Ω and Z₀ = 50 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.11. If Z_via = 30 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.25. This shows that a larger impedance mismatch between the via and transmission line generally results in stronger local reflections. For this reason, via optimization in high-speed PCB design is not simply about avoiding vias. The goal is to minimize the impedance discontinuity between the via structure and the transmission line. 4. Why Should You Consider the Return Path During Layer Transitions? （Layer Transition and Return Current Path） A via can affect not only the signal itself but also its return-current path. When a signal changes layers, its reference plane may also change. For example, a signal may transition between routing layers associated with different reference planes. If there is no suitable return path near the layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer route, creating a larger current loop. This can lead to: Increased loop inductance Increased EMI radiation Degraded signal integrity Increased crosstalk Therefore, high-speed via design needs to consider not only how the signal travels, but also how its return current flows back. 5. When Do Vias Significantly Affect High-Speed Signals? Many engineers have the same question: if the parasitic parameters of a via are so small, can a via really affect a high-speed signal? When evaluating the impact of a PCB via, data rate alone is not enough. Signal rise time, via propagation delay, and via stub resonance also need to be considered. Rise Time vs. Via Propagation Delay The propagation delay of a via can be approximately expressed as: For a typical via with L = 1.2 nH and C = 0.4 pF: This time scale is usually relatively small. Therefore, for many common high-speed digital signals, the impact of the via's lumped L/C parameters alone may not be as significant as the resonance caused by a long via stub. However, as signal edges become faster, via geometry, impedance discontinuity, and return-path design become increasingly important to signal integrity. Via Stub Resonance vs. Signal Spectrum Instead of using data rate alone as the criterion, it is more important to consider whether the via stub resonance falls within the main frequency range of the signal. When these frequencies become close, the via stub can create a significant notch in the frequency response, affecting insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, there is no single data-rate threshold that determines whether a via will cause problems. The actual design should consider data rate, rise time, via stub length, Nyquist frequency, and channel loss together. 6. Why Is a Via a Weak Point in a High-Speed Link? A PCB trace can be designed as a relatively continuous transmission structure by controlling parameters such as trace width, dielectric thickness, and copper thickness. A via, however, has to perform a three-dimensional transition over a very short distance. As a result, a single PCB via may introduce: Parasitic capacitance Parasitic inductance Impedance discontinuity Via stub resonance Return-path discontinuity The trace is like a “highway,” while the via is more like a combination of a “toll station + sharp turn + dead-end road.” A single via may not cause a significant problem by itself. However, when multiple discontinuities appear along the same high-speed link, their effects can accumulate and eventually appear as increased insertion loss, return loss, or eye-diagram degradation. 7. How Can You Reduce the Impact of Vias? Minimize Unnecessary Vias High-speed signals should avoid unnecessary layer transitions and multiple vias within a short routing distance. During BGA fanout, optimize the component placement and routing-layer strategy to minimize the number of layer transitions for critical high-speed signals. Use Back Drilling For high-speed SerDes links and other applications with demanding signal integrity requirements, if the via stub enters the effective frequency range of the signal, back drilling can be used to remove most of the unused plated barrel. The primary purpose of back drilling is to shorten the via stub and reduce the impact of via stub resonance on high-speed signals. The required back-drilling depth and remaining stub length should be determined based on the PCB stackup, signal characteristics, and manufacturing capabilities rather than a fixed data-rate threshold. Optimize Via Anti-Pads The anti-pad affects the parasitic capacitance between the via and the reference plane. Anti-pad too small: Higher parasitic capacitance, which may reduce the local impedance. Anti-pad too large: Although it can reduce some parasitic capacitance, it may also create a larger opening in the reference plane and affect the return path. Therefore, via anti-pad dimensions should be optimized based on via size, stackup, reference-plane spacing, and target impedance, rather than using a fixed dimension. Add Ground Return Vias During a high-speed layer transition, ground vias can be placed near the signal via to provide a shorter, lower-inductance return-current path. For differential signals, the ground vias should also be arranged as symmetrically as practical to avoid significant differences in the return environment of the two traces. Optimize Via Dimensions Within the limits of manufacturing capability, via diameter, pad size, and via length can be optimized to reduce parasitic effects. For example: A smaller drill diameter can reduce some parasitic effects. A smaller pad can reduce coupling to the reference plane. A shorter via can reduce parasitic inductance and via stub length. However, smaller is not always better. Very small vias can increase PCB manufacturing difficulty and cost. Choose an Appropriate Stackup High-speed signal layers should be placed close to continuous reference planes to maintain strong coupling between the signal and its return path. For high-density, high-speed designs, blind vias, buried vias, and HDI structures can also be used to shorten the via length and reduce the impact of through-hole via stubs. Conclusion A via is not simply a “vertical wire.” In high-speed PCB design , it is a complex three-dimensional interconnect structure involving parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, impedance discontinuity, via stub resonance, and return-path changes. In many cases, the lumped parasitic parameters of a single via are not the dominant source of signal degradation. However, when a via creates a significant impedance discontinuity or its via stub resonance enters the effective frequency range of the signal, it can have a noticeable impact on insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, the key question in high-speed PCB design is not simply whether a via can be used, but: Will this via structure introduce an unacceptable discontinuity within the effective frequency range of the target signal? Minimizing unnecessary vias, controlling via stub length, using back drilling or HDI structures when appropriate, and maintaining a continuous return path are all effective ways to improve signal integrity in high-speed links. PCB Conformal Coating: Which Components Need Masking? by: Mila Sep 23,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB conformal coating circuit board conformal coating pcb protection coating Applying a conformal coating to the PCB during PCB assembly process can enhance the PCB's resistance to moisture, salt spray, dust, and corrosive environments. However, it is essentially an insulating protective film. For this reason, not every area of a PCB is suitable for direct coating. Areas that require electrical contact, mechanical movement, heat dissipation, or optical transmission can actually develop new reliability issues if they are improperly coated. Especially for the following components, applying conformal coating directly without proper masking can lead to a situation where the PCB has been coated for protection, but the product develops problems because critical areas were coated when they should not have been. So, let’s take a closer look at where PCB conformal coating needs special attention. 1. Connectors: Protect Electrical Contact Areas Connectors are usually one of the most important components to keep clear of conformal coating. The reason is simple: their contacts need to maintain reliable electrical contact. For example, if a connector contact normally has a contact resistance of only a few tens of mΩ, allowing conformal coating to enter the contact area essentially adds an insulating film between the mating surfaces. The problem can be even more complicated because some connectors may still work after the first few mating cycles, as the coating can be scraped away from the contact area. But that does not mean the connection will remain reliable. Over time, vibration, temperature and humidity cycling, coating residue, contamination, and oxidation of the contact surface can all increase contact resistance or cause intermittent contact. In actual PCB conformal coating applications, the electrical contact area, mating area, and other surfaces that must maintain reliable contact generally need to be masked. The exact masking area should be determined according to the connector manufacturer's coating requirements. This is especially important in automotive electronics and industrial control equipment that operate under long-term vibration. Being able to conduct electricity once does not necessarily mean the connection will remain reliable. （Connectors component） 2. Relays and Switches: Keep Contacts and Moving Parts Clear Contacts and moving mechanisms also require special attention, making relays another type of component that needs careful consideration during conformal coating. PCB Conformal Coating: Which Components Need Masking? by: Mila Sep 23,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB conformal coating circuit board conformal coating pcb protection coating Applying a conformal coating to the PCB during PCB assembly process can enhance the PCB's resistance to moisture, salt spray, dust, and corrosive environments. However, it is essentially an insulating protective film. For this reason, not every area of a PCB is suitable for direct coating. Areas that require electrical contact, mechanical movement, heat dissipation, or optical transmission can actually develop new reliability issues if they are improperly coated. Especially for the following components, applying conformal coating directly without proper masking can lead to a situation where the PCB has been coated for protection, but the product develops problems because critical areas were coated when they should not have been. So, let’s take a closer look at where PCB conformal coating needs special attention. 1. Connectors: Protect Electrical Contact Areas Connectors are usually one of the most important components to keep clear of conformal coating. The reason is simple: their contacts need to maintain reliable electrical contact. For example, if a connector contact normally has a contact resistance of only a few tens of mΩ, allowing conformal coating to enter the contact area essentially adds an insulating film between the mating surfaces. The problem can be even more complicated because some connectors may still work after the first few mating cycles, as the coating can be scraped away from the contact area. But that does not mean the connection will remain reliable. Over time, vibration, temperature and humidity cycling, coating residue, contamination, and oxidation of the contact surface can all increase contact resistance or cause intermittent contact. In actual PCB conformal coating applications, the electrical contact area, mating area, and other surfaces that must maintain reliable contact generally need to be masked. The exact masking area should be determined according to the connector manufacturer's coating requirements. This is especially important in automotive electronics and industrial control equipment that operate under long-term vibration. Being able to conduct electricity once does not necessarily mean the connection will remain reliable. （Connectors component） 2. Relays and Switches: Keep Contacts and Moving Parts Clear Contacts and moving mechanisms also require special attention, making relays another type of component that needs careful consideration during conformal coating. A relay typically contains contacts, an armature, springs, and other mechanical structures. If conformal coating enters the moving mechanism, it may affect the mechanical action of the relay. More importantly, the contacts themselves are critical because a relay relies on mechanical contacts to make and break an electrical circuit. If the contact surfaces are contaminated by coating, contact resistance, arcing characteristics, and long-term reliability may all be affected. Therefore, it does not mean that the entire relay must always be left uncoated. For sealed relays that have been verified as compatible with conformal coating, the outside of the component and the surrounding PCB may still be coated for protection. The areas that require particular attention are the contacts, moving mechanisms, and any areas specifically designated as coating-prohibited by the manufacturer. For high-voltage relays, additional considerations include creepage distance, clearance, and the effect of the coating on insulation performance. It should not simply be assumed that conformal coating automatically provides sufficient electrical isolation. 3. Buttons and Potentiometers: Avoid Coating Moving Contacts Components that contain moving or contacting mechanisms also require special attention. Mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components can be affected if conformal coating enters their internal moving or contact areas. For example, a potentiometer contains sliding contacts. If conformal coating penetrates into the mechanism, it can form a thin insulating contamination layer over the sliding contacts. What can happen? Resistance jumps, poor contact, and increased noise are all possible. This can be particularly troublesome in analog circuits because the problem may not appear as an obvious component failure. Instead, it may show up as increased output noise, ADC reading drift, or other intermittent problems that are difficult to trace. Therefore, for mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components, the masking area should be determined based on the component structure and manufacturer's requirements rather than simply applying full-component coating. （Buttons component） 4. Power Components: Consider Thermal Performance MOSFETs, DC-DC converters, LDOs, and other power components often have large copper areas around them to help dissipate heat. The effect of conformal coating on thermal performance cannot simply be described as "coating always causes the temperature to increase by a certain amount." Instead, the entire thermal path needs to be considered. For power components that rely on PCB copper, thermal vias, thermal pads, or external heat sinks for heat dissipation, the coating location, coating thickness, and overall mechanical design may all affect the final thermal performance. For example, assume a power component dissipates 2 W and its junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is 30 °C/W. Under this simplified model, the temperature rise is approximately: ΔT = P × θJA = 2 × 30 = 60 °C If the overall thermal conditions cause the effective thermal resistance to increase to 40 °C/W: ΔT = 2 × 40 = 80 °C Under this assumption, the temperature rise increases by 20 °C. It is important to note that this is only a simplified example showing how changes in thermal resistance affect temperature rise. It does not mean that conformal coating itself will necessarily increase θJA from 30 °C/W to 40 °C/W. The actual result depends on factors such as PCB copper area, thermal vias, component package, airflow, heat sink design, coating material, and coating thickness. Therefore, for high-power MOSFETs, power inductors, rectifier diodes, DC-DC converters, and similar components, the key question is whether the overall thermal path becomes less effective after coating. For thermal pads, thermal vias, exposed heat-dissipation surfaces, and areas that contact a heat sink, the need for masking should be determined based on the component and mechanical design rather than coating everything simply to achieve complete coverage. 5. Optical Components: Protect Optical Paths Conformal coating can also directly affect the performance of optical components. LEDs, photoelectric sensors, infrared receivers, cameras, light-sensitive devices, and similar components require particular attention. Conformal coating can change the transmittance, reflectivity, or surface condition of an optical window. For example, if a photoelectric sensor is calibrated for a specific optical window and an additional coating layer is applied to that surface, the optical path may change. As a result, sensors in the same production batch may produce inconsistent outputs. For components involving an optical path, first confirm with the component manufacturer whether conformal coating is permitted and what materials, coating thicknesses, and coverage areas are allowed. Do not assume that a coating will have no optical impact simply because the coating itself is transparent. 6. PCB Conformal Coating Is Not About Complete Coverage One of the most common mistakes in PCB conformal coating is treating complete coverage as the ultimate goal. A better approach is simple: protect the areas that need protection, and keep critical areas free of coating. During the PCB design stage, the coating requirements for different areas should be defined in advance. In general, they can be considered in three categories: Areas That Should Be Coated Exposed copper Solder joints General passive components and their soldered areas Areas that are vulnerable to moisture, salt spray, and corrosion Areas That Should Be Kept Free of Coating or Masked Electrical contact areas of connectors Moving or contacting mechanisms in buttons and potentiometers Test points Optical windows Other areas that need to maintain electrical or mechanical contact Components That Require Specification-Based Evaluation Power components Relays Transformers Sensors Crystals and oscillators Other specialized components The third category should not simply be classified as "coat" or "do not coat." The decision should be based on the component manufacturer's datasheet, coating compatibility, and the actual application environment. 7. How to Define Conformal Coating Areas During PCB Design Conformal coating should not be considered only after the PCB has been manufactured. The design stage should clearly define which areas require coating, which areas require masking, and what coating requirements need to be met. Coating Area Areas that require protection from moisture, contamination, corrosion, or other environmental factors. Keep-Out Area Areas that must remain free of conformal coating, such as connector contacts, test points, and optical windows. Masking Area Areas that need to be protected during manufacturing using masking tape, fixtures, or other masking methods. Thickness Requirement The target thickness of the conformal coating should be specified according to the application and material requirements. Inspection Requirement Quality requirements should be defined for coating coverage, missed coating, runs, bubbles, and other appearance or process-related defects. If you are sending your design for PCB production , it is recommended to clearly indicate the required coating and masking areas in the Gerber files, assembly drawings, or other production documentation. Conclusion Finally, do not rely only on the conformal coating manufacturer's documentation. The coating requirements of individual component manufacturers also need to be considered. For example, some connectors may allow coating while others explicitly prohibit it. Likewise, some MOSFETs may tolerate full coating, while others have thermal structures that require special treatment. Good PCB conformal coating design is not simply about maximizing coverage or increasing coating thickness. It is about clearly defining where coating should be applied, where it should not be applied, and why. The purpose of conformal coating is to improve PCB reliability in harsh environments, not to make the entire board look completely covered. By defining the Coating Area, Keep-Out Area, and Masking Area during the PCB design stage, the coating process and subsequent quality control can be much clearer and more reliable. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. PCB Layout Examples: From high-speed and RF to HDI, BGA, and rigid-flex designs, we handle a wide range of complex PCB layout requirements. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC by: Mila Sep 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design DCDC PCB layout power supply layout LDO layout guidelines Power supply design is not simply about choosing the right regulator and adding enough copper. The PCB layout directly affects thermal performance, noise, EMI, stability, and overall power integrity. LDOs and DCDC converters have different layout priorities: LDOs require careful attention to heat dissipation, capacitor placement, and power loss, while DCDC converters are more sensitive to high-frequency current loops, feedback routing, and grounding. When both are used in the same system, power-stage isolation and decoupling become equally important. In this guide, we’ll break down the key power supply layout considerations and common mistakes for LDOs, DCDC converters, and mixed power architectures. 1. LDO (Low-Dropout Regulator): Quiet but Sensitive to Heat （LDO regulator） Advantages: Low noise, no switching interference, and simple peripheral circuitry Disadvantages: Efficiency depends on the input-to-output voltage difference, and large voltage drops or high load currents can generate significant heat. Three Common LDO PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Poor Thermal Management → Excessive Temperature Rise Incorrect: Leaving the exposed pad floating without sufficient copper area or thermal vias. Consequence: Higher thermal resistance can increase junction temperature, potentially triggering thermal protection or affecting long-term reliability. Correct: Connect the exposed pad to a sufficiently large copper area. Add thermal vias according to the package and datasheet recommendations, connecting them to internal or bottom-layer copper planes. Avoid routing signal traces underneath the thermal pad. Evaluate the required copper area and thermal performance based on actual power dissipation. Mistake 2: Input/Output Capacitors Too Far from the Pins → Reduced Stability and Transient Performance Incorrect: Placing the input and output capacitors far away from the LDO pins. Consequence: Increased parasitic impedance can affect stability, transient response, and high-frequency noise performance. Correct: Place Cin and Cout as close as possible to the corresponding LDO pins. Select capacitor values, quantities, and ESR according to the device datasheet. Prefer low-ESR capacitors recommended by the manufacturer. Keep the feedback path short and avoid unnecessary routing and noise coupling. Mistake 3: Ignoring Voltage Drop and Power Dissipation → Efficiency and Thermal Issues Incorrect: Using an LDO for high input voltage and high current without evaluating power dissipation. Consequence: Higher LDO power dissipation increases junction temperature and may trigger thermal protection or reduce system reliability. Correct: The main power dissipation of an LDO can be estimated using: P ≈ (Vin − Vout) × Iout The larger the voltage drop and output current, the higher the LDO power dissipation. For high-power applications, evaluate efficiency, junction temperature, and PCB thermal performance together. When the voltage drop or load current is high, consider using a DCDC converter first and an LDO for downstream regulation and noise reduction. 2. DCDC (Switching Power Supply): Efficient but Noisy （dc-dc converter） Advantages: High conversion efficiency, higher output current capability, and suitability for a wide range of input and output voltages Disadvantages: Switching nodes and high di/dt currents can generate noise, making DCDC PCB layout critical to EMI, stability, and overall power performance. Five Common DCDC PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Long Power Loops → Increased Ringing and EMI Incorrect: Placing the input capacitor, power switch, inductor, and other key components too far apart, resulting in a large high-frequency current loop. Consequence: Increased parasitic inductance can produce more pronounced voltage spikes and ringing under high di/dt conditions, increasing EMI and component stress. Correct: Minimize the area of critical high-frequency power loops. Place input bypass capacitors, power devices, and inductors as close together as possible. Use sufficiently wide power traces. The required width should be determined by current, copper thickness, and allowable temperature rise. Avoid unnecessarily long high di/dt return paths. Mistake 2: Noisy Feedback Path → Output Voltage Fluctuation Incorrect: Routing the FB trace close to or parallel with the SW node, inductor, or other noisy areas. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into the feedback network, affecting output voltage regulation and system stability. Correct: Keep the FB trace short and away from the SW node and high di/dt current paths. Place the feedback resistors close to the IC's FB pin. Sense the output voltage from a stable, low-noise point. For high-precision applications, consider Kelvin sensing or other methods recommended by the device manufacturer to reduce voltage drop and noise. Mistake 3: Improper Ground Plane Design → Increased EMI and Noise Incorrect: Improper AGND, PGND, or high-current return-path routing causes sensitive control circuitry to share impedance with power return currents. Consequence: Ground bounce and common-impedance coupling can affect control signals, feedback, and output voltage. Correct: Follow the DCDC IC manufacturer's recommended method for connecting AGND and PGND. Provide a low-impedance return path for PGND. Keep sensitive analog ground areas away from high-current power return paths whenever possible. Prevent high di/dt currents from passing through sensitive signal areas. Mistake 4: Improper Input Capacitor Placement → Increased Input Ripple Incorrect: Relying on a single bulk capacitor while placing it far from the VIN and GND pins. Consequence: A larger high-frequency current loop can increase input ripple and noise. Correct: Configure input capacitors according to the DCDC converter datasheet. Use capacitors with different values when necessary to address different frequency ranges. Place input capacitors as close as possible to the VIN and GND pins. Keep the input capacitor loop short and compact. Mistake 5: Ignoring the Freewheeling Path → Reduced Efficiency and Poorer EMI Performance Incorrect: Placing the freewheeling diode, synchronous MOSFET, or related circuitry too far apart. Consequence: Increased parasitic parameters can lead to additional losses, ringing, and EMI. Correct: Optimize the freewheeling and synchronous rectification paths according to the specific converter topology. Minimize high-current return paths. For multiphase DCDC converters, keep the power paths of each phase well organized and reasonably symmetrical. 3. LDO + DCDC Mixed Power Supply: Balancing Efficiency and Low Noise （power supply pcb） In practical systems, DCDC converters and LDOs are often used together rather than as alternatives. For example: DCDC: 12V → 3.3V for efficient voltage conversion LDO: 3.3V → 1.8V for noise-sensitive circuits such as ADCs, PLLs, and clocks This approach combines the efficiency of a DCDC converter with the low-noise characteristics of an LDO, making it useful for applications that require both power efficiency and clean power rails. Three Common Mixed Power Supply Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Insufficient Filtering at the LDO Input → Upstream Noise May Reach the Downstream Rail Incorrect: Connecting the DCDC output directly to an LDO-powered sensitive load without evaluating the DCDC switching noise and the LDO's PSRR. Correct: Connect the exposed pad to a sufficiently large copper area. Add thermal vias according to the package and datasheet recommendations, connecting them to internal or bottom-layer copper planes. Avoid routing signal traces underneath the thermal pad. Consequence: Increased parasitic impedance can affect stability, transient response, and high-frequency noise performance. The PCB layout directly affects thermal performance, noise, EMI, stability, and overall power integrity. LDOs and DCDC converters have different layout priorities: LDOs require careful attention to heat dissipation, capacitor placement, and power loss, while DCDC converters are more sensitive to high-frequency current loops, feedback routing, and grounding. When both are used in the same system, power-stage isolation and decoupling become equally important. In this guide, we’ll break down the key power supply layout considerations and common mistakes for LDOs, DCDC converters, and mixed power architectures. 1. LDO (Low-Dropout Regulator): Quiet but Sensitive to Heat （LDO regulator） Advantages: Low noise, no switching interference, and simple peripheral circuitry Disadvantages: Efficiency depends on the input-to-output voltage difference, and large voltage drops or high load currents can generate significant heat. Three Common LDO PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Poor Thermal Management → Excessive Temperature Rise Incorrect: Leaving the exposed pad floating without sufficient copper area or thermal vias. Consequence: Higher thermal resistance can increase junction temperature, potentially triggering thermal protection or affecting long-term reliability. Correct: Connect the exposed pad to a sufficiently large copper area. Add thermal vias according to the package and datasheet recommendations, connecting them to internal or bottom-layer copper planes. Avoid routing signal traces underneath the thermal pad. Evaluate the required copper area and thermal performance based on actual power dissipation. Mistake 2: Input/Output Capacitors Too Far from the Pins → Reduced Stability and Transient Performance Incorrect: Placing the input and output capacitors far away from the LDO pins. Consequence: Increased parasitic impedance can affect stability, transient response, and high-frequency noise performance. Correct: Place Cin and Cout as close as possible to the corresponding LDO pins. Select capacitor values, quantities, and ESR according to the device datasheet. Prefer low-ESR capacitors recommended by the manufacturer. Keep the feedback path short and avoid unnecessary routing and noise coupling. Mistake 3: Ignoring Voltage Drop and Power Dissipation → Efficiency and Thermal Issues Incorrect: Using an LDO for high input voltage and high current without evaluating power dissipation. Consequence: Higher LDO power dissipation increases junction temperature and may trigger thermal protection or reduce system reliability. Correct: The main power dissipation of an LDO can be estimated using: P ≈ (Vin − Vout) × Iout The larger the voltage drop and output current, the higher the LDO power dissipation. For high-power applications, evaluate efficiency, junction temperature, and PCB thermal performance together. When the voltage drop or load current is high, consider using a DCDC converter first and an LDO for downstream regulation and noise reduction. 2. DCDC (Switching Power Supply): Efficient but Noisy （dc-dc converter） Advantages: High conversion efficiency, higher output current capability, and suitability for a wide range of input and output voltages Disadvantages: Switching nodes and high di/dt currents can generate noise, making DCDC PCB layout critical to EMI, stability, and overall power performance. Five Common DCDC PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Long Power Loops → Increased Ringing and EMI Incorrect: Placing the input capacitor, power switch, inductor, and other key components too far apart, resulting in a large high-frequency current loop. Consequence: Increased parasitic inductance can produce more pronounced voltage spikes and ringing under high di/dt conditions, increasing EMI and component stress. Correct: Minimize the area of critical high-frequency power loops. Place input bypass capacitors, power devices, and inductors as close together as possible. Use sufficiently wide power traces. The required width should be determined by current, copper thickness, and allowable temperature rise. Avoid unnecessarily long high di/dt return paths. Mistake 2: Noisy Feedback Path → Output Voltage Fluctuation Incorrect: Routing the FB trace close to or parallel with the SW node, inductor, or other noisy areas. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into the feedback network, affecting output voltage regulation and system stability. Correct: Keep the FB trace short and away from the SW node and high di/dt current paths. Place the feedback resistors close to the IC's FB pin. Sense the output voltage from a stable, low-noise point. For high-precision applications, consider Kelvin sensing or other methods recommended by the device manufacturer to reduce voltage drop and noise. Mistake 3: Improper Ground Plane Design → Increased EMI and Noise Incorrect: Improper AGND, PGND, or high-current return-path routing causes sensitive control circuitry to share impedance with power return currents. Consequence: Ground bounce and common-impedance coupling can affect control signals, feedback, and output voltage. Correct: Follow the DCDC IC manufacturer's recommended method for connecting AGND and PGND. Provide a low-impedance return path for PGND. Keep sensitive analog ground areas away from high-current power return paths whenever possible. Prevent high di/dt currents from passing through sensitive signal areas. Mistake 4: Improper Input Capacitor Placement → Increased Input Ripple Incorrect: Relying on a single bulk capacitor while placing it far from the VIN and GND pins. Consequence: A larger high-frequency current loop can increase input ripple and noise. Correct: Configure input capacitors according to the DCDC converter datasheet. Use capacitors with different values when necessary to address different frequency ranges. Place input capacitors as close as possible to the VIN and GND pins. Keep the input capacitor loop short and compact. Mistake 5: Ignoring the Freewheeling Path → Reduced Efficiency and Poorer EMI Performance Incorrect: Placing the freewheeling diode, synchronous MOSFET, or related circuitry too far apart. Consequence: Increased parasitic parameters can lead to additional losses, ringing, and EMI. Correct: Optimize the freewheeling and synchronous rectification paths according to the specific converter topology. Minimize high-current return paths. For multiphase DCDC converters, keep the power paths of each phase well organized and reasonably symmetrical. 3. LDO + DCDC Mixed Power Supply: Balancing Efficiency and Low Noise （power supply pcb） In practical systems, DCDC converters and LDOs are often used together rather than as alternatives. For example: DCDC: 12V → 3.3V for efficient voltage conversion LDO: 3.3V → 1.8V for noise-sensitive circuits such as ADCs, PLLs, and clocks This approach combines the efficiency of a DCDC converter with the low-noise characteristics of an LDO, making it useful for applications that require both power efficiency and clean power rails. Three Common Mixed Power Supply Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Insufficient Filtering at the LDO Input → Upstream Noise May Reach the Downstream Rail Incorrect: Connecting the DCDC output directly to an LDO-powered sensitive load without evaluating the DCDC switching noise and the LDO's PSRR. Consequence: Switching ripple from the upstream converter may couple into downstream sensitive circuits through the power path, affecting ADC, PLL, and other noise-sensitive devices. Correct: Evaluate whether additional filtering is required based on the DCDC switching frequency, LDO PSRR, and load noise requirements. When necessary, add a ferrite bead, LC filter, or π filter between the two power stages. Place filtering components close to the corresponding power input and keep the filter loop area under control. Avoid adding filtering components blindly; select them based on the actual noise frequency range. Mistake 2: Poor Power Region Layout → Noise Coupling Incorrect: Placing the high-noise DCDC switching area too close to sensitive LDO power areas or creating unnecessary coupling between different power regions. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into sensitive power rails through parasitic capacitance, electromagnetic coupling, or shared impedance. Correct: Properly separate the DCDC power stage, LDO area, and sensitive load areas. Keep high-noise SW nodes away from sensitive power rails and signals. Maintain a solid reference ground plane beneath the LDO output power area whenever possible. Keep sensitive power traces away from high di/dt return paths of the DCDC converter. Mistake 3: Poorly Designed Decoupling Network → Insufficient High-Frequency Response Incorrect: Placing all capacitors at the DCDC output while providing insufficient local decoupling near sensitive loads. Consequence: Parasitic impedance in the power path can reduce high-frequency decoupling effectiveness, preventing the load from receiving transient current quickly enough. Correct: Configure DCDC output capacitors according to the converter requirements. Use the required input and output capacitors at the LDO according to the datasheet. Add local decoupling capacitors close to sensitive loads such as ADCs, PLLs, and MCUs. Design each power stage's decoupling network according to the actual load and frequency requirements rather than simply adding more capacitors. Conclusion Although LDOs and DCDC converters are both power management devices, their power supply layout priorities are different. LDO layout guidelines focus more on thermal management, capacitor placement, and power dissipation. DCDC PCB layout focuses more on high-frequency power loops, feedback paths, grounding, and EMI. Mixed power supplies require additional attention to noise isolation and decoupling between different power stages. A good power supply pcb design is not simply about adding more copper. It is about giving current the shortest and most appropriate path, keeping noise away from sensitive areas, and placing every critical component where it can perform properly. Mistake 4: Improper Input Capacitor Placement → Increased Input Ripple Incorrect: Relying on a single bulk capacitor while placing it far from the VIN and GND pins. Consequence: A larger high-frequency current loop can increase input ripple and noise. Correct: Configure input capacitors according to the DCDC converter datasheet. Use capacitors with different values when necessary to address different frequency ranges. Place input capacitors as close as possible to the VIN and GND pins. Keep the input capacitor loop short and compact. Mistake 5: Ignoring the Freewheeling Path → Reduced Efficiency and Poorer EMI Performance Incorrect: Placing the freewheeling diode, synchronous MOSFET, or related circuitry too far apart. Consequence: Increased parasitic parameters can lead to additional losses, ringing, and EMI. Correct: Optimize the freewheeling and synchronous rectification paths according to the specific converter topology. Minimize high-current return paths. For multiphase DCDC converters, keep the power paths of each phase well organized and reasonably symmetrical. 3. LDO + DCDC Mixed Power Supply: Balancing Efficiency and Low Noise （power supply pcb） In practical systems, DCDC converters and LDOs are often used together rather than as alternatives. For example: DCDC: 12V → 3.3V for efficient voltage conversion LDO: 3.3V → 1.8V for noise-sensitive circuits such as ADCs, PLLs, and clocks This approach combines the efficiency of a DCDC converter with the low-noise characteristics of an LDO, making it useful for applications that require both power efficiency and clean power rails. Consequence: Switching ripple from the upstream converter may couple into downstream sensitive circuits through the power path, affecting ADC, PLL, and other noise-sensitive devices. Correct: Evaluate whether additional filtering is required based on the DCDC switching frequency, LDO PSRR, and load noise requirements. When necessary, add a ferrite bead, LC filter, or π filter between the two power stages. Place filtering components close to the corresponding power input and keep the filter loop area under control. Avoid adding filtering components blindly; select them based on the actual noise frequency range. Mistake 2: Poor Power Region Layout → Noise Coupling Incorrect: Placing the high-noise DCDC switching area too close to sensitive LDO power areas or creating unnecessary coupling between different power regions. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into sensitive power rails through parasitic capacitance, electromagnetic coupling, or shared impedance. Correct: Properly separate the DCDC power stage, LDO area, and sensitive load areas. Keep high-noise SW nodes away from sensitive power rails and signals. Maintain a solid reference ground plane beneath the LDO output power area whenever possible. Keep sensitive power traces away from high di/dt return paths of the DCDC converter. Mistake 3: Poorly Designed Decoupling Network → Insufficient High-Frequency Response Incorrect: Placing all capacitors at the DCDC output while providing insufficient local decoupling near sensitive loads. Consequence: Parasitic impedance in the power path can reduce high-frequency decoupling effectiveness, preventing the load from receiving transient current quickly enough. Correct: Configure DCDC output capacitors according to the converter requirements. Use the required input and output capacitors at the LDO according to the datasheet. Add local decoupling capacitors close to sensitive loads such as ADCs, PLLs, and MCUs. Design each power stage's decoupling network according to the actual load and frequency requirements rather than simply adding more capacitors. Conclusion Although LDOs and DCDC converters are both power management devices, their power supply layout priorities are different. LDO layout guidelines focus more on thermal management, capacitor placement, and power dissipation. DCDC PCB layout focuses more on high-frequency power loops, feedback paths, grounding, and EMI. Mixed power supplies require additional attention to noise isolation and decoupling between different power stages. A good power supply pcb design is not simply about adding more copper. It is about giving current the shortest and most appropriate path, keeping noise away from sensitive areas, and placing every critical component where it can perform properly.
