Verify Now Blog > Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 21,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity PCB antipad high-speed PCB design anti pad pcb In high-speed PCB design , via antipads are often treated as simple clearance features. In fact, the size of a PCB antipad directly affects the parasitic capacitance and local impedance around a via, making it an important parameter for maintaining impedance continuity and signal integrity. If the antipad is too small, it can introduce excessive capacitive loading and cause local impedance to drop. If it is too large, it may affect the integrity of the power or ground plane. Especially in Gbps-level high-speed links, simply using the default parameters in PCB design software can result in significant impedance discontinuities around the via transition, potentially affecting signal integrity. The purpose of an anti pad PCB design is not limited to preventing electrical shorts. By changing the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, a properly designed antipad can reduce via parasitic capacitance, optimize local impedance, and minimize signal reflections. Therefore, antipad design is an important part of optimizing high-speed vias. What Is a PCB Antipad Actually “Removing”? Let's put aside the abstract definition and look at it from a straightforward engineering perspective. When a PCB via changes layers, its metal barrel and pad pass through portions of the power and ground planes. The metal conductor, dielectric material, and surrounding plane copper naturally form parasitic capacitance. The impedance of a transmission line is mainly determined by the dielectric material, trace width, and stackup. However, the additional parasitic capacitance around a via introduces extra capacitive loading, causing the local via impedance to deviate from the target impedance of the transmission line. This creates an impedance discontinuity that can affect high-speed signal transmission. A PCB antipad is a copper clearance area created around the via pad on the power or ground plane layers through which the via passes. Its main purposes are: Increase the distance between the via barrel and plane copper to prevent electrical shorts; Reduce the parasitic capacitance between the via and reference plane, optimize local via impedance, and reduce reflections caused by impedance discontinuity. A high-speed signal trace can be compared to a smooth road with a constant speed limit. The via is an unavoidable intersection, while parasitic capacitance is like a sudden dip in the road. When the signal travels through this discontinuity at high speed, impedance changes can cause reflections, ringing, and waveform distortion. The purpose of an antipad is to adjust the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, reducing the impact of this “dip” and making the via transition smoother. （Anti-pad Structure） How Does Parasitic Capacitance Affect Via Impedance? A via is not an ideal conductor. Its equivalent model can include parasitic inductance L and parasitic capacitance C. For high-speed signals, the actual impedance characteristics of a via are also affected by factors such as via length, hole diameter, pad size, antipad size, reference plane position, and via stub. The antipad size is one of the important parameters affecting via parasitic capacitance. If the antipad is too small, the distance between the via barrel or pad and the reference plane becomes smaller, increasing the capacitive loading between the via and plane. This can cause a more significant drop in local via impedance. For example, when a transmission line with a target impedance of 50 Ω passes through an unoptimized via structure, the local impedance may decrease around the via transition, creating a structure such as: 50 Ω trace → lower impedance at via → 50 Ω trace. This impedance discontinuity can cause signal reflections, energy loss, and waveform distortion. Therefore, an antipad is not simply a matter of making the clearance as large or as small as possible. In high-speed PCB design, its size needs to be optimized together with the stackup, via structure, and target impedance. （Small antipad vs Large antipad） What Problems Can Improper Antipad Design Cause? It is easy to assume that a small dimensional difference will not matter. However, in Gbps-level high-speed links, even small geometric changes in the via structure can affect impedance and signal integrity. 1. Impedance Discontinuity, Signal Reflection, and Reduced Eye Opening A smaller antipad → higher parasitic capacitance → potentially lower local via impedance. When a high-speed signal reaches this region, a significant impedance change can cause signal reflection, edge distortion, increased jitter, and reduced eye opening. These effects may ultimately degrade the performance of the high-speed link. 2. Poorer Return Loss and Reflected Signal Energy Impedance discontinuities increase signal reflection, causing part of the signal energy to return toward the transmitter instead of reaching the receiver effectively. For high-speed SerDes links, reflections from multiple vias, connectors, and package structures can accumulate. Therefore, maintaining impedance continuity across the via transition is an important part of signal integrity optimization. 3. Via Resonance and Stub Effects Can Increase Loss at Specific Frequencies The parasitic inductance and capacitance of a via, together with unused via stubs, can create frequency-dependent resonance and reflection characteristics. When the effective frequency range of a high-speed signal approaches these resonant regions, return loss and insertion loss may deteriorate significantly. This is one reason why some links may work normally at lower speeds but show degraded performance at higher data rates. Therefore, in addition to PCB antipad design, high-speed via design also needs to consider via stubs. For loss-sensitive high-speed links, techniques such as back drilling, blind vias, or buried vias can be used to shorten or eliminate unnecessary via stubs. 4. Reference Plane Discontinuity and Poorer Return Current Paths An antipad should not simply be made as large as possible. If the plane clearance becomes excessively large, it may affect the continuity of the local reference plane and force the high-speed return current to take a longer path. This can increase return-path inductance and introduce additional impedance discontinuities. In high-density high-speed PCB design, the locations of adjacent vias, return vias, and reference planes should also be considered together to avoid creating new signal integrity or EMI problems through excessive plane clearance. Not Just Vias: BGA Areas Also Need Attention Most high-speed PCB designs focus heavily on via antipads, but in high-density BGA regions, the parasitic capacitance between component pads and reference planes also deserves attention. A typical high-speed trace may be only 3–4 mil wide, while a BGA pad is usually much larger than the trace. The larger the pad area and the closer it is to the reference plane, the greater the potential capacitive loading. A large pad located close to a reference plane can introduce additional capacitive loading, making the BGA breakout region another potential impedance transition in a high-speed signal path. Therefore, high-speed BGA design should consider: BGA pad size; Distance between the pad and reference plane; Trace width and impedance; Breakout method; Reference plane continuity. When necessary, local plane clearance can be used to reduce the parasitic capacitance associated with the pad. However, not every BGA pad requires an enlarged antipad. Excessive plane clearance can also disrupt reference plane continuity and force the return current to detour. Therefore, the appropriate clearance should be determined based on the stackup, pad geometry, target impedance, and simulation results. How Should a Differential Via Antipad Be Designed? A single-ended signal via can typically use a circular antipad, but differential vias should not simply follow the same design approach. 1. Separate Circular Antipads May Introduce Additional Coupling If the positive and negative differential vias each use an independent circular antipad, a narrow strip of reference plane copper may remain between the two antipads. This remaining copper can change the electromagnetic coupling between the two vias. For high-speed differential signals, such a structural change may affect: Differential impedance Symmetry between the two signal paths Differential-to-common-mode conversion Insertion loss and return loss around the via transition 2. Connected Oval or “Dog-Bone” Antipad When space allows and simulation confirms the design, the antipads around the two differential vias can be partially connected to form an oval or “dog-bone” clearance area. This approach can reduce unnecessary plane copper between the two vias and create a more symmetrical electromagnetic environment around the differential via pair. The main benefits include: Better control of differential impedance toward the target value; Improved structural symmetry and reduced risk of differential-to-common-mode conversion; Reduced unnecessary local electromagnetic coupling between the vias. However, a dog-bone-shaped antipad is not a universal solution for every differential via structure. The final shape and dimensions should still be determined based on via spacing, stackup, target impedance, and simulation results. How Large Should a PCB Antipad Be? Antipad design is a typical case of “too much of a good thing.” If the antipad is too small, electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane increases, potentially increasing parasitic capacitance. If it is too large, reference plane continuity may be affected. Therefore, the PCB antipad needs to balance impedance control, return current paths, and manufacturing capability. Key Guidelines for High-Speed PCB Antipad Design 1. Do Not Simply Apply a Fixed Mil Value There is no universal antipad size that works for every high-speed PCB. The actual dimensions should be optimized according to via hole diameter, pad size, dielectric thickness, material Dk, reference plane position, and target impedance. 2. Meet Manufacturing Rules Before Optimizing Impedance An initial antipad size can be established according to the PCB manufacturer's design rules and then refined through impedance calculation or simulation. 3. Maintain Symmetry in Differential Vias For differential via structures, the geometry and electromagnetic environment around the positive and negative vias should be as symmetrical as possible to maintain differential impedance and reduce mode conversion. 4. Simulate the Complete Via Transition for High-Speed Links For high-speed links above 10 Gbps, as well as interfaces such as PCIe, USB, and SerDes that have strict requirements for channel loss and impedance continuity, fixed empirical dimensions should not be applied directly. The complete stackup, material Dk/Df, via geometry, reference planes, return vias, and target impedance should be considered together. For complex three-dimensional via structures, tools such as HFSS, CST, or Simbeor can be used for electromagnetic analysis, while tools such as Polar SI9000 are more suitable for PCB stackup and transmission-line impedance analysis. The acceptable impedance variation should ultimately be determined according to the specific interface specification and channel budget rather than applying a single universal ±10% requirement. Conclusion Effective high-speed PCB design is not simply about creating an antipad around a via. It requires an understanding of the relationship between parasitic capacitance, via impedance, reference planes, return current paths, and signal integrity. An antipad that is too small may increase capacitive loading and cause local impedance to decrease, while an oversized antipad may affect reference plane continuity. For high-speed differential vias, designers must also consider structural symmetry, differential impedance, and mode conversion. Therefore, there is no single antipad size that is suitable for every PCB. A properly designed PCB antipad should be optimized according to the target impedance and signal integrity requirements, together with the PCB stackup, via geometry, manufacturing capability, and simulation results. This helps maintain a more continuous and stable electromagnetic environment throughout the high-speed signal path. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 21,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity PCB antipad high-speed PCB design anti pad pcb In high-speed PCB design , via antipads are often treated as simple clearance features. In fact, the size of a PCB antipad directly affects the parasitic capacitance and local impedance around a via, making it an important parameter for maintaining impedance continuity and signal integrity. If the antipad is too small, it can introduce excessive capacitive loading and cause local impedance to drop. If it is too large, it may affect the integrity of the power or ground plane. Especially in Gbps-level high-speed links, simply using the default parameters in PCB design software can result in significant impedance discontinuities around the via transition, potentially affecting signal integrity. The purpose of an anti pad PCB design is not limited to preventing electrical shorts. By changing the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, a properly designed antipad can reduce via parasitic capacitance, optimize local impedance, and minimize signal reflections. Therefore, antipad design is an important part of optimizing high-speed vias. What Is a PCB Antipad Actually “Removing”? Let's put aside the abstract definition and look at it from a straightforward engineering perspective. When a PCB via changes layers, its metal barrel and pad pass through portions of the power and ground planes. The metal conductor, dielectric material, and surrounding plane copper naturally form parasitic capacitance. The impedance of a transmission line is mainly determined by the dielectric material, trace width, and stackup. However, the additional parasitic capacitance around a via introduces extra capacitive loading, causing the local via impedance to deviate from the target impedance of the transmission line. This creates an impedance discontinuity that can affect high-speed signal transmission. A PCB antipad is a copper clearance area created around the via pad on the power or ground plane layers through which the via passes. Its main purposes are: Increase the distance between the via barrel and plane copper to prevent electrical shorts; Reduce the parasitic capacitance between the via and reference plane, optimize local via impedance, and reduce reflections caused by impedance discontinuity. A high-speed signal trace can be compared to a smooth road with a constant speed limit. The via is an unavoidable intersection, while parasitic capacitance is like a sudden dip in the road. When the signal travels through this discontinuity at high speed, impedance changes can cause reflections, ringing, and waveform distortion. The purpose of an antipad is to adjust the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, reducing the impact of this “dip” and making the via transition smoother. （Anti-pad Structure） How Does Parasitic Capacitance Affect Via Impedance? A via is not an ideal conductor. Its equivalent model can include parasitic inductance L and parasitic capacitance C. For high-speed signals, the actual impedance characteristics of a via are also affected by factors such as via length, hole diameter, pad size, antipad size, reference plane position, and via stub. The antipad size is one of the important parameters affecting via parasitic capacitance. If the antipad is too small, the distance between the via barrel or pad and the reference plane becomes smaller, increasing the capacitive loading between the via and plane. This can cause a more significant drop in local via impedance. For example, when a transmission line with a target impedance of 50 Ω passes through an unoptimized via structure, the local impedance may decrease around the via transition, creating a structure such as: 50 Ω trace → lower impedance at via → 50 Ω trace. This impedance discontinuity can cause signal reflections, energy loss, and waveform distortion. Therefore, an antipad is not simply a matter of making the clearance as large or as small as possible. In high-speed PCB design, its size needs to be optimized together with the stackup, via structure, and target impedance. （Small antipad vs Large antipad） What Problems Can Improper Antipad Design Cause? It is easy to assume that a small dimensional difference will not matter. However, in Gbps-level high-speed links, even small geometric changes in the via structure can affect impedance and signal integrity. 1. Impedance Discontinuity, Signal Reflection, and Reduced Eye Opening A smaller antipad → higher parasitic capacitance → potentially lower local via impedance. When a high-speed signal reaches this region, a significant impedance change can cause signal reflection, edge distortion, increased jitter, and reduced eye opening. These effects may ultimately degrade the performance of the high-speed link. 2. Poorer Return Loss and Reflected Signal Energy Impedance discontinuities increase signal reflection, causing part of the signal energy to return toward the transmitter instead of reaching the receiver effectively. For high-speed SerDes links, reflections from multiple vias, connectors, and package structures can accumulate. Therefore, maintaining impedance continuity across the via transition is an important part of signal integrity optimization. 3. Via Resonance and Stub Effects Can Increase Loss at Specific Frequencies The parasitic inductance and capacitance of a via, together with unused via stubs, can create frequency-dependent resonance and reflection characteristics. When the effective frequency range of a high-speed signal approaches these resonant regions, return loss and insertion loss may deteriorate significantly. This is one reason why some links may work normally at lower speeds but show degraded performance at higher data rates. Therefore, in addition to PCB antipad design, high-speed via design also needs to consider via stubs. For loss-sensitive high-speed links, techniques such as back drilling, blind vias, or buried vias can be used to shorten or eliminate unnecessary via stubs. 4. Reference Plane Discontinuity and Poorer Return Current Paths An antipad should not simply be made as large as possible. If the plane clearance becomes excessively large, it may affect the continuity of the local reference plane and force the high-speed return current to take a longer path. This can increase return-path inductance and introduce additional impedance discontinuities. In high-density high-speed PCB design, the locations of adjacent vias, return vias, and reference planes should also be considered together to avoid creating new signal integrity or EMI problems through excessive plane clearance. Not Just Vias: BGA Areas Also Need Attention Most high-speed PCB designs focus heavily on via antipads, but in high-density BGA regions, the parasitic capacitance between component pads and reference planes also deserves attention. A typical high-speed trace may be only 3–4 mil wide, while a BGA pad is usually much larger than the trace. The larger the pad area and the closer it is to the reference plane, the greater the potential capacitive loading. A large pad located close to a reference plane can introduce additional capacitive loading, making the BGA breakout region another potential impedance transition in a high-speed signal path. Therefore, high-speed BGA design should consider: BGA pad size; Distance between the pad and reference plane; Trace width and impedance; Breakout method; Reference plane continuity. When necessary, local plane clearance can be used to reduce the parasitic capacitance associated with the pad. However, not every BGA pad requires an enlarged antipad. Excessive plane clearance can also disrupt reference plane continuity and force the return current to detour. Therefore, the appropriate clearance should be determined based on the stackup, pad geometry, target impedance, and simulation results. How Should a Differential Via Antipad Be Designed? A single-ended signal via can typically use a circular antipad, but differential vias should not simply follow the same design approach. 1. Separate Circular Antipads May Introduce Additional Coupling If the positive and negative differential vias each use an independent circular antipad, a narrow strip of reference plane copper may remain between the two antipads. This remaining copper can change the electromagnetic coupling between the two vias. For high-speed differential signals, such a structural change may affect: Differential impedance Symmetry between the two signal paths Differential-to-common-mode conversion Insertion loss and return loss around the via transition 2. Connected Oval or “Dog-Bone” Antipad When space allows and simulation confirms the design, the antipads around the two differential vias can be partially connected to form an oval or “dog-bone” clearance area. This approach can reduce unnecessary plane copper between the two vias and create a more symmetrical electromagnetic environment around the differential via pair. The main benefits include: Better control of differential impedance toward the target value; Improved structural symmetry and reduced risk of differential-to-common-mode conversion; Reduced unnecessary local electromagnetic coupling between the vias. However, a dog-bone-shaped antipad is not a universal solution for every differential via structure. The final shape and dimensions should still be determined based on via spacing, stackup, target impedance, and simulation results. How Large Should a PCB Antipad Be? Antipad design is a typical case of “too much of a good thing.” If the antipad is too small, electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane increases, potentially increasing parasitic capacitance. If it is too large, reference plane continuity may be affected. Therefore, the PCB antipad needs to balance impedance control, return current paths, and manufacturing capability. Key Guidelines for High-Speed PCB Antipad Design 1. Do Not Simply Apply a Fixed Mil Value There is no universal antipad size that works for every high-speed PCB. The actual dimensions should be optimized according to via hole diameter, pad size, dielectric thickness, material Dk, reference plane position, and target impedance. 2. Meet Manufacturing Rules Before Optimizing Impedance An initial antipad size can be established according to the PCB manufacturer's design rules and then refined through impedance calculation or simulation. 3. Maintain Symmetry in Differential Vias For differential via structures, the geometry and electromagnetic environment around the positive and negative vias should be as symmetrical as possible to maintain differential impedance and reduce mode conversion. 4. Simulate the Complete Via Transition for High-Speed Links For high-speed links above 10 Gbps, as well as interfaces such as PCIe, USB, and SerDes that have strict requirements for channel loss and impedance continuity, fixed empirical dimensions should not be applied directly. The complete stackup, material Dk/Df, via geometry, reference planes, return vias, and target impedance should be considered together. For complex three-dimensional via structures, tools such as HFSS, CST, or Simbeor can be used for electromagnetic analysis, while tools such as Polar SI9000 are more suitable for PCB stackup and transmission-line impedance analysis. The acceptable impedance variation should ultimately be determined according to the specific interface specification and channel budget rather than applying a single universal ±10% requirement. Conclusion Effective high-speed PCB design is not simply about creating an antipad around a via. It requires an understanding of the relationship between parasitic capacitance, via impedance, reference planes, return current paths, and signal integrity. An antipad that is too small may increase capacitive loading and cause local impedance to decrease, while an oversized antipad may affect reference plane continuity. For high-speed differential vias, designers must also consider structural symmetry, differential impedance, and mode conversion. Therefore, there is no single antipad size that is suitable for every PCB. A properly designed PCB antipad should be optimized according to the target impedance and signal integrity requirements, together with the PCB stackup, via geometry, manufacturing capability, and simulation results. This helps maintain a more continuous and stable electromagnetic environment throughout the high-speed signal path. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Why Do PCBs Need Stitching Vias Along the Board Edge? by: Mila Oct 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias PCB EMI shielding PCB return path PCB via stitching Anyone who has worked on PCB layout has probably experienced this: after finishing the layout, you hand the board over to a senior engineer for review. They take a quick look around the board and ask, “Where are the ground vias along the edge?” At first, this may seem unnecessary. After all, the board edge does not carry signal traces. So why are stitching vias placed there? The answer lies in what happens around the edge of a PCB. Properly placed grounding vias can help control electromagnetic coupling, provide a more continuous high-frequency return path, and improve PCB edge shielding. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive designs, that simple row of vias can make a noticeable difference. （Stitching Vias） What Do Ground Vias Along the PCB Edge Actually Do? This row of vias is commonly known as a ground via fence, via fence, or stitching vias. It is not simply a matter of placing a row of vias around the board. Instead, the vias connect ground structures on different PCB layers and create a more continuous electromagnetic boundary along the board edge. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. Why Do PCBs Need Stitching Vias Along the Board Edge? by: Mila Oct 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias PCB EMI shielding PCB return path PCB via stitching Anyone who has worked on PCB layout has probably experienced this: after finishing the layout, you hand the board over to a senior engineer for review. They take a quick look around the board and ask, “Where are the ground vias along the edge?” At first, this may seem unnecessary. After all, the board edge does not carry signal traces. So why are stitching vias placed there? The answer lies in what happens around the edge of a PCB. Properly placed grounding vias can help control electromagnetic coupling, provide a more continuous high-frequency return path, and improve PCB edge shielding. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive designs, that simple row of vias can make a noticeable difference. （Stitching Vias） What Do Ground Vias Along the PCB Edge Actually Do? This row of vias is commonly known as a ground via fence, via fence, or stitching vias. It is not simply a matter of placing a row of vias around the board. Instead, the vias connect ground structures on different PCB layers and create a more continuous electromagnetic boundary along the board edge. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. Why No Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator in PCB Layout? by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb routing crystal oscillator pcb layout pcb crystal oscillator When designing a PCB, many engineers have heard the rule: no traces should run under a crystal oscillator. But why? Can a low-speed signal trace really affect a crystal oscillator? And can a guard ring with grounding vias completely eliminate interference? Although a crystal oscillator provides the clock signal for digital circuits, its oscillation loop is highly sensitive to parasitic capacitance and external noise. Poor crystal oscillator PCB layout and PCB routing can cause frequency shifts, startup problems, or unstable clock signals, and may even increase EMI risks. So, why should traces be kept away from the area beneath a crystal? How should the guard ring and grounding vias be designed? Let's start with how a crystal oscillator works and then look at the key considerations for its PCB layout and routing. 1. How Does a Crystal Oscillator Work? A crystal oscillator uses the piezoelectric properties of a quartz crystal to generate a stable periodic signal. When an alternating voltage is applied to the crystal, it mechanically vibrates at a specific resonant frequency. The electrical and mechanical characteristics of the crystal allow it to provide a highly stable frequency reference for the circuit. In many digital systems, the crystal is connected to an oscillator circuit inside an MCU, processor, or other IC. A common configuration is the Pierce oscillator, where the crystal works together with two load capacitors to form the oscillation loop. The crystal itself can be considered as a high-Q resonant component. This means that even small changes in the surrounding circuit can affect its behavior. Therefore, crystal oscillator PCB layout is not simply about placing the component close to the IC. The routing, ground plane, surrounding copper, and parasitic effects also need to be considered. （Piezoelectric Effect） 2. Why Should You Avoid Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator? The area around a crystal oscillator may look electrically simple, but PCB routing underneath the crystal can introduce several unwanted effects. Parasitic Capacitance A PCB trace running underneath the crystal or its oscillator pins can form parasitic capacitance with the copper layers below or above it. This additional capacitance changes the effective load seen by the oscillator circuit. As a result, the crystal's oscillation frequency may shift, and the startup characteristics can also be affected. This is especially important because the crystal oscillator circuit usually operates with relatively small signal levels and is sensitive to its load conditions. Keeping unnecessary copper and traces away from the crystal area helps reduce these unpredictable parasitic effects. （recommend pcb layout） Noise Coupling High-speed signal traces can generate rapidly changing electric fields. If these traces pass beneath or too close to the crystal oscillator, noise can couple into the sensitive oscillation loop through parasitic capacitance. The problem becomes more noticeable when the nearby traces carry high-speed clocks, switching signals, or other signals with large voltage transitions. For this reason, good PCB routing practice is to keep noisy signal traces away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. EMI and Signal Integrity The crystal oscillator area should also be treated as a sensitive clock source. Poor routing can increase unwanted coupling between the oscillator and nearby circuits. At the same time, the crystal circuit itself can become a source of electromagnetic radiation if its return path and surrounding copper are not properly controlled. A compact layout with short connections and a clean reference plane can help reduce both noise coupling and EMI risks. （Sources of EMI Issues） 3. Why Use a Guard Ring and Grounding Vias? In addition to keeping signal traces away, some designs use a grounded copper guard ring around the crystal oscillator. Guard Ring A guard ring is a copper area surrounding the sensitive crystal circuit and connected to ground. Its purpose is to provide a low-impedance ground barrier around the oscillator area, helping reduce coupling from nearby signals. The guard ring should not replace the basic keep-out requirements. It is an additional measure for improving isolation and controlling the electromagnetic environment around the crystal. （Ground Guard Ring） Grounding Via Stitching Grounding vias can be placed around the guard ring to connect the surrounding ground copper to the ground planes on other layers. This via stitching helps maintain a more continuous ground structure and can reduce the path through which external noise couples into the oscillator area. However, adding more vias does not automatically make the design better. The via placement should be coordinated with the crystal package, oscillator pins, routing space, and PCB manufacturing requirements. （Ground Stitching Vias） Keep-Out Area The most basic rule is still to keep unnecessary signal traces and copper away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. The exact keep-out size depends on the crystal, IC, PCB stackup, operating frequency, and layout requirements. Therefore, the IC or crystal manufacturer's recommendations should be followed whenever available. A typical layout can be organized as: Crystal → Short oscillator traces → Load capacitors → IC. The surrounding area can then use a grounded guard ring and stitching vias where necessary. （typical crystal pcb layout） 4. Crystal Oscillator PCB Layout and Routing Tips Good crystal oscillator PCB layout focuses on keeping the oscillation loop short, quiet, and predictable. Place the Crystal Close to the IC The crystal should normally be placed as close as practical to the corresponding oscillator pins of the MCU or other IC. Shorter connections reduce parasitic capacitance and inductance and help minimize the area of the sensitive oscillator loop. Avoid placing the crystal far away and routing long traces back to the IC. Keep Oscillator Routing Short and Symmetrical The traces between the crystal and the oscillator pins should be as short as practical. Avoid unnecessary vias, sharp detours, and long parallel runs with noisy signals. When possible, keep the two oscillator connections reasonably symmetrical to reduce differences in parasitic effects. Place Load Capacitors Close to the Oscillator Pins Load capacitors are normally placed close to the crystal and IC oscillator pins. Long traces between the capacitors and the IC add parasitic inductance and capacitance, making the actual load different from the nominal capacitor value. Therefore, component placement and PCB routing should be considered together rather than separately. Avoid High-Speed Traces Near the Crystal During PCB routing, keep high-speed clocks, switching nodes, power converters, and other noisy signals away from the crystal area whenever possible. If a high-speed signal must cross the region, consider whether the routing can be changed to maintain sufficient physical separation. This is particularly important for dense multilayer boards where signals on adjacent layers may also couple through the dielectric. Provide a Clean Ground Reference A continuous ground plane can provide a stable reference for the surrounding circuit and help control return-current paths. However, avoid routing unrelated signals through the sensitive crystal area on other layers. The goal is not simply to create as much copper as possible, but to create a predictable electromagnetic environment around the oscillator. Consider the Crystal Package and Shielding For some applications, the crystal oscillator may be enclosed in a metal package or shielded structure. If shielding is used, make sure its connection to ground is reliable and that the mechanical structure does not introduce unexpected parasitic effects. For designs with strict clock stability or EMI requirements, testing should be used to verify the actual performance rather than relying only on layout rules. 5. Common Mistakes in Crystal Oscillator PCB Routing Several layout mistakes can make an otherwise functional crystal oscillator less stable. Running signal traces directly underneath the crystal. Routing high-speed or switching signals too close to the oscillator loop. Placing the crystal too far from the IC. Using unnecessarily long oscillator traces. Placing load capacitors far from the oscillator pins. Adding excessive vias or complicated routing around the crystal. Ignoring the IC manufacturer's crystal layout recommendations. These problems may not always cause an immediate failure. In some designs, the oscillator may still start normally but show frequency deviation, increased sensitivity to noise, or different behavior between PCB revisions. That is why crystal oscillator layout should be treated as a complete circuit rather than simply a component placement rule. The rule of “no traces under the crystal oscillator” is not an absolute manufacturing requirement. Its purpose is to reduce parasitic capacitance, noise coupling, and interference around a sensitive oscillator circuit. In practical PCB routing , the most important principles are to keep the crystal close to the IC, minimize the oscillator loop, keep noisy signals away, place load capacitors properly, and provide a clean ground environment. For more demanding designs, a grounded guard ring and via stitching can provide additional isolation. Ultimately, the recommended layout from the IC and crystal manufacturers should be used as the primary reference, with actual testing used to verify oscillator stability and EMI performance. Why No Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator in PCB Layout? by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb routing crystal oscillator pcb layout pcb crystal oscillator When designing a PCB, many engineers have heard the rule: no traces should run under a crystal oscillator. But why? Can a low-speed signal trace really affect a crystal oscillator? And can a guard ring with grounding vias completely eliminate interference? Although a crystal oscillator provides the clock signal for digital circuits, its oscillation loop is highly sensitive to parasitic capacitance and external noise. Poor crystal oscillator PCB layout and PCB routing can cause frequency shifts, startup problems, or unstable clock signals, and may even increase EMI risks. So, why should traces be kept away from the area beneath a crystal? How should the guard ring and grounding vias be designed? Let's start with how a crystal oscillator works and then look at the key considerations for its PCB layout and routing. 1. How Does a Crystal Oscillator Work? A crystal oscillator uses the piezoelectric properties of a quartz crystal to generate a stable periodic signal. When an alternating voltage is applied to the crystal, it mechanically vibrates at a specific resonant frequency. The electrical and mechanical characteristics of the crystal allow it to provide a highly stable frequency reference for the circuit. In many digital systems, the crystal is connected to an oscillator circuit inside an MCU, processor, or other IC. A common configuration is the Pierce oscillator, where the crystal works together with two load capacitors to form the oscillation loop. The crystal itself can be considered as a high-Q resonant component. This means that even small changes in the surrounding circuit can affect its behavior. Therefore, crystal oscillator PCB layout is not simply about placing the component close to the IC. The routing, ground plane, surrounding copper, and parasitic effects also need to be considered. （Piezoelectric Effect） 2. Why Should You Avoid Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator? The area around a crystal oscillator may look electrically simple, but PCB routing underneath the crystal can introduce several unwanted effects. Parasitic Capacitance A PCB trace running underneath the crystal or its oscillator pins can form parasitic capacitance with the copper layers below or above it. This additional capacitance changes the effective load seen by the oscillator circuit. As a result, the crystal's oscillation frequency may shift, and the startup characteristics can also be affected. This is especially important because the crystal oscillator circuit usually operates with relatively small signal levels and is sensitive to its load conditions. Keeping unnecessary copper and traces away from the crystal area helps reduce these unpredictable parasitic effects. （recommend pcb layout） Noise Coupling High-speed signal traces can generate rapidly changing electric fields. If these traces pass beneath or too close to the crystal oscillator, noise can couple into the sensitive oscillation loop through parasitic capacitance. The problem becomes more noticeable when the nearby traces carry high-speed clocks, switching signals, or other signals with large voltage transitions. For this reason, good PCB routing practice is to keep noisy signal traces away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. EMI and Signal Integrity The crystal oscillator area should also be treated as a sensitive clock source. Poor routing can increase unwanted coupling between the oscillator and nearby circuits. At the same time, the crystal circuit itself can become a source of electromagnetic radiation if its return path and surrounding copper are not properly controlled. A compact layout with short connections and a clean reference plane can help reduce both noise coupling and EMI risks. （Sources of EMI Issues） 3. Why Use a Guard Ring and Grounding Vias? In addition to keeping signal traces away, some designs use a grounded copper guard ring around the crystal oscillator. Guard Ring A guard ring is a copper area surrounding the sensitive crystal circuit and connected to ground. Its purpose is to provide a low-impedance ground barrier around the oscillator area, helping reduce coupling from nearby signals. The guard ring should not replace the basic keep-out requirements. It is an additional measure for improving isolation and controlling the electromagnetic environment around the crystal. （Ground Guard Ring） Grounding Via Stitching Grounding vias can be placed around the guard ring to connect the surrounding ground copper to the ground planes on other layers. This via stitching helps maintain a more continuous ground structure and can reduce the path through which external noise couples into the oscillator area. However, adding more vias does not automatically make the design better. The via placement should be coordinated with the crystal package, oscillator pins, routing space, and PCB manufacturing requirements. （Ground Stitching Vias） Keep-Out Area The most basic rule is still to keep unnecessary signal traces and copper away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. The exact keep-out size depends on the crystal, IC, PCB stackup, operating frequency, and layout requirements. Therefore, the IC or crystal manufacturer's recommendations should be followed whenever available. A typical layout can be organized as: Crystal → Short oscillator traces → Load capacitors → IC. The surrounding area can then use a grounded guard ring and stitching vias where necessary. （typical crystal pcb layout） 4. Crystal Oscillator PCB Layout and Routing Tips Good crystal oscillator PCB layout focuses on keeping the oscillation loop short, quiet, and predictable. Place the Crystal Close to the IC The crystal should normally be placed as close as practical to the corresponding oscillator pins of the MCU or other IC. Shorter connections reduce parasitic capacitance and inductance and help minimize the area of the sensitive oscillator loop. Avoid placing the crystal far away and routing long traces back to the IC. Keep Oscillator Routing Short and Symmetrical The traces between the crystal and the oscillator pins should be as short as practical. Avoid unnecessary vias, sharp detours, and long parallel runs with noisy signals. When possible, keep the two oscillator connections reasonably symmetrical to reduce differences in parasitic effects. Place Load Capacitors Close to the Oscillator Pins Load capacitors are normally placed close to the crystal and IC oscillator pins. Long traces between the capacitors and the IC add parasitic inductance and capacitance, making the actual load different from the nominal capacitor value. Therefore, component placement and PCB routing should be considered together rather than separately. Avoid High-Speed Traces Near the Crystal During PCB routing, keep high-speed clocks, switching nodes, power converters, and other noisy signals away from the crystal area whenever possible. If a high-speed signal must cross the region, consider whether the routing can be changed to maintain sufficient physical separation. This is particularly important for dense multilayer boards where signals on adjacent layers may also couple through the dielectric. Provide a Clean Ground Reference A continuous ground plane can provide a stable reference for the surrounding circuit and help control return-current paths. However, avoid routing unrelated signals through the sensitive crystal area on other layers. The goal is not simply to create as much copper as possible, but to create a predictable electromagnetic environment around the oscillator. Consider the Crystal Package and Shielding For some applications, the crystal oscillator may be enclosed in a metal package or shielded structure. If shielding is used, make sure its connection to ground is reliable and that the mechanical structure does not introduce unexpected parasitic effects. For designs with strict clock stability or EMI requirements, testing should be used to verify the actual performance rather than relying only on layout rules. 5. Common Mistakes in Crystal Oscillator PCB Routing Several layout mistakes can make an otherwise functional crystal oscillator less stable. Running signal traces directly underneath the crystal. Routing high-speed or switching signals too close to the oscillator loop. Placing the crystal too far from the IC. Using unnecessarily long oscillator traces. Placing load capacitors far from the oscillator pins. Adding excessive vias or complicated routing around the crystal. Ignoring the IC manufacturer's crystal layout recommendations. These problems may not always cause an immediate failure. In some designs, the oscillator may still start normally but show frequency deviation, increased sensitivity to noise, or different behavior between PCB revisions. That is why crystal oscillator layout should be treated as a complete circuit rather than simply a component placement rule. The rule of “no traces under the crystal oscillator” is not an absolute manufacturing requirement. Its purpose is to reduce parasitic capacitance, noise coupling, and interference around a sensitive oscillator circuit. In practical PCB routing , the most important principles are to keep the crystal close to the IC, minimize the oscillator loop, keep noisy signals away, place load capacitors properly, and provide a clean ground environment. For more demanding designs, a grounded guard ring and via stitching can provide additional isolation. Ultimately, the recommended layout from the IC and crystal manufacturers should be used as the primary reference, with actual testing used to verify oscillator stability and EMI performance. That is why crystal oscillator layout should be treated as a complete circuit rather than simply a component placement rule. The rule of “no traces under the crystal oscillator” is not an absolute manufacturing requirement. Its purpose is to reduce parasitic capacitance, noise coupling, and interference around a sensitive oscillator circuit. In practical PCB routing , the most important principles are to keep the crystal close to the IC, minimize the oscillator loop, keep noisy signals away, place load capacitors properly, and provide a clean ground environment. For more demanding designs, a grounded guard ring and via stitching can provide additional isolation. Ultimately, the recommended layout from the IC and crystal manufacturers should be used as the primary reference, with actual testing used to verify oscillator stability and EMI performance.
