Why No Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator in PCB Layout? by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb routing crystal oscillator pcb layout pcb crystal oscillator When designing a PCB, many engineers have heard the rule: no traces should run under a crystal oscillator. But why? Can a low-speed signal trace really affect a crystal oscillator? And can a guard ring with grounding vias completely eliminate interference? Although a crystal oscillator provides the clock signal for digital circuits, its oscillation loop is highly sensitive to parasitic capacitance and external noise. Poor crystal oscillator PCB layout and PCB routing can cause frequency shifts, startup problems, or unstable clock signals, and may even increase EMI risks. So, why should traces be kept away from the area beneath a crystal? How should the guard ring and grounding vias be designed? Let's start with how a crystal oscillator works and then look at the key considerations for its PCB layout and routing. 1. How Does a Crystal Oscillator Work? A crystal oscillator uses the piezoelectric properties of a quartz crystal to generate a stable periodic signal. When an alternating voltage is applied to the crystal, it mechanically vibrates at a specific resonant frequency. The electrical and mechanical characteristics of the crystal allow it to provide a highly stable frequency reference for the circuit. In many digital systems, the crystal is connected to an oscillator circuit inside an MCU, processor, or other IC. A common configuration is the Pierce oscillator, where the crystal works together with two load capacitors to form the oscillation loop. The crystal itself can be considered as a high-Q resonant component. This means that even small changes in the surrounding circuit can affect its behavior. Therefore, crystal oscillator PCB layout is not simply about placing the component close to the IC. The routing, ground plane, surrounding copper, and parasitic effects also need to be considered. （Piezoelectric Effect） 2. Why Should You Avoid Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator? The area around a crystal oscillator may look electrically simple, but PCB routing underneath the crystal can introduce several unwanted effects. Parasitic Capacitance A PCB trace running underneath the crystal or its oscillator pins can form parasitic capacitance with the copper layers below or above it. This additional capacitance changes the effective load seen by the oscillator circuit. As a result, the crystal's oscillation frequency may shift, and the startup characteristics can also be affected. This is especially important because the crystal oscillator circuit usually operates with relatively small signal levels and is sensitive to its load conditions. Keeping unnecessary copper and traces away from the crystal area helps reduce these unpredictable parasitic effects. （recommend pcb layout） Noise Coupling High-speed signal traces can generate rapidly changing electric fields. If these traces pass beneath or too close to the crystal oscillator, noise can couple into the sensitive oscillation loop through parasitic capacitance. The problem becomes more noticeable when the nearby traces carry high-speed clocks, switching signals, or other signals with large voltage transitions. For this reason, good PCB routing practice is to keep noisy signal traces away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. EMI and Signal Integrity The crystal oscillator area should also be treated as a sensitive clock source. Poor routing can increase unwanted coupling between the oscillator and nearby circuits. At the same time, the crystal circuit itself can become a source of electromagnetic radiation if its return path and surrounding copper are not properly controlled. A compact layout with short connections and a clean reference plane can help reduce both noise coupling and EMI risks. （Sources of EMI Issues） 3. Why Use a Guard Ring and Grounding Vias? In addition to keeping signal traces away, some designs use a grounded copper guard ring around the crystal oscillator. Guard Ring A guard ring is a copper area surrounding the sensitive crystal circuit and connected to ground. Its purpose is to provide a low-impedance ground barrier around the oscillator area, helping reduce coupling from nearby signals. The guard ring should not replace the basic keep-out requirements. It is an additional measure for improving isolation and controlling the electromagnetic environment around the crystal. （Ground Guard Ring） Grounding Via Stitching Grounding vias can be placed around the guard ring to connect the surrounding ground copper to the ground planes on other layers. This via stitching helps maintain a more continuous ground structure and can reduce the path through which external noise couples into the oscillator area. However, adding more vias does not automatically make the design better. The via placement should be coordinated with the crystal package, oscillator pins, routing space, and PCB manufacturing requirements. （Ground Stitching Vias） Keep-Out Area The most basic rule is still to keep unnecessary signal traces and copper away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. The exact keep-out size depends on the crystal, IC, PCB stackup, operating frequency, and layout requirements. Therefore, the IC or crystal manufacturer's recommendations should be followed whenever available. A typical layout can be organized as: Crystal → Short oscillator traces → Load capacitors → IC. The surrounding area can then use a grounded guard ring and stitching vias where necessary. （typical crystal pcb layout） 4. Crystal Oscillator PCB Layout and Routing Tips Good crystal oscillator PCB layout focuses on keeping the oscillation loop short, quiet, and predictable. Place the Crystal Close to the IC The crystal should normally be placed as close as practical to the corresponding oscillator pins of the MCU or other IC. Shorter connections reduce parasitic capacitance and inductance and help minimize the area of the sensitive oscillator loop. Avoid placing the crystal far away and routing long traces back to the IC. Keep Oscillator Routing Short and Symmetrical The traces between the crystal and the oscillator pins should be as short as practical. Avoid unnecessary vias, sharp detours, and long parallel runs with noisy signals. When possible, keep the two oscillator connections reasonably symmetrical to reduce differences in parasitic effects. Place Load Capacitors Close to the Oscillator Pins Load capacitors are normally placed close to the crystal and IC oscillator pins. Long traces between the capacitors and the IC add parasitic inductance and capacitance, making the actual load different from the nominal capacitor value. Therefore, component placement and PCB routing should be considered together rather than separately. Avoid High-Speed Traces Near the Crystal During PCB routing, keep high-speed clocks, switching nodes, power converters, and other noisy signals away from the crystal area whenever possible. If a high-speed signal must cross the region, consider whether the routing can be changed to maintain sufficient physical separation. This is particularly important for dense multilayer boards where signals on adjacent layers may also couple through the dielectric. Provide a Clean Ground Reference A continuous ground plane can provide a stable reference for the surrounding circuit and help control return-current paths. However, avoid routing unrelated signals through the sensitive crystal area on other layers. The goal is not simply to create as much copper as possible, but to create a predictable electromagnetic environment around the oscillator. Consider the Crystal Package and Shielding For some applications, the crystal oscillator may be enclosed in a metal package or shielded structure. If shielding is used, make sure its connection to ground is reliable and that the mechanical structure does not introduce unexpected parasitic effects. For designs with strict clock stability or EMI requirements, testing should be used to verify the actual performance rather than relying only on layout rules. 5. Common Mistakes in Crystal Oscillator PCB Routing Several layout mistakes can make an otherwise functional crystal oscillator less stable. Running signal traces directly underneath the crystal. Routing high-speed or switching signals too close to the oscillator loop. Placing the crystal too far from the IC. Using unnecessarily long oscillator traces. Placing load capacitors far from the oscillator pins. Adding excessive vias or complicated routing around the crystal. Ignoring the IC manufacturer's crystal layout recommendations. These problems may not always cause an immediate failure. In some designs, the oscillator may still start normally but show frequency deviation, increased sensitivity to noise, or different behavior between PCB revisions. That is why crystal oscillator layout should be treated as a complete circuit rather than simply a component placement rule. The rule of “no traces under the crystal oscillator” is not an absolute manufacturing requirement. Its purpose is to reduce parasitic capacitance, noise coupling, and interference around a sensitive oscillator circuit. In practical PCB routing , the most important principles are to keep the crystal close to the IC, minimize the oscillator loop, keep noisy signals away, place load capacitors properly, and provide a clean ground environment. For more demanding designs, a grounded guard ring and via stitching can provide additional isolation. Ultimately, the recommended layout from the IC and crystal manufacturers should be used as the primary reference, with actual testing used to verify oscillator stability and EMI performance. How to Generate Gerber Files in Fusion 360? by: Mia Nov 23,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design Tutorial Gerber Fusion 360 Autodesk Once you have completed the PCB design in Fusion 360, the next step is to export production files to prepare for PCB manufacturing. Therefore, this tutorial will guide you on how to export Gerber files and Drill files in Autodesk Fusion 360. This guide uses the demo board example in Fusion 360 named "Air_Quality_Sensor." In Fusion 360, there are three options for exporting Gerber files: CAM Preview, CAM Processor, and Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs. As shown in the following image: Method One: Click on "CAM Preview" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "CAM Preview" • The Manufacturing Preview window will appear, then click on the CAM Processor button in the bottom right corner, as shown in the following image. • After the CAM Processor window appears, click on the document icon next to the CAM file name, then choose "Load CAM jobs" -> "examples" and select the CAM file that suits your design. Since it is a 2-layer board, we select "example_2_layer.cam." • On the left side of the window, select "Gerber", and keep the Output Type as the default "Gerber RS-274X". Click on the "Process Job" button in the bottom right corner, and choose the desired pathway for saving. • The generated files are as follows: Method Two: Click on "CAM Processor" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "CAM Processor" After clicking, the CAM Processor window will appear. The subsequent steps are the same as the steps in Method One. Method Three: Click on "Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs" • After clicking, the CAM Export File List window will appear. You can see various files such as profile, copper, soldermask, solderpaste, drill files, and more, which are the Gerber files. • Click OK, select the destination where you want to save the files, then click Save. And then the Gerber files will be exported and saved. • A ZIP folder containing all the necessary PCB Gerber files will be generated. • If you want to check what is inside this ZIP folder, simply right-click on the ZIP folder and extract all the files. At this point, you have completed all the steps on how to generate Gerber and drill files using Autodesk Fusion 360. Therefore, this tutorial will guide you on how to export Gerber files and Drill files in Autodesk Fusion 360. This guide uses the demo board example in Fusion 360 named "Air_Quality_Sensor." In Fusion 360, there are three options for exporting Gerber files: CAM Preview, CAM Processor, and Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs. As shown in the following image: Method One: Click on "CAM Preview" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "CAM Preview" • The Manufacturing Preview window will appear, then click on the CAM Processor button in the bottom right corner, as shown in the following image. • After the CAM Processor window appears, click on the document icon next to the CAM file name, then choose "Load CAM jobs" -> "examples" and select the CAM file that suits your design. Since it is a 2-layer board, we select "example_2_layer.cam." • On the left side of the window, select "Gerber", and keep the Output Type as the default "Gerber RS-274X". Click on the "Process Job" button in the bottom right corner, and choose the desired pathway for saving. • The generated files are as follows: Method Two: Click on "CAM Processor" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "CAM Processor" After clicking, the CAM Processor window will appear. The subsequent steps are the same as the steps in Method One. Method Three: Click on "Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs" • After clicking, the CAM Export File List window will appear. You can see various files such as profile, copper, soldermask, solderpaste, drill files, and more, which are the Gerber files. • Click OK, select the destination where you want to save the files, then click Save. And then the Gerber files will be exported and saved. • A ZIP folder containing all the necessary PCB Gerber files will be generated. • If you want to check what is inside this ZIP folder, simply right-click on the ZIP folder and extract all the files. At this point, you have completed all the steps on how to generate Gerber and drill files using Autodesk Fusion 360. How to Set Shortcut Key in Cadence Allegro PCB Editor? by: Mia Sep 25,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design Tutorial shortcut key Allegro PCB Editor Setting shortcut key in Allegro can significantly improve work efficiency and lower body burden. In this article, we will introduce the three methods to set shortcut key: Directly defined in the Allegro PCB Editor command window; By modifying the user variable env file; Define strokes as shortcut keys. Directly Defined in the Allegro PCB Editor Command Window This kind of shortcut key can only be used in the present design and will be invalid if restarting the software. The command format is as follows: alias F2 add connect funckey a add connect For example, set the shortcut key for routing command. As shown in the figure below, enter alias F2 add connect in the command window, and press Enter to use it. There are two ways that allow us to check which commands can be set as shortcut keys: 1.Directly enter alias or funckey in the command window, and press Enter to pop up the shortcut key dialog box, as shown below: 2.View it by executing the Tools->Utilities->Keyboard Commands command, as shown below: By Modifying the User Variable env File There are two modes for this: alias and funckey. If you use alias to define letters, you will need to enter the letter and press Enter for the shortcut to take effect. It is recommended not to define letters and instead use something like Fn or Del for quicker access. The funckey command can be used to define individual shortcut key, and it is more powerful than alias. Anything that can be defined with alias can also be defined with funckey. Funckey definitions are case-sensitive. For example, funckey C 'dbdoctor' assigns dbdoctor to the uppercase C, while funckey c 'copy' assigns copy to the lowercase c. Funckey can also define two letters. For example, when we move the device and align the structure, select the center of the positioning hole, and set it as follows: funckey sa "prepopup;pop dyn_option_select 'Snap pick to@:@Arc/Circle Center'", which is quite convenient. env File Path Taking my computer as an example, in D:\Cadence\SPB_Data\pcbenv, open the env file with Notepad and you can add your own shortcut. Note: Please back up the env file before modifying it. Open the env file with Notepad, as shown in the picture below. In the red box are several of my customized shortcut keys. Users can define shortcut keys according to their own operating habits. Define Strokes as Shortcut Keys Create allegro stroke. Execute Tools->Utilities->Stroke Editor command. After that, a window like the one below will pop up. You can use the right mouse button to draw the strokes you want to define in the blank area of the window and enter the content for the command, as shown in the figure below. In my case, I drew a line with the right mouse button and set the command as oops. After setting it up, if we want to perform the oops operation in the future, we can simply draw a line with the right mouse button. Make sure the stroke is activated. Setup->User Preferences Editor>UI>input Check the no_dragpopup option, otherwise, you need to hold down the Ctrl key to take effect. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. How to generate Gerber files from CircuitMaker 2.2.1.6? by: Mia Jun 27,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design Tutorial CircuitMaker Gerber PCB This guide is about how to export Gerber file from CircuitMaker 2.2.1.6. Step 1 : Open the PCB design file first, and then open the "Project" menu and click "Generate outputs", as shown below. Step 2 : After clicking, the dialog box shown below will appear. Check the boxes next to Gerber Files and NC Drill Files. Step 3 : Click the "Configure" link next to "Gerber Files". In the dialog that opens, configure the following options in the "General" tab: Use the 2:3 format, as the milling precision is 1mm. It's fine to use a higher format if you prefer. And it does not matter whether you choose inches or millimeters as the unit. Remember the settings you choose here, as you will need to use the same settings when configuring your NC Drill file. Step 4 : In the "Layer" tab, select as shown below and do not check any boxes in the right panel. Step 5 : In the "Advanced" tab (skip "Drill Drawing" and "Apertures"), configure the following options: "Film Size" and "Aperture Matching Tolerance" can keep the default settings without changing. Uncheck all options in "other" (such as G54, optimize change location commands, etc.). Select "Separate file per layer" in Batch Mode for generating Gerber files. For advanced settings, such as leading/trailing zeroes, vector/raster, and absolute/relative, just use the same settings when configuring the NC Drill settings. Step 6 : Click "OK" to return to the "Generate output files" dialog box, and then click the "Configure" link next to "NC Drill Files". Configuring the following settings in the "NC Drill Setup" dialog box. Step 7 : Click "OK" and then close "NC Drill Setup" dialog box. Step 8 : Click "Generate" in the "Generate Output Files" dialog box. Step 9 : A dialog box shown as below will pop up after clicking "Generate", select "Save and Commit changes". Step 10 : Click "OK" in the "Save to Saver" dialog box poped up. Step 11 : Click the "Release" button in the "Generate output files" dialog box, which will save the generated files to the cloud. Step 12 : A window called "Confirm Release" will appear,write "Release Note" as needed and click "OK". A new window will show: Project has been released successfully, open in Web Browser. Step 13 : Click "open in Web Browser" which will open the published files in the web browser. Click "Show Files" to display the files and then click the download icon to download the Gerber and drill files. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Sheet Metal Cutting Design Guidelines Sheet Metal Cutting Design Guidelines by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Sheet Cutting This guide is designed to help engineers and designers prepare CAD and STEP files that meet manufacturing standards. Following these design requirements prior to order submission helps prevent file rejections, shorten lead times, and reduce overall manufacturing costs. Note: Material-specific values—including minimum hole size, internal radius, and thickness limits—vary by material and process. 1. File Formats & Submission Requirements Select the appropriate file format based on whether your part is flat or contains 3D forms/bends. Unsupported Formats Mesh Files: .stl, .obj, etc., are not accepted for flat/formed sheet cutting. Raster Images: .jpg, .png, .tif, .bmp, etc. All raster artwork must be converted to vector geometry prior to submission. 2. Vector & CAD File Cleaning A production file should contain only the closed cutting geometry required to manufacture the part. Clean all construction elements and annotations before exporting. Scale & Units 1:1 Scale: Build files at full final cut size. Written dimensions inside drawings are ignored by automated processing systems. Units: Imperial (inches) is preferred. Metric (millimeters) is acceptable when used consistently between the file and quote. Centimeters and meters are not supported. Manufacturing Geometry Only Remove all dimensions, title blocks, borders, guides, notes, and annotations. Convert Text to Outlines Convert all text to vector outlines (or explode/expand text in CAD). Editable fonts/text boxes cannot be recognized as cutting geometry. Closed Cutting Profiles Every cut path must form a fully closed shape. Inspect geometry in wireframe/outline mode before export to detect unclosed paths or tiny gaps. Duplicate & Overlapping Lines Delete duplicate, overlapping, or intersecting vector entities. In multi-entity geometry, duplicated lines can be interpreted as double-cutting paths and ruin cut quality. Dedicated Layer Usage Place all final cut paths on a designated cut layer. Move construction geometry or annotations to separate layers or delete them entirely prior to export. Bridging Floating Interiors Internal "islands" (e.g., the centers of letters like O, A, B, or donut-shaped cutouts) will become detached during cutting. Add bridges or stencil connections to retain them. Bridge width depends on material thickness. 3. Part Dimensions & Multi-Part Nesting Establish part envelopes and multi-part arrangements early to avoid sizing and production rejection issues. Part Size Limits Size limits vary by material and manufacturing process. CNC Routing Size Limits: ○ Minimal part size: 2mm (0.08in) ○ Maximal part size: 1000 mm (40in) ○ Minimal diameter: 0.3mm (0.01in) These are general size restrictions; the specific restrictions vary depending on the material. For details, please upload your file and wait for an engineer to review it to determine if it is acceptable. Multi-Part Ordering & Pre-Nesting Single File Upload (Recommended): For multiple copies of the same part, upload one file containing a single part and set the desired quantity at checkout. Pre-Nesting Rules: Pre-nested layouts are permitted only when: All parts share the same material and thickness. The file is a supported 2D vector format (.dxf, .dwg). Pre-nested 3D formats (.step/.stp/.iges/.igs/.sldprt) are not accepted. Bending, tapping, or hardware-inserted parts must be uploaded as individual single-part files. No Common-Line Nesting Do not share a cutting line between adjacent parts. Common-line cutting does not account for kerf, beam width, tool diameter, or stream width (which introduces a gap ranging from ~0.006″ to 0.012″ depending on material). Separate each part geometry according to process tolerance limits. Directional & Mirrored Materials Materials with distinct surface finishes (e.g., brushed ACM, mirrored acrylic, textured ABS, hardboard) require specific top/bottom orientation. Save mirrored variations as separate files when orientation matters. 4. Feature Design Tolerances & Limits Check hole sizes, internal corners, narrow walls, and cutout density against process limitations before finalizing artwork. Feature Limits Summary Narrow Walls & Isolated Features Extremely narrow walls or small isolated features tend to distort or overheat during cutting. Maintain minimum feature dimensions as specified for your target material and process. Dense Cutout Patterns Intricate patterns (e.g., grilles, speaker grates) increase cutting times and heat buildup, potentially causing warping or thermal marks in thin stock. If burn marks occur on fiber laser cut samples, increase the line/web thickness between cutouts. 5. Process-Specific Design Guidelines Selection of laser, waterjet, or CNC routing depends on material composition, stock thickness, and required edge quality. Laser Cutting Ideal for sheet metals, acrylic, and select boards. Mind the heat-affected zone (HAZ) and kerf allowance on small, intricate features. Waterjet Cutting Preferred for heat-sensitive or thick materials (composites, rubber, foam). Internal corner radii are constrained by the ~0.032″ waterjet stream diameter. CNC Routing CNC routing uses a rotating bit for flatbed cutting on materials like ACM, plastics, wood, and boards. 2D Flatbed Limitation: CNC routers perform 2D flatbed cut-throughs only. They cannot produce V-grooves, 3D surface contours, partial-depth cuts, double-sided cuts, or counterbores. Tapping and countersinking are handled via separate post-processing services. Dogbone Fillets for Square Corners: Because a rotating bit leaves an internal radius (min. 0.063″), a square peg will not seat flush into a standard routed pocket. Add dogbone fillets (corner over-cuts) to provide proper clearance for mating components. Standard chamfers do not eliminate the tool radius.\ Sizing Formula: Dogbone Diameter ≥ Tool Bit Diameter+ 0.005″(0.13mm) (Example: When routing with a standard 0.125″ bit, design your dogbone circles with a diameter of at least 0.130″.) Fixturing Tabs: Small perimeter tabs retain routed parts during cutting. ○Tab size: ~0.1875″ wide × 50% material thickness deep. ○Tabs are removed/sanded post-process and do not alter functional geometry. ○Edge geometry must allow at least 0.400″ spacing between vertex nodes for tab placement. Material Removal Limit: Do not remove more than 50% of total material on perforated or skeletal designs to prevent parts from shifting or breaking during routing. Edge Finish: Routed edges may display minor witness marks, steps, or friction discoloration. These are standard for the process and do not affect structural performance. 6. Formed & Bent Sheet Metal Parts When submitting parts that require bending, folding, or forming, follow true sheet-metal modeling rules. One Solid Body Per File Each .step or .stp file must contain exactly one solid sheet-metal body. Multi-body solids or assemblies cannot be processed within a single part file. Model True Sheet-Metal Geometry Use dedicated sheet-metal design tools in your CAD software. Extruded solids or mesh objects are not valid substitutes for sheet-metal bodies. Uniform Thickness & Simple Features Maintain uniform material thickness throughout the part. Include a flat edge face at every boundary. Do not model partial-depth features, tapered edges, or countersinks directly into the 3D model. Model simple through-holes only; specify secondary services (tapping, countersinks) during quoting. Reference Plane Alignment Align at least one major flat face parallel to a primary CAD reference plane to ensure accurate flat-pattern unfolding. Material Rules & Bend Parameters Apply a sheet-metal rule matching your target material thickness, bend radius, and K-factor. Mismatched bend parameters cause open-contour or flat-pattern export errors. STEP Export Verification Ensure the single sheet-metal body is selected before exporting. A file reading as 0″ × 0″ upon upload indicates an unselected body or missing solid geometry. Bending Geometric Guardrails (Keepout Zones) Placing holes or small features too close to a bend line will cause material stretching and feature distortion during die press braking. Follow these minimum spacing requirements: Hole-to-Bend Line Minimum Distance: Minimum Clearance= (2 × Material Thickness) + Bend Radius (Holes placed closer than this limit will deform into ovals during bending.) Minimum Flange Height (Bend Leg Length): Minimum Flange Length= 4 × Material Thickness (Flanges shorter than this limit cannot sit stably across the lower press brake die during forming.) Cutout Relief at Bends: When a cutout intersects a bend line, add bend relief slots extending at least 1× Material Thickness beyond the bend line on both sides to prevent material tearing. 7. Troubleshooting Common File Errors 8. Pre-Submission Checklist Verify the following before uploading your production file: File Format: Vector (.dxf, .dwg) for flat parts; 3D Solid (.step, .stp, .iges, .igs, .sldprt) for bent parts. Scale & Units: Created at 1:1 scale using consistent Inches or Millimeters. Clean Geometry: All dimensions, notes, construction lines, and borders removed. Text Outlined: All text converted to vector paths. Closed Paths: All cutting profiles form fully closed shapes. No Duplicate Lines: Overlapping and shared geometry removed. Islands Bridged: Floating interior cutouts connected with stencil bridges. Feature Limits: Hole diameters and internal radii satisfy selected process minimums. CNC Requirements: Dogbones added to internal square corners; material removal ≤ 50%. 3D Sheet Metal: Exactly one solid sheet-metal body per file with uniform thickness. Nesting Setup: Single part per file (no common-line cutting); separate directional or mirrored parts into distinct files. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Sheet Metal Tapping Design Guidelines Sheet Metal Tapping Design Guidelines by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Tapping This guideline aims to provide structural engineers and mechanical designers with Design for Manufacturability (DFM) specifications for thread tapping in sheet metal fabrication and CNC milling/turning processes. It helps designers effectively avoid tool chipping, thread stripping, bend deformation, and engineering question (EQ) delays during the design phase—thereby significantly improving the automated DFM review approval rate, eliminating redundant back-and-forth communication, and substantially reducing order lead times and processing schedules. 1. Key Sheet Metal Tapping Parameters In sheet metal cutting and CNC machining, tapping is a critical process that creates internal threads in pre-machined pilot holes to allow direct fastening with bolts and screws. Compared to traditional methods like adding clinching nuts (PEM Nuts) or using clearance holes with standard nuts, direct tapping significantly reduces the bill of materials (BOM), lowers assembly labor, and achieves exceptional surface flatness. Thread Engagement: The percentage of overlapping profile depth between the external and internal threads. Thread engagement directly determines the pull-out strength of the threaded connection and the difficulty of machining. Thread Pitch: The axial distance between corresponding points on adjacent thread teeth. Metric threads express this as pitch in millimeters (e.g., M4 × 0.7), while Imperial threads express it as threads per inch (TPI, e.g., 1/4-20). Tap Drill Size (Pilot Hole Diameter): The pre-drilled or laser-cut hole diameter prior to tapping. An undersized hole can cause tap breakage or binding, whereas an oversized hole results in insufficient thread height and stripped threads. 2. Thread Engagement & Geometric Calculations When designing tapped parts, avoid blindly striving for 100% thread height. Research and engineering practice demonstrate that a thread engagement of 60% to 75% provides 100% of the bolt's ultimate tensile strength; further increasing engagement exponentially increases cutting torque and tap breakage risks. Thread Engagement Formula Thread Engagement (%) = [ (D_major - D_hole) / (1.08253 × P) ] × 100% (Note: Major Thread Diameter D_major and Pilot Hole Diameter D_hole are in mm; Pitch P is in mm) Recommended Thread Engagement by Material Soft Materials (Aluminum 6061-T6, Copper, Engineering Plastics POM/PA): A 70% to 75% thread engagement is recommended to achieve higher shear strength. Hard Materials (Stainless Steel 304/316, Carbon Steel, Titanium Alloys): A 50% to 60% thread engagement is recommended to significantly reduce tool wear and work-hardening risks. Sheet Thickness to Engagement Depth Ratio The optimal effective thread engagement length should reach 1.0 to 1.5 times the nominal bolt diameter (e.g., the effective depth for an M4 thread should be between 4 mm and 6 mm). For thin sheet metal where the plate thickness is less than 1.0 times the thread diameter, extruded/flanged hole tapping processes can be used to extend engagement depth. 3. Sheet Metal vs. CNC Machining Tapping Guidelines Laser-cut sheet metal and solid CNC machined parts differ fundamentally in tapping processes and must follow distinct geometric constraints: 4. Core Sheet Metal Tapping DFM Rules Clearance from Bends and Features When placing tapped holes near sheet metal bend lines, tensile stresses during bending cause thread distortion, preventing proper bolt insertion. Bend Clearance Rule: The distance from the tapped hole center to the bend line must be ≥ (1/2 × Bend Die Opening Width + 2 × Sheet Thickness). Feature Clearance Rule: Tapped hole edges must maintain a distance of at least 1.5 × Sheet Thickness from other cut features (e.g., large cutouts, slots). Tool Clearance and Fixture Interference Automated tapping machines and CNC tapping heads require adequate clearance. If a tapped hole is close to high vertical walls or internal cavity corners, the tapping chuck will collide. Geometric Interference Warning: Ensure a cylindrical clearance area above the tapped hole axis with a radius of at least 20 mm and no height obstructions to allow unhindered spindle entry. Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ) & Thermal Expansion Compensation Strategy: Laser cutting creates a micro-hardened layer (HAZ) along the hole wall. To prevent this hardened layer from breaking taps, for aluminum alloys and carbon steel, it is recommended to enlarge the pilot hole in the CAD model by 0.05 mm to 0.08 mm (0.002" to 0.003") over standard pre-drilled sizes to compensate for thermal expansion, contraction, and tool wear. 5. Recommended Sheet Metal Tapping Drill Size Chart The table below lists common metric and imperial tap sizes along with their recommended pre-drilled hole diameters in 2D/3D models: 6. CAD File Preparation Model Setup: In 3D CAD (STEP) or 2D (DXF), do not model physical thread geometry! Draw smooth, plain cylindrical pilot holes. Modeling physical 3D threads causes CAM toolpath parsing errors. Diameter Identification: Set the hole diameter to be tapped to the target thread's nominal major diameter or standard tap drill size. Upon cloud system upload, intelligent algorithms will automatically identify and prompt tap assignment. Surface Finish Margins: If the part requires subsequent anodizing or powder coating, specify in advance on order notes: "Tap before anodizing" or request thread masking. 7. Pre-Manufacturing Checklist File Format Verification: 2D submitted in .dxf or .dwg (1:1 scale, free of overlapping or broken lines); 3D submitted as a single solid .step / .stp file. Smooth Pilot Holes: All holes intended for tapping are plain smooth cylinders without helical curves or 3D thread meshes. Thickness-to-Depth Ratio: Sheet metal thickness meets effective engagement requirements (if plate thickness < 1× Thread Diameter, PEM nuts or extruded tapping have been evaluated). Edge & Bend Clearance: Hole center to edge ≥ 2.0× Thread Diameter; hole center to bend line ≥ (1/2 × Die Opening Width + 2 × Sheet Thickness). Blind Hole Clearance (CNC): For CNC blind holes, the total drill depth extends at least 3× Pitch (3P) beyond the effective thread depth for chip relief. Perpendicularity Confirmation: All tapping axes are strictly perpendicular to their respective faces. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Threaded Holes in CNC Machining: Thread Types, Depth, and Design Tips Threaded Holes in CNC Machining: Thread Types, Depth, and Design Tips by: Mila Sep 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Tapping Threaded Holes CNC machined parts CNC Machining Threaded holes are widely used in CNC machined parts for fastening, assembly, and maintenance. From simple mounting holes to precision mechanical connections, properly designed threads help ensure reliable assembly and long-term performance. However, designing a threaded hole involves more than selecting a screw size. Thread type, tap drill diameter, hole depth, material, and machining method all affect the final result. This guide covers common thread types, machining methods, and essential CNC thread design guidelines to help you create parts that are easier to manufacture, inspect, and assemble. 1. What Are Threaded Holes? （Thread Nomenclature） A threaded hole is a hole with internal helical grooves designed to engage with an external thread, such as a bolt or screw. In CNC machining, internal threads are commonly produced through tapping or thread milling. Threaded holes allow components to be fastened without requiring a separate nut on the opposite side. They are widely used in machine housings, brackets, fixtures, enclosures, and precision mechanical components. Depending on the part geometry and assembly requirements, threaded holes can be classified into two main types. Blind Holes vs. Through Holes （Blind Holes vs. Through Holes） Through holes extend completely through the workpiece. They generally provide better chip evacuation and allow greater flexibility for tapping tools. However, the exit side may require deburring, and the entire hole length does not automatically need to be threaded. Blind holes terminate within the material and are commonly used when the opposite surface must remain intact or when a screw is installed from only one side. Blind threaded holes require more careful depth planning because the tapping tool needs additional space at the bottom of the hole. The drilled depth must account for the drill point, incomplete threads, and tool clearance. The choice between blind and through holes depends on the component geometry, available space, fastening requirements, and manufacturing method. 2. Common Thread Types for CNC Machining Different thread profiles and standards serve different applications. Selecting the right thread type ensures compatibility with fasteners and avoids unnecessary machining complexity. Metric and Unified Threads ISO Metric Threads (M) and Unified Threads (UNC/UNF) are widely used for mechanical fastening. Metric threads use a 60° thread profile and are specified by nominal diameter and pitch, such as M6 × 1.0. Unified threads are commonly used in North American applications and are specified by nominal diameter, threads per inch (TPI), and thread series. UNC (Unified National Coarse): Commonly used for general-purpose fastening. UNF (Unified National Fine): Used in applications requiring finer thread pitch or specific fastening characteristics. Metric and Unified threads should not be treated as interchangeable simply because their nominal diameters are similar. Always follow the thread standard specified by the mating component or engineering drawing. Pipe and Power Transmission Threads Pipe threads, such as NPT, NPTF, and BSP series, are used in fluid, gas, and piping connections. Their sealing requirements depend on the thread form, taper, and sealing method. Power transmission threads, including trapezoidal, square, and buttress threads, are designed for applications involving motion transmission or substantial axial loads. For general CNC machined parts, standard metric or Unified threads are usually sufficient. Specialized thread profiles should be specified when the application requires them. Coarse vs. Fine Threads Coarse threads have a larger pitch, while fine threads have a smaller pitch for the same nominal diameter. Coarse threads are commonly used for general fastening because they are practical for routine assembly and relatively tolerant of handling and minor contamination. Fine threads provide finer axial adjustment and, for comparable nominal diameters, may offer a larger tensile stress area. However, they require appropriate machining and inspection and can be more sensitive to thread damage. The choice depends on material, loading conditions, available engagement length, and the mating fastener. Thread pitch alone does not determine joint strength or resistance to loosening. For detailed thread profiles, standards, and specifications, refer to our CNC Thread Standards and Types Guide . 3. Tap Drill Sizes and Thread Hole Preparation Before cutting an internal thread, a hole must be drilled to the appropriate diameter. This is known as the tap drill hole. The tap drill diameter is smaller than the nominal thread diameter, leaving enough material to form the internal thread profile. If the hole is too large, the resulting thread may have insufficient engagement. If it is too small, tapping forces increase, potentially causing poor thread quality or tool breakage. How to Calculate Tap Drill Diameter For standard ISO metric threads, a commonly used preliminary estimate for cutting taps is: Tap drill diameter ≈ Major diameter − Pitch For example, an M6 × 1.0 thread has a nominal diameter of 6 mm and a pitch of 1.0 mm. 6 − 1.0 = 5.0 mm. A 5.0 mm drill is therefore a common starting point for an M6 × 1.0 internal thread. This formula is a practical estimate, not a substitute for standard tap drill tables. The appropriate hole diameter depends on the thread standard, required thread engagement, material, tolerance, and tapping method. Form taps also require different hole preparation because they displace material rather than remove it. For actual machining, always refer to the recommended tap drill size for the specified thread and material. See our CNC Thread Tap Drill Size Chart for detailed metric, Unified, and pipe thread dimensions. Prepare the Hole Entrance Before tapping, the hole entrance is often chamfered to remove burrs and provide a smoother entry for the tap or fastener. A suitable chamfer can help guide the tool into the hole and improve fastener assembly. However, an excessively large chamfer reduces the available full thread length near the entrance. For CNC machined parts, the chamfer should be appropriate for the thread size, fastener geometry, and assembly requirements. If the entrance geometry is critical, specify it in the engineering drawing. 4. How to Create Threaded Holes CNC threaded holes are commonly produced through drilling followed by tapping or thread milling. The appropriate method depends on thread size, material, hole geometry, production quantity, and required accuracy. Step 1: Drill the Tap Hole The first step is to drill a hole to the recommended tap drill diameter. The hole must be large enough for the selected threading method while leaving sufficient material to form the required thread profile. For blind holes, the drilled depth must exceed the required effective thread depth to accommodate the drill point, incomplete threads, and necessary tool clearance. Step 2: Select the Appropriate Tap Tapping uses a cutting or forming tool to produce internal threads in a prepared hole. Common cutting tap types include: These taps differ mainly in their lead geometry and ability to form threads near the bottom of a hole. A bottoming tap does not eliminate the need for clearance at the bottom of a blind hole. Actual tool suitability depends on the tap design, thread size, material, and machining conditions. Cutting taps remove material to form the thread profile. Forming taps displace material without producing conventional cutting chips and are suitable for certain ductile materials when the hole diameter and material conditions are appropriate. Step 3: Consider Thread Milling （thread milling internal hole） Thread milling uses a rotating milling cutter to generate the thread profile through a controlled toolpath. Compared with conventional tapping, thread milling can provide greater flexibility for different thread diameters and may offer better control over thread dimensions through toolpath adjustments. It can also be useful for certain large-diameter, deep, or specialized threads. In suitable machining setups, it can reduce the risk of a broken tap becoming trapped in a workpiece. However, thread milling may require more programming and machining time, particularly for simple standard threads in high-volume production. The final method should be selected according to the part geometry, material, thread specifications, and production requirements. 5. CNC Thread Design Guidelines Good CNC thread design considers tool access, material strength, hole geometry, and the intended assembly. The following guidelines help reduce machining difficulty and improve the reliability of threaded components. Thread Engagement and Hole Depth （thread depth vs drill depth） Thread engagement length is the actual length over which the internal and external threads engage. It is different from the total drilled depth. For blind holes, distinguish between effective thread depth and total drill depth. The drilled depth should allow for the drill point, incomplete threads, and necessary tool clearance. A thread engagement length of approximately 1 to 1.5 times the nominal diameter is sometimes used as an initial guideline for metal fastening applications. For an M6 thread, this corresponds to approximately 6–9 mm of engagement. However, this is not a universal strength requirement. The required length depends on the workpiece material, fastener strength, loading conditions, and the risk of internal thread stripping. Softer materials, high loads, and repeated assembly may require a different design. Where joint strength is critical, calculate the required engagement rather than relying solely on a diameter ratio. Ensure Adequate Tool Access and Edge Distance Threaded holes should be positioned where drilling and tapping tools can approach the surface properly. Holes located on angled or curved surfaces may require a suitable flat or machined seating surface to ensure consistent tool entry and proper fastener seating. Also, avoid placing threaded holes too close to part edges, thin walls, or adjacent features. Insufficient surrounding material can weaken the component and make machining more difficult. The required edge distance and wall thickness depend on the thread diameter, material, loading conditions, and part geometry. There is no single minimum distance suitable for every application. Consider Material and Surface Finishing Different materials have different machining characteristics and thread strength. Aluminum alloys are generally machinable, but internal threads may be more susceptible to stripping under high loads or repeated assembly. For plastic components or parts requiring frequent disassembly, threaded inserts may provide a more durable fastening interface. Surface treatments also require attention. Anodizing, powder coating, and other coatings can affect thread fit and clearance. Where necessary, specify whether threaded holes should be masked during finishing or receive post-processing. For critical threaded features, consider the effect of the coating thickness on the required fit and inspection. 6. CNC Threads vs. 3D Printed Threads CNC machining and 3D printing can both produce threaded features, but their design considerations differ. CNC machined metal threads are commonly produced through tapping or thread milling and can be specified according to established thread standards. In 3D printing, thread quality depends more heavily on printing technology, material, layer orientation, and feature resolution. Threaded inserts may be useful for plastic parts that require repeated assembly. When designing parts that combine CNC machined and 3D printed components, consider thread compatibility, tolerances, material behavior, and assembly loads. For more information on printed threads, inserts, and mechanical joints, see our guide to Designing Threads, Inserts & Joints for 3D Printing . Conclusion Successful CNC thread design starts with selecting the appropriate thread standard, specifying the correct tap drill size, and allowing sufficient space for machining and fastener engagement. Clear engineering drawings and practical design decisions can help reduce machining risks, improve assembly reliability, and avoid unnecessary manufacturing costs. Verify Now Blog > Welded Sheet Metal Parts Design Guidelines Welded Sheet Metal Parts Design Guidelines by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Welding This guide is designed to help mechanical engineers and product designers optimize laser-cut and bent sheet metal parts for welding processes. By adhering to Design for Manufacturability (DFM) standards during the CAD modeling stage, you can significantly enhance structural strength, eliminate thermal distortion, reduce assembly tooling costs, and shorten production lead times. 1. Allowed and Recommended Weld Joint Types To ensure the mechanical strength of weld joints and effectively control heat input, we recommend using the following two standardized joint configurations: Corner Weld Two bent edges meet at a 90° right angle. Outside Corner Weld (Recommended): The welding torch is applied to the outside of the corner joint, yielding superior penetration, better fill, and a fuller weld appearance. Inside Corner Weld: The welding torch is applied to the inside concave corner, suitable for applications with external assembly interference where weld protrusions are not permitted. T-Joint Weld One bent edge meets perpendicularly with the flat surface of another extending flange. Also divided into Inside Fillet Weld and Outside Fillet Weld. T-Joints offer excellent shear strength and are ideal for stiffeners, gussets, or baffle structures. Unsupported Weld Types: Butt welds, lap welds, spot welds, stitch welds, and complex multi-part assembly welds are currently not available for standardized automated online quoting and processing, and require manual engineering review. 2. CAD Modeling & Design Rules "Design for Bending First" Principle All welded parts must first satisfy standard sheet metal bending specifications. Design should complete 3D bend modeling first, as welding is a secondary process performed after bending. Always check clearance for bending tooling to prevent welding flanges from obstructing the bending stroke. Do NOT Model Weld Geometry Never draw fillet welds, weld beads, or weld cutouts in your CAD model. The model must reflect true, un-welded sheet metal bend geometry. The factory CAM system will automatically calculate weld compensation and joint normalization based on the selected material and thickness. Bend Reliefs and Unsealed Corners Laser welding is primarily used for structural connection and positioning alignment; it does not guarantee watertight or gastight seals. Bend relief gaps and open bend seams will not be automatically filled. If sealing is required, post-process sealant must be applied or manual full-fill grinding specified. 3. Innovative Features: Fixtureless Self-Alignment & Thermal Control Structures To eliminate reliance on expensive welding fixtures and resolve thermal distortion issues in thin sheet metal welding, this guide introduces the following innovative DFM techniques: Tab-and-Slot Self-Alignment Design Incorporate interlocking tabs and slots directly into mating parts during the laser cutting phase. Engineering Advantage: Parts achieve precise interlocking alignment without fixtures, eliminating cumulative assembly errors and manual measurement setup time. Design Rule: Tab width is recommended to be 3x to 5x the sheet thickness, with a unilateral clearance allowance of 0.1mm~0.15mm. Integrated Locating Holes and Alignment Pins Place laser-cut locating holes（3.0mm~5.0mm）on non-welded datum surfaces to accept standard dowel/spring pins or locating bolts. This improves high-volume assembly consistency and serves as a inspection measurement datum. Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ) Relief Cuts & Anti-Distortion Design Thin sheet metal welding (e.g., 1.5mm aluminum alloy) is prone to "oil-canning" or wave distortion due to localized thermal expansion. Stress Relief Slots: Incorporate elongated stress-relief slots in non-load-bearing areas adjacent to the weld to block thermal stress propagation across large flat surfaces. Pulsed Laser Welding: Utilizing pulsed laser welding reduces the heat-affected zone to only 1/5 that of traditional TIG/MIG welding, drastically reducing residual stress while producing a visually appealing "stack-of-dimes" surface finish. 4. Finished Appearance, Delivery Expectations, and Post-Processing 5. Design Checklist Please review and verify the following items prior to order submission or production release: CAD Model Specification: Correct bending parameters have been applied to the part model, and no 3D weld beads or fillets have been modeled. Root Gap: The assembly gap (root gap) at the target weld joint is controlled within 0.020'' （0.5mm） in CAD. Self-Alignment Features: Tab-and-slot features or locating holes have been prioritized to reduce assembly and fixture alignment difficulty. Torch Clearance: Weld locations avoid complex multi-bend intersections or tight internal enclosures, ensuring adequate torch accessibility and line of sight. Coating Allowance: If powder coating or anodizing is required later, coating thickness allowances have been factored into mating tolerances (e.g., adding 0.05~0.1mm per side for powder coat). Verify Now Blog > How to Generate BOM and Centroid File in Eagle How to Generate BOM and Centroid File in Eagle by: PCBWay Jan 11,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Help Center In Eagle, we usually find that the file format is often confusing when using the normal way to export BOM and Centroid files. To solve the problem, this article will introduce how to export correctly formatted BOM and Centroid files by using ULP. First of all, download the ULP on your computer: https://pcbwayfile.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/msgfile/23/01/11/1457344260842.zip Generate Controid file: Click ULP Then find Browse... Choose eagle_smt.ulp Click Save and the Centroid file will be generated automatically. Generate BOM file: The initial step to generate BOM file is similar to that for Centroid file. Switch to the Schematics page, click ULP -> Browse... But remember to choose eagle_bom.ulp this time. Make sure to choose Values , CSV and , The output result is a BOM file in csv format. Finished. Verify Now Blog > How to Place PCBWay Orders from Online 3D Viewer Directly？ How to Place PCBWay Orders from Online 3D Viewer Directly？ by: PCBWay Jan 13,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Help Center Online 3D Viewer ( https://3dviewer.net/ ) is popular among 3D Printing hobbyists for its simple page and excellent viewing capabilities. For the convenience of all, we have good news: PCBWay has partnered with Online 3D Viewer to include a built-in plugin that allows designers to place PCBWay orders directly from the viewer. This article is going to show the steps: 1. Enter Online 3D Viewer and open your file. 2. Find the icon indicated by the arrow and click it. 3. Click Print and enter PCBWay. 4. Select the appropriate parameters according to the specific needs of the project, and the system will conduct a rough quotation. 5. Click Submit Request , the staff will give a final price based on the parts to be printed and the parameters selected. 6. Finished. PCBWay has always been committed to providing customers with better services. In the future, we will also work hard to reach cooperation with more software and practice the goal of one-stop service. Verify Now Blog > How to Use Payoneer to Pay for Orders How to Use Payoneer to Pay for Orders by: Mila Jan 13,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Help Center PCBWay now supports Payoneer as a payment method for your orders. Payoneer is a secure and convenient way to pay for your orders. This guide will walk you through the steps to complete your payment quickly and safely. Instructions： 1. On the order page, select “Payoneer” as the payment method and click “Place Order.” A awaiting payment order package will be created. 2. Our sales representative will send you a Payoneer payment link via email. If you do not receive it, please contact your sales representative or find their contact in the top-right corner of your account page. 3. Click the payment link to go to the Payoneer payment page. If you are a new user, you will need to sign up for a Payoneer account before making the payment. 4. During registration, verify that the order number is correct and create your payer account password. 5. Click “Add Payment Method” and enter your credit card information to add the card. 6. Use your credit card to pay for the request and you can track the payment status of each payment request. 7. After the payment is completed, our finance team will verify whether the payment has been received. Once confirmed, your sales representative will help finalize the payment for the order package, and production will begin. If you have any questions, please contact your sales representative or online Live Chat. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Join us Wanna be a dedicated PCBWay writer? We definately look forward to having you with us. Verify Now Blog > When vibration meets LoRa (and bandwidth fights back) When vibration meets LoRa (and bandwidth fights back) by: Engineer Sep 22,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Technology Micropython Meshtastic Custom PCB Vibration sensor Summary： Using off the shelf hardware to measure vibration and transmit using LoRa. Here we are again. I’ve been working on a little clandestine project, I can’t fully name. Who is it for? The real application? What I can talk about is the tech. It’s a sensor project over a wireless protocol. Pretty standard for me. The short version: environment readings and vibration measurement using Meshtastic and LoRa. Completely enclosed local environment with web sockets, no cloud involvement at all. Before we get into the firmware wars, Let me tell you about what hardware I am using. The base platform I built the node around RAK Wireless WisBlock gear (ordered through Rokland): RAK4631 — Nordic nRF52840 BLE core + LoRa SX1262 RAK19007 — WisBlock Base Board 2nd Gen RAK1921 — WisBlock OLED display RAK1904 — 3-axis acceleration sensor For sensitivity tuning I needed an I²C rotary encoder. Adafruit’s STEMMA QT Rotary Encoder Breakout was one of the few low-cost I²C options that did exactly what I needed. Solid docs, worked flawlessly. A word of caution here, RAKWireless sells an I2C rotary encoder as well, but it is not compatible with the 3-axis sensor. I could get either one to work, but not both. I believe they must share an interrupt, that is my theory. I tried moving the 3-axis sensor to another slot, same problem. So, I went with the Adafruit rotary encoder instead. It has an added bonus of having a Neopixel mounted on the board which comes in handy later. Since the rotary encoder and OLED both use the I2C bus, I designed a small PCB to mount both and attach to the main board with JST connectors. (I hate JST connectors so much, I ended up just soldering wires from the boards because I just struggle with crimping the pins. Maybe someone smarter than this dumb hillbilly, with more patience, can tell me what I am doing wrong) Anyhoo.. Here is the board I designed to hold the OLED and the rotary encoder. The software (and the headaches) Architecture-wise, the node collects temperature, humidity, pressure, air quality, and vibration, then sends that data using Meshtastic over LoRa to a LoRa-to-Ethernet gateway that I built. Maybe another blog post on that one soon. The LoRa to Ethernet gateway forwards packets to a websocket on a NodeRed server. Sensor nodes stay mesh-connected so delivery stays reliable. Everything lives in one closed environment — nodes, collection, retention. Nothing over the internet. No cloud. 100% local and encrypted. Meshtastic’s built-in encryption is a nice bonus. Less time spent worrying about who might be listening in and really easy to configure. The problem Meshtastic is great but, there are limitations and they make perfect sense. The biggest one is bandwidth. LoRa means each node only gets to send a little data at a time. That’s fine for periodic temperature updates or a simple state change. Not so fine for data streaming. Everyone shares the airwaves. One chatty node can drown out the rest. For temp, humidity, pressure, and air quality, that’s easy, dial the transmit interval so everybody gets a turn. The standard environmental transmission interval is 15-30 minutes in the stock firmware. I changed that interval to 2 minutes in the firmware. This is a closed system; I only care what my nodes are saying. A note of caution though, if you make all the nodes talk a lot, you limit the number of nodes you can have on the mesh, in theory. Vibration is different. How do you capture vibration from multiple sources, get it across the mesh, and store it without chewing through all the bandwidth? The iterations I went through several versions. Some worked. Some taught me things the hard way. Attempt 1: The firehose. Stream live vibration data. One sensor was fine. Two sent too much data and consumed all the bandwidth, overloading the gateway. It listens for packets, then forwarded them serially to the web socket. I needed a faucet, not a firehose. Lesson one: don’t pour a lake through a straw. Attempt 2: Duty-cycled sampling. Stream for a few seconds, rest, stream, rest. Fine if you care about long-term trends. I wanted short-term anomalies too — What if i wanted to know if a truck was rolling past the house, or the dogs going full gladiator with a toy. Lesson two: selective data, not just less data. Attempt 3: Baseline + sensitivity. If the thing is already vibrating, what counts as an anomaly? You need a baseline. I set the firmware to wait 30 seconds after boot (so power-on bumps don’t poison the sample), then it collects ambient vibration for 30 seconds and builds a baseline. I used that baseline to compare any readings, used the rotary encoder to set sensitivity (how much above or below baseline is an actual anomaly?) and send 5 packets per anomaly with a 1ms wait between the packets. Below you can see the initial “bump”, then it goes back to almost normal for the remaining 4 packets. This should tell me if there are any resonant frequencies caused by the vibration over time. We will see though. More testing is needed here. The RAK1904 is a 3-axis accelerometer measuring force in G’s. Range and sample rate both matter when sampling. The sensor has several settings for how it measures force. After the usual loop of fail → fail → finally works, I landed on a 2g range setting (about 4 mg to trigger) and a high sample rate so quick spikes don’t get missed. (See my resonant frequency statement above) Slight variations still showed up in the baseline. At this point I was just reading X, Y, Z G-force though. I summed the three axes (X+Y+Z) and converted to an RMS-style reading (using 2 mm/s2), which gave me a baseline RMS with a peak. I also added a function where a single out of range sample doesn’t fire on a reading over peak, it wants two consecutive events which is more real world. A vibration doesn’t happen in one direction, see Newtons law. This sampling method is used so a random blip doesn’t spam the mesh. I could see this happening if the power was not clean so, wanted to assure that only real movement generated triggers. The firmware sends five consecutive readings using custom protobufs inside Meshtastic. I found that there are a bunch of unused protobufs set aside for “custom” work like this. So, I set the protobuf to 255. That way I can filter the data coming into the web socket (after decryption) by what protobuf it was using and that would tell me what was vibration data. Easy filtering into a NodeRed flow.. The rotary encoder adjusts sensitivity between about 0.5 and 15 mm/s², and the OLED shows the sensitivity setting you’re using/changing to. I setup the Neopixel to flash red on boot, until the baseline is complete. Once complete, the Neopixel changes to a solid green (armed, ready and sensing). When it is triggered, the Neopixel changes to a flashing blue. After it sends the data and the cooldown period, it changes back to green (armed) I have some real world testing to do, but I believe the sensor ready to be deployed. I am capturing data currently sending it to a local database and using Grafana to review the data. Here are some images of everything put together in a custom 3D printed enclosure. I used Fusion to design the enclosure and 3D printed in PLA for the prototype. Here we are again. I’ve been working on a little clandestine project, I can’t fully name. Who is it for? The real application? What I can talk about is the tech. Adafruit’s STEMMA QT Rotary Encoder Breakout was one of the few low-cost I²C options that did exactly what I needed. Solid docs, worked flawlessly. I believe they must share an interrupt, that is my theory. I tried moving the 3-axis sensor to another slot, same problem. So, I went with the Adafruit rotary encoder instead. It has an added bonus of having a Neopixel mounted on the board which comes in handy later. Since the rotary encoder and OLED both use the I2C bus, I designed a small PCB to mount both and attach to the main board with JST connectors. (I hate JST connectors so much, I ended up just soldering wires from the boards because I just struggle with crimping the pins. Meet the Winners of PCBWay's 12th Badge Design Contest Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity.
