FDM represents a process classification recognized within industry standards to define extrusion-based printing that relies on controlled thermal input, coordinated motion systems, and sequential layer deposition to convert digital toolpaths into physical geometry. The term refers directly to filament deposition, thermal bonding, and stacked layers, which are fundamental principles of desktop material extrusion 3D printers. What is the Full Form of FDM in 3D Printing? The full form of FDM in 3D printing is Fused Deposition Modeling, a material extrusion technology classified under additive manufacturing. FDM describes a process in which solid thermoplastic filament is fed into a temperature-controlled nozzle, transitions into a molten or semi-molten state, and is extruded in sequential layers to construct three-dimensional objects from digital design data. FDM gained widespread adoption in desktop and industrial 3D printing due to a mechanically simple system design, predictable thermoplastic behavior, and a layer-by-layer fabrication method that clearly links digital toolpaths to physical part geometry. Is FDM the same as Fused Deposition Modeling? Yes, FDM is the same as Fused Deposition Modeling in 3D printing, where FDM serves as the standard abbreviation for the full technical term. Fused Deposition Modeling describes a material extrusion additive manufacturing process that builds three-dimensional parts through controlled deposition of heated thermoplastic in sequential layers. Fused Deposition Modeling appears consistently in professional and consumer contexts because FDM is an industry-recognized abbreviation formalized through technical documentation, standards usage, and long term adoption within additive manufacturing workflows. How Does FDM Work? FDM works by heating solid thermoplastic filament and depositing the material along precise paths to construct parts layer by layer. FDM begins when a drive mechanism feeds filament into a temperature-controlled nozzle, where thermal energy softens the polymer and coordinated motion systems extrude a continuous bead onto the build surface following digital toolpaths. The layers of FDM are formed by cooling and diffusion, which allows interlayer bonding. Incremental vertical movement builds three-dimensional geometry with mechanical performance influenced by layer height, extrusion width, and deposition sequence. What is the FDM 3D Printing Process? The FDM 3D printing process converts a digital design into a physical object through controlled material extrusion and sequential layering. FDM begins with a CAD model that is sliced into horizontal layers, producing machine instructions that define extrusion paths, motion coordinates, and process parameters. FDM proceeds when thermoplastic filament is fed into a temperature-controlled nozzle, extruded along programmed toolpaths, and deposited in successive layers, where controlled cooling and thermal diffusion enable interlayer bonding until the complete three-dimensional geometry is formed. What are the Working Principles of FDM? The working principles of FDM are listed below. Filament Heating : Solid thermoplastic filament enters a heated nozzle where temperature rises above the polymer melting range, enabling controlled viscous flow without chemical transformation. Material Extrusion : Pressurized filament extrudes through a calibrated nozzle opening, producing a continuous bead whose width depends on nozzle diameter, extrusion rate, layer height, and deposition speed. Toolpath Deposition : Motion systems guide the nozzle along predefined paths generated from sliced digital models, placing material in controlled horizontal patterns. Thermal Bonding : Deposited material transfers heat into the previous layer, allowing molecular diffusion and polymer chain entanglement across layer interfaces that form interlayer adhesion during controlled cooling. Layer Solidification : Cooling stabilizes each deposited layer while incremental vertical movement repositions the nozzle for subsequent layers, allowing cumulative layer stacking to produce the final three-dimensional geometry. Can FDM print complex 3D shapes? Yes, FDM can print complex 3D shapes within defined mechanical, thermal, and material constraints. FDM achieves geometric complexity through controlled extrusion paths, fine layer heights, and coordinated motion systems that reproduce curved surfaces, enclosed cavities, and detailed external features. FDM faces limitations with steep overhangs and unsupported spans because molten thermoplastic requires structural support during deposition. Support structures increase post processing requirements and affect surface finish, while material stiffness and thermal behavior constrain minimum feature size and bridge length. Printer resolution, nozzle diameter, layer height, cooling efficiency, toolpath strategy, and material selection collectively define the level of geometric complexity achievable through FDM printing. Industrial FDM Printers : Industrial FDM printers support large build volumes, extended duty cycles, and high-temperature extrusion systems, with many configurations incorporating heated chambers for tooling, fixtures, and end-use manufacturing. Large-Format FDM Printers : Large-format FDM printers extend industrial scale extrusion with oversized build volumes for molds, jigs, fixtures, and architectural components. High-Temperature FDM Printers : High-temperature FDM printers support advanced thermoplastics (PEEK, PEKK, ULTEM) through reinforced frames, high-temperature hotends, and actively heated build environments. Continuous Fiber FDM Systems : Continuous fiber FDM systems integrate continuous carbon fiber, glass fiber, or aramid reinforcement during extrusion to increase part strength and stiffness. Pellet-Fed FDM Printers : Pellet-fed FDM printers replace filament with thermoplastic pellets, enabling higher deposition rates and lower material cost for large-scale parts. Hybrid FDM Systems : Hybrid FDM systems combine extrusion-based additive manufacturing with Computer Numerical Control (CNC0 machining or secondary processes to improve dimensional accuracy and surface finish. Multi-Axis FDM Systems : Multi-axis FDM systems use additional rotational axes to reduce support requirements and improve mechanical performance through nonplanar layer deposition. Hotend : Hotend applies heat to melt thermoplastic and guides the molten material through a calibrated nozzle to form consistent extrusion beads. Heated Bed : Heated bed maintains controlled surface temperature to promote first-layer adhesion and reduce thermal distortion during printing. Motion System : The motion system uses linear rails, belts, or lead screws to position the nozzle and build platform according to commanded coordinates with repeatable motion control. Stepper Motors : Stepper motors provide incremental rotational motion for extrusion, horizontal travel, and vertical layer positioning through controlled step sequences. Controller Board : The controller board interprets digital instructions and coordinates heaters, motors, and sensors to execute the programmed printing process. Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) : ABS provides higher impact resistance and improved heat resistance compared to PLA, supporting enclosures, housings, and functional components when printed under controlled thermal conditions. Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol (PETG) : PETG combines strength, moderate flexibility, and chemical resistance, supporting mechanical parts and containers with improved moisture resistance. Nylon (Polyamide) : Nylon delivers high toughness, wear resistance, and fatigue strength, supporting gears, bearings, and load-bearing components under repeated stress. Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) : TPU exhibits elasticity and abrasion resistance, supporting seals, gaskets, and flexible mechanical assemblies. Carbon Fiber Reinforced Filaments : Carbon fiber reinforced filaments increase stiffness and dimensional stability through chopped fiber reinforcement, supporting lightweight structural parts and tooling. Glass Fiber Reinforced Filaments : Glass fiber reinforced filaments improve stiffness and heat deflection performance, supporting fixtures and mechanically stressed components. Are all FDM printers suitable for beginners? No, not all FDM printers are suitable for beginners because machine complexity, material handling, and setup requirements vary widely. Beginner-friendly printers feature simple assembly, intuitive interfaces, and reliable auto-leveling or calibration systems, which reduce errors and learning time. Entry-level FDM printers are low-cost, support open filament systems, and offer moderate build volumes, making them suitable for education, hobbyist projects, and initial prototyping. Advanced FDM printers for professional or industrial use feature high-temperature nozzles, enclosed chambers, dual extrusion, and complex software controls, requiring operator experience for effective use. Reliability, ease of use, and affordability distinguish beginner models from advanced systems, guiding selection based on user skill and application requirements. How Does Xometry Handle Quality Control and Testing for FDM-Manufactured Parts? Xometry handles quality control and testing for FDM-manufactured parts by enforcing rigorous monitoring and inspection throughout production to ensure part reliability and precision. Xometry’s quality assurance framework includes structured oversight of print parameters (temperature, layer height, and print speed) to maintain consistent accuracy and dimensional fidelity during FDM production. The company partners with certified manufacturers and applies engineering checks before printing to confirm material suitability and process readiness, verifying that thermoplastic filaments comply with performance and application requirements. Xometry performs post-production inspections to evaluate surface finish, dimensional accuracy, and proper support removal under controlled quality assurance procedures after printing. The structured approach to quality control and testing ensures FDM parts produced through Xometry meet performance requirements and customer expectations for additive manufacturing output. What Are the Health and Safety Concerns Associated With Fused Deposition Modeling? The health and safety concerns associated with Fused Deposition Modeling are related to material emissions, chemical exposure, and thermal hazards during printing and post-processing. The melting of thermoplastic filaments through the nozzle can release volatile organic compounds, with higher emission levels from ABS and composite filaments, creating inhalation risks during operation. Post-processing using chemicals, including acetone for smoothing or finishing, introduces additional hazards for operators handling printed parts. Microscopic particles from polymers and additives (ceramic, composite, and metal) may be released during extrusion, potentially causing respiratory issues with prolonged exposure. Accidental contact with the hot nozzle or heated bed poses burn hazards, making enclosed safety chambers, adequate ventilation, and personal protective equipment essential for safe FDM operation. What Are Examples of Fused Deposition Modeling? The examples of fused deposition modeling are listed below. Personalized Prosthetic Limbs : FDM-produced prosthetic devices tailored to the patient's anatomy, for functional prototypes or low-stress applications requiring improved fit and basic functionality. Custom Jigs, Fixtures, and Tools : Manufacturing aids created to support assembly, alignment, and production processes. Functional Accessories : Items such as phone cases, holders, and other practical devices created with durable thermoplastic materials. Anatomical Models : Medical training models representing organs, bones, and systems for educational purposes. Geological Formations : Scaled FDM models of terrain and geological structures for research, teaching, and visualization purposes. Educational Aids : Learning tools that illustrate engineering principles, mechanical systems, or scientific concepts. Dental Models : FDM-printed training aids for dental education and prototype appliances, supporting practice and design verification rather than final certified devices. Automotive Components : Car parts and accessories, including prototypes, brackets, and custom fittings. Housings : Enclosures for devices or machinery, providing protection and structural support. Electronic Devices : Functional components or casings for consumer electronics, sensors, and prototypes. What Is the Difference Between Fused Deposition Modeling and Stereolithography? The difference between Fused Deposition Modeling and Stereolithography is in materials, printing process, accuracy, and cost. FDM extrudes melted thermoplastic filaments through a nozzle, depositing material layer by layer to build parts, resulting in moderate resolution and visible layer lines. Stereolithography uses liquid photopolymer resin cured by ultraviolet light to form solid layers, producing parts with higher resolution and smoother surfaces. SLA may require more safety precautions (handling uncured resin, alcohol wash, UV curing), and resins can be more expensive than common FDM filaments. The choice between FDM and SLA depends on the required surface quality, precision, cost constraints, and intended application of the printed parts. What Is the Difference Between Fused Deposition Modeling and Selective Laser Sintering? The difference between Fused Deposition Modeling and Selective Laser Sintering is in materials, printing process, part detail, and cost. Fused Deposition Modeling extrudes melted thermoplastic filaments through a nozzle, depositing material layer by layer, producing moderate surface detail and visible layer lines. Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) uses a high-powered laser to sinter powdered polymers within a powder bed, enabling complex geometries without the need for support structures. Metals and ceramics require specialized additive processes. FDM is more cost-effective and suited for rapid prototyping and functional parts with simpler geometries, whereas SLS supports intricate and dense designs but requires higher-cost equipment, materials, and post-processing to remove excess powder. The differences make FDM ideal for accessible prototyping and general part production, while SLS is suitable for advanced designs requiring strength, detail, and support-free geometries. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / Understanding Lattice Structure for 3D Printing Understanding Lattice Structure for 3D Printing Written by Joel Schadegg Updated by Greg Paulsen 5 min read Published October 12, 2021 Updated September 3, 2026 One of the most impressive characteristics of 3D printing is the ability to manufacture parts with complex internal lattice structures that would be impossible with traditional manufacturing techniques. What is a Lattice Structure for 3D printing? Simply put, a lattice structure for 3D printing is a repeating or non-repeating 3-dimensional assemblage of connected nodes. In its simplest form, multiple lattice nodes get connected to one another by beams. In the case of a repeating 3D structure, the collection of beams and nodes take on regular and repeating 3D shapes such as cubes or tetrahedrons. These shapes are often referred to as cells. The shape and density of these cells will determine how the part behaves when loads are applied. A 3D printed lattice structure makes optimal use of both material and the printer’s unique capabilities by only putting mass where it is structurally necessary. The overall item is thus significantly lighter than if it would be if completely solid. This is one reason why lattice structures are very common in the natural world. For many years this principle could only be implemented on large-scale constructions like steel buildings. However, with the advent and growing accessibility of 3D printing, it has become possible to create smaller and more mundane parts and products with internal lattice structures of their own. It can be done both for mechanical strength and aesthetic appeal. This method significantly reduces the mass of a part and has almost endless applications in the aerospace and automotive industries where reduced mass directly translates to improved fuel efficiency. Generating Lattice Structures Due to the complexity of lattice structures, it is impractical to model them into the part using typical CAD tools. In most cases, the part is drawn in CAD as if it were solid. Then, after the part has been designed (with DFAM principles in mind) the model is imported into another software package to generate a lattice structure. Among the more common programs for this purpose are Netfabb or nTopology. Another method of generating a 3D printed lattice structure is through generative design. In this case, a part’s connection points, mass limitations, and expected loads are defined. An algorithm then generates hundreds of solutions that would meet the requirements. From there, the most optimal lattice cell structure and cell density can be selected from among the solutions or generated through further iteration. When creating a lattice structure, it’s important to understand what factors will affect the overall function of the final part. These factors are listed below: Lattice Material: When 3D printing in metal , the lattice is often the same material as the overall part. However, if a flexible lattice is required then multi-material parts can be considered. Some products use soft flexible materials for the lattice and more resilient material as a shell to protect the lattice. One common example of this is a running shoe sole. Lattice Structure: The most basic 3D printed lattice structures feature repeating and uniform patterns throughout the entire part. However, more advanced methods will vary the cell and beam structure to be denser in areas that need additional strength and keep the lattice less dense in areas that experience less loading. The individual shape of the cells also has a significant effect on part performance since different structures will have different mechanical properties. Cell Orientation: The orientation of individual cells in a 3D printed lattice structure can affect the complexity of the print. For example, it is best practice to orient the cells in such a way that they can support themselves during the printing process itself without the need for support structures. Attempting to remove supports from hundreds of small cells is not advised. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Lattice 3D print with DMLS Benefits of Lattice Structures Lattice structures for 3D printing offer a wide range of benefits. Some of the most important are listed below. Reduced part cost: Depending on the material, 3D printing can be an expensive process. This is especially the case with materials like titanium or inconel that are common in the aerospace industry. The introduction of a lattice structure means that less material will be used, thus making the part cheaper overall without sacrificing structural integrity. Improved strength-to-weight ratio: If designed according to accepted DFAM (Design for Additive Manufacturing) principles, parts with lattice structures can have unparalleled strength-to-weight ratios. This makes them ideal in automotive and aerospace applications (among others) in which it’s critical to minimize mass. Shock absorption: Lattice structures are extremely efficient at dissipating impact and shock loads because the cell configuration helps the whole construction flex and disburse energy. Some lightweight lattices can effectively stop bullets. Increased surface area: Some applications focus on maximizing surface area rather than mechanical strength. Heat transfer or chemical reactions, for example, may be the primary goal. Lattice structures are useful here because they give the part more surfaces without increasing its overall footprint. Osseointegration: This refers to the method of creating lattice structures in medical implants that promote bone growth. The resulting implants form much stronger bonds with the patient's own bone structure. Are Lattice Structures Worth the Extra Complexity? In general, lattice structures for 3D printing allow engineers to push the limits of material science while simultaneously reducing overall part mass. Lattice structures have only recently started moving from advanced aerospace applications to more common consumer products thanks to the growing availability of 3D printers and reductions in material costs. This style of design is here to stay simply because lattices are so efficient. It is wise to learn how to incorporate them into your designs to leverage their benefits. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / Metal 3D Printing Technologies Are Rapidly Evolving: Here's How You Can Take Advantage Without Risk Metal 3D Printing Technologies Are Rapidly Evolving: Here's How You Can Take Advantage Without Risk Written by Dean McClements 12 min read Published March 22, 2022 Updated September 3, 2026 Explore the Rapidly Changing Landscape of Metal Additive Manufacturing Industrial metal 3D printing has continued to penetrate the market at break-neck rates, thanks to evolutio­­ns in technology and outside factors like supply chain disruptions. We’ve covered the evolving ways metal 3D­ printing is being incorporated into industrial production before. However, due to the fast-moving nature of additive manufacturing development, we’re bringing you an update on how this technology is being increasingly adopted and how you can access it. What is Metal 3D Printing? First, the basics: there are multiple metal additive manufacturing methods, including the more widespread DMLS (direct metal laser sintering) as well as the more recently popular method of metal binder jetting. In DMLS, metal powder is directly melted (or sintered) by a laser layer by layer to create parts. However, metal binder jetting layers adhesive in a tray of metal powder, enabling printed pieces to be sifted out of the raw material when finished without having to remove support structures. From here parts can be baked and sintered or infused with a metal (like bronze) to reach their final form. This enables more mass production of metal parts once the initial design optimization is finished. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo How Metal Additive Manufacturing is Evolving Supply chain disruptions from the past couple of years have drastically increased the popularity of an already fast-growing field, especially for medical and aerospace companies. 2018 and 2019 predictions by Deloitte and PwC predicted 3D printing would continue to grow in popularity partly because metal and other non-plastic materials were becoming available for use in 3D printing. PwC specifically predicted the growth of an entire metal additive manufacturing supply chain, including companies that produce the printers and software themselves, printing material suppliers, and service companies. This has come into fruition in niche markets as more technology to complement 3d metal printing is being offered, a sign of the sector’s maturity. While metal 3D printing was first limited to massive industrial DMLS printers, it has evolved into more complex and smaller machines that allow for a greater range of production. More small metal 3D printers, including metal binder jetting models , are coming onto the market. These take up less space on a factory floor and cost far less, breaking down the barrier for entry for companies that want to start metal additive manufacturing. At the same time, manufacturers of larger industrial printers are creating larger print beds to enable more parts created per print. They’re also continually adding more and more lasers to large DMLS printers, which increase the speed and consistency of a print, making it easier to predict. Predicting the outcomes of metal additive manufacturing is getting easier too. While originally the user could only see how the part would turn out by printing it, newer printers have better software to predict design outcomes. Concepts like digital twins, which simulate how a 3D printed part will turn out before the print ever starts, will also help prevent errors creeping in as they continue to advance. Someday these twins will also be able to work across multiple programs and machines as a part goes through numerous manufacturing processes. Metal material itself is becoming more available for additive manufacturing. Metal filament and powder costs have been predicted to drop. Additionally, some printers have come into the market that use polymer encapsulated metal injection molding material, which is less expensive than traditional 3D printing metals. At the same time, companies are already showing a growing interest in high-performance metals like refractory metals such as tungsten. In the future more high-performance metals will be available for industrial applications, including high entropy alloys . However, additive manufacturing plastics continue to evolve and may eventually replace metals for some properties as a cheaper alternative to expensive and rare alloys. Metal 3D Printing Advantages Why is metal additive manufacturing gaining so much ground? As you’ll see in the next section, different industries find different aspects of it valuable. In general, however, this newer production method allows for: efficient energy and material usage on-demand creation of a part at the point of use shortened supply chains more freedom in design less setup than for any other type of manufacturing (this includes increased flexibility and less expense than multiple sets of tooling.) Metal Additive Manufacturing Applications Metal 3D printing has become most popular in markets where short timelines are important, as well as where there are a lot of expensive metals used to make small parts. Aerospace and defense companies were some of the first to adopt 3D metal printing, followed closely by the medical and dental industries. These industries first adopted metal 3D printing because it addresses the factors that make standard parts for these sectors cost more than in other sectors. Aerospace parts are historically expensive for several reasons, including the rare materials used, the necessity for short lead times, and the extra precision required to ensure they perform to specifications. They also need to be as lightweight as possible. Metal additive manufacturing addresses all of these factors in a less expensive way than more traditional manufacturing processes. A 3D printed metal part can weigh as much as 70% less than the identical part produced by other methods. Since a printer uses only the material it needs, the waste of expensive materials like titanium and nickel alloy is kept to a minimum compared to subtractive manufacturing processes. At the same time, already tight lead times for products like jet engine turbines are cut down and additional accuracy is possible with less effort (and therefore cost). Additionally, complex systems in aerospace can be more easily redesigned, simplified, and tested through 3D printing, as printing can reduce the number of components required and quicken the time to create a complex prototype system. Medical and dental manufacturers also use 3D printing for its ability to create accurate, lightweight parts with short lead times. However, these fields also need to attain a high degree of customization at a lower cost, which is necessary for products like artificial hip joints and dental implants. Additionally, automotive companies have been using metal additive manufacturing for high-end parts to a limited extent<dynamic-value> in aerospace and defense, printing in metal offers automotive businesses easier redesign of systems to increase performance. It also allows for metal component weight reduction to improve fuel efficiency, and creation of specialized aftermarket parts. However, most automotive parts are less expensive than aerospace or medical parts, and additive manufacturing has yet to catch up to the speed of other processes, so 3D printing only fits in certain situations for these manufacturers. In the future, industries like mining and oil and gas may also adopt metal 3D printing, as this process can help with the speed of delivery, an essential factor for these fields. According to one report, 83% of oil and gas firms are thinking about adopting 3D printing or on-demand manufacturing for spare parts. A stainless steel part printed with Xometry's DMLS service. Metal Additive Manufacturing Examples What does this look like in concrete terms? In aerospace, NASA and SpaceX have used metal additive manufacturing to make spaceship parts. NASA used the technique to create a rocket engine turbopump that contained 45% fewer parts. In SpaceX’s case, 3D printed parts went into its SuperDraco ship’s engine combustion chamber. There are also metal additive manufacturing examples in the medical field. By 2016 the FDA had approved metal 3D printed implants for medical procedures, and they’ve been used since not only in hip implants, but for a custom artificial rib cage and a skull implant. Xometry has helped build new surgical robot prototypes through its 3D printing and other manufacturing services, creating medically validated parts. There are some notable examples of other companies adopting this technology; Ford recently installed an autonomous robot to control printers creating end-use parts so it could scale up printing production. Meanwhile, Volkswagen has implemented binder jet printing in its headquarters plant in Germany. Multiple oil and gas suppliers are also experimenting with or implementing metal 3D printing, including PGV, which has been printing parts like tool slips and pistons on-demand enough to reduce lead times by 50-80% and physical inventory by 50%. Metal Additive Manufacturing Disadvantages To catch on in more industries, metal 3D printing will still need to overcome some hurdles. Both types of printing are limited in the amount of parts that can be printed simultaneously by the size of the build plate. For DMLS, the post-processing required to remove support structures is time-consuming and adds cost. Binder jetting doesn’t have support structures, allowing faster production in bigger batches. However, neither method has yet reached the speed and output of more traditional manufacturing processes like stamping or forging. Because of this, it’s essential to choose carefully which parts to produce using this method to ensure it provides an economic benefit. Getting Into Metal 3D Printing While metal 3D printing offers various benefits, it only makes sense to implement it in certain circumstances. It’s important to investigate whether your company will benefit from using this manufacturing process, and secondly, whether you should outsource the process or bring it in-house. Any company can start using 3D printed parts, but those that aren’t able to make an upfront investment in the equipment and supporting processes will often use third party additive manufacturers to have parts made. Companies that want to create in-house additive manufacturing facilities will need to account for additional equipment and training for DMLS printers (such as support structure removal and DMLA safety procedures) and binder jet printers (such as baking and sintering or infusing the printed parts). To determine if 3D printing is worth it, ask yourself: Which parts that you currently produce will benefit from being 3D printed? What will be the benefit in costs? What impact will 3D printing have on your business strategy? What impact will this process have on your supply chains? What regulatory considerations will you need to account for? Any company that wants to start using additive manufacturing should first set up a team to talk to people in various departments so you know who the stakeholders are and which parts should be 3D printed first. If you’ve determined your company can go forward with incorporating 3D printing, there are further decisions to be made about whether to use a 3D printing manufacturer or set up this process in your own company. Companies that invest in up-front costs for 3D printing will find they save money in the long run, and they’ll have more control over the process. Though a good additive manufacturer will provide intellectual property protection and cyber security, this additional control may appeal to companies that want to avoid sharing information. Companies that wish to manufacture in-house should consider whether their production will be centralized from one location or distributed from multiple locations. Many companies that decide to take 3D printing in-house will also start with third-party additive manufacturers to get advice about what’s possible and transfer knowledge to their own employees before setting up their own printers. Companies that may benefit more from permanent outsourcing will include those without the budget for the upfront cost of buying and setting up all the necessary equipment and training. Additionally, companies who want low volume production or that simply want to experiment with short runs of products will also benefit. Finally, if parts must be tested or analyzed , it may be easier to work with an additive manufacturer who can do that for you. Any company that does want to outsource 3D printing should decide whether the 3D printed parts are coming from OEMs , tier 1 suppliers, or others. Start Your Instant Quote STEP · STP · SLDPRT · STL · DXF · IPT · X_T · X_B · 3DXML · CATPART · PRT · SAT · 3MF · JT Upload Your Design All uploads are secure and confidential How to Design for 3D Printing in Metal Whether you’re designing new parts to be 3D printed, or creating parts you already produce with a manufacturing process, it’s vital to design parts specifically for the printing process instead of porting over designs from other processes. Otherwise printed parts will at best cost more , and at worst not perform as well as the same parts made using other processes. We cover more details on designing for 3D printing in our in-depth guides to metal binder jetting design , DMLS design , and general 3D printing design. However, briefly, there are a few points it’s important to remember: Wall thickness should be at least .7 mm (.024 inches) on self-supporting features, and at least 1.2mm (.048 inches) on unsupported or load-bearing features. Wall thickness should also remain uniform. Keep at least a .5 mm (.020 inch) gap between part features. Get rid of confined hollows in the part design, as this is where trapped material or support structures can remain and block material that needs to leave during post-processing. Round corners to reduce stress points and increase the part’s performance over its lifetime. Be careful with cantilevers, as these are delicate on 3D printed parts, especially large, heavy ones. events.after: Resources / 3D Printing Design / Metal 3D Printing Technologies Are Rapidly Evolving: Here's How You Can Take Advantage Without Risk Metal 3D Printing Technologies Are Rapidly Evolving: Here's How You Can Take Advantage Without Risk Written by Dean McClements 12 min read Published March 22, 2022 Updated September 3, 2026 Explore the Rapidly Changing Landscape of Metal Additive Manufacturing Industrial metal 3D printing has continued to penetrate the market at break-neck rates, thanks to evolutio­­ns in technology and outside factors like supply chain disruptions. We’ve covered the evolving ways metal 3D­ printing is being incorporated into industrial production before. However, due to the fast-moving nature of additive manufacturing development, we’re bringing you an update on how this technology is being increasingly adopted and how you can access it. What is Metal 3D Printing? First, the basics: there are multiple metal additive manufacturing methods, including the more widespread DMLS (direct metal laser sintering) as well as the more recently popular method of metal binder jetting. In DMLS, metal powder is directly melted (or sintered) by a laser layer by layer to create parts. However, metal binder jetting layers adhesive in a tray of metal powder, enabling printed pieces to be sifted out of the raw material when finished without having to remove support structures. From here parts can be baked and sintered or infused with a metal (like bronze) to reach their final form. This enables more mass production of metal parts once the initial design optimization is finished. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo How Metal Additive Manufacturing is Evolving Supply chain disruptions from the past couple of years have drastically increased the popularity of an already fast-growing field, especially for medical and aerospace companies. 2018 and 2019 predictions by Deloitte and PwC predicted 3D printing would continue to grow in popularity partly because metal and other non-plastic materials were becoming available for use in 3D printing. PwC specifically predicted the growth of an entire metal additive manufacturing supply chain, including companies that produce the printers and software themselves, printing material suppliers, and service companies. This has come into fruition in niche markets as more technology to complement 3d metal printing is being offered, a sign of the sector’s maturity. While metal 3D printing was first limited to massive industrial DMLS printers, it has evolved into more complex and smaller machines that allow for a greater range of production. More small metal 3D printers, including metal binder jetting models , are coming onto the market. These take up less space on a factory floor and cost far less, breaking down the barrier for entry for companies that want to start metal additive manufacturing. At the same time, manufacturers of larger industrial printers are creating larger print beds to enable more parts created per print. They’re also continually adding more and more lasers to large DMLS printers, which increase the speed and consistency of a print, making it easier to predict. Predicting the outcomes of metal additive manufacturing is getting easier too. While originally the user could only see how the part would turn out by printing it, newer printers have better software to predict design outcomes. Concepts like digital twins, which simulate how a 3D printed part will turn out before the print ever starts, will also help prevent errors creeping in as they continue to advance. Someday these twins will also be able to work across multiple programs and machines as a part goes through numerous manufacturing processes. Metal material itself is becoming more available for additive manufacturing. Metal filament and powder costs have been predicted to drop. Additionally, some printers have come into the market that use polymer encapsulated metal injection molding material, which is less expensive than traditional 3D printing metals. At the same time, companies are already showing a growing interest in high-performance metals like refractory metals such as tungsten. In the future more high-performance metals will be available for industrial applications, including high entropy alloys . However, additive manufacturing plastics continue to evolve and may eventually replace metals for some properties as a cheaper alternative to expensive and rare alloys. Metal 3D Printing Advantages Why is metal additive manufacturing gaining so much ground? As you’ll see in the next section, different industries find different aspects of it valuable. In general, however, this newer production method allows for: efficient energy and material usage on-demand creation of a part at the point of use shortened supply chains more freedom in design less setup than for any other type of manufacturing (this includes increased flexibility and less expense than multiple sets of tooling.) Metal Additive Manufacturing Applications Metal 3D printing has become most popular in markets where short timelines are important, as well as where there are a lot of expensive metals used to make small parts. Aerospace and defense companies were some of the first to adopt 3D metal printing, followed closely by the medical and dental industries. These industries first adopted metal 3D printing because it addresses the factors that make standard parts for these sectors cost more than in other sectors. Aerospace parts are historically expensive for several reasons, including the rare materials used, the necessity for short lead times, and the extra precision required to ensure they perform to specifications. They also need to be as lightweight as possible. Metal additive manufacturing addresses all of these factors in a less expensive way than more traditional manufacturing processes. A 3D printed metal part can weigh as much as 70% less than the identical part produced by other methods. Since a printer uses only the material it needs, the waste of expensive materials like titanium and nickel alloy is kept to a minimum compared to subtractive manufacturing processes. At the same time, already tight lead times for products like jet engine turbines are cut down and additional accuracy is possible with less effort (and therefore cost). Additionally, complex systems in aerospace can be more easily redesigned, simplified, and tested through 3D printing, as printing can reduce the number of components required and quicken the time to create a complex prototype system. Medical and dental manufacturers also use 3D printing for its ability to create accurate, lightweight parts with short lead times. However, these fields also need to attain a high degree of customization at a lower cost, which is necessary for products like artificial hip joints and dental implants. Additionally, automotive companies have been using metal additive manufacturing for high-end parts to a limited extent<dynamic-value> in aerospace and defense, printing in metal offers automotive businesses easier redesign of systems to increase performance. It also allows for metal component weight reduction to improve fuel efficiency, and creation of specialized aftermarket parts. However, most automotive parts are less expensive than aerospace or medical parts, and additive manufacturing has yet to catch up to the speed of other processes, so 3D printing only fits in certain situations for these manufacturers. In the future, industries like mining and oil and gas may also adopt metal 3D printing, as this process can help with the speed of delivery, an essential factor for these fields. According to one report, 83% of oil and gas firms are thinking about adopting 3D printing or on-demand manufacturing for spare parts. A stainless steel part printed with Xometry's DMLS service. Metal Additive Manufacturing Examples What does this look like in concrete terms? In aerospace, NASA and SpaceX have used metal additive manufacturing to make spaceship parts. NASA used the technique to create a rocket engine turbopump that contained 45% fewer parts. In SpaceX’s case, 3D printed parts went into its SuperDraco ship’s engine combustion chamber. There are also metal additive manufacturing examples in the medical field. By 2016 the FDA had approved metal 3D printed implants for medical procedures, and they’ve been used since not only in hip implants, but for a custom artificial rib cage and a skull implant. Xometry has helped build new surgical robot prototypes through its 3D printing and other manufacturing services, creating medically validated parts. There are some notable examples of other companies adopting this technology; Ford recently installed an autonomous robot to control printers creating end-use parts so it could scale up printing production. Meanwhile, Volkswagen has implemented binder jet printing in its headquarters plant in Germany. Multiple oil and gas suppliers are also experimenting with or implementing metal 3D printing, including PGV, which has been printing parts like tool slips and pistons on-demand enough to reduce lead times by 50-80% and physical inventory by 50%. Metal Additive Manufacturing Disadvantages To catch on in more industries, metal 3D printing will still need to overcome some hurdles. Both types of printing are limited in the amount of parts that can be printed simultaneously by the size of the build plate. For DMLS, the post-processing required to remove support structures is time-consuming and adds cost. Binder jetting doesn’t have support structures, allowing faster production in bigger batches. However, neither method has yet reached the speed and output of more traditional manufacturing processes like stamping or forging. Because of this, it’s essential to choose carefully which parts to produce using this method to ensure it provides an economic benefit. Getting Into Metal 3D Printing While metal 3D printing offers various benefits, it only makes sense to implement it in certain circumstances. It’s important to investigate whether your company will benefit from using this manufacturing process, and secondly, whether you should outsource the process or bring it in-house. Any company can start using 3D printed parts, but those that aren’t able to make an upfront investment in the equipment and supporting processes will often use third party additive manufacturers to have parts made. Companies that want to create in-house additive manufacturing facilities will need to account for additional equipment and training for DMLS printers (such as support structure removal and DMLA safety procedures) and binder jet printers (such as baking and sintering or infusing the printed parts). To determine if 3D printing is worth it, ask yourself: Which parts that you currently produce will benefit from being 3D printed? What will be the benefit in costs? What impact will 3D printing have on your business strategy? What impact will this process have on your supply chains? What regulatory considerations will you need to account for? Any company that wants to start using additive manufacturing should first set up a team to talk to people in various departments so you know who the stakeholders are and which parts should be 3D printed first. If you’ve determined your company can go forward with incorporating 3D printing, there are further decisions to be made about whether to use a 3D printing manufacturer or set up this process in your own company. Companies that invest in up-front costs for 3D printing will find they save money in the long run, and they’ll have more control over the process. Though a good additive manufacturer will provide intellectual property protection and cyber security, this additional control may appeal to companies that want to avoid sharing information. Companies that wish to manufacture in-house should consider whether their production will be centralized from one location or distributed from multiple locations. Many companies that decide to take 3D printing in-house will also start with third-party additive manufacturers to get advice about what’s possible and transfer knowledge to their own employees before setting up their own printers. Companies that may benefit more from permanent outsourcing will include those without the budget for the upfront cost of buying and setting up all the necessary equipment and training. Additionally, companies who want low volume production or that simply want to experiment with short runs of products will also benefit. Finally, if parts must be tested or analyzed , it may be easier to work with an additive manufacturer who can do that for you. Any company that does want to outsource 3D printing should decide whether the 3D printed parts are coming from OEMs , tier 1 suppliers, or others. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / PLA vs. ABS: Differences between ABS and PLA Filaments PLA vs. ABS: Differences between ABS and PLA Filaments Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Dr. Mahder Tewolde PhD 18 min read Published August 15, 2022 Updated September 3, 2026 Learn all about these two materials that are commonly used in 3D printing applications. PLA and ABS are two of the commonly used 3D printing filaments, but they differ in key areas (strength, ease of use, and heat resistance). Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) is stronger and more impact-resistant than Polylactic acid (PLA). ABS is ideal for parts exposed to mechanical stress (automotive or tool components) in terms of strength and durability. PLA is more suited for decorative or non-functional items where strength is not a priority in terms of heat resistance. ABS has a higher glass transition temperature, allowing it to withstand higher temperatures without warping. PLA has lower heat resistance and deforms under heat, making it unsuitable for high-temperature applications. PLA is easier to print than ABS because it does not require a heated print bed and is less prone to warping. ABS needs a heated bed and shrink, leading to potential print failures if not appropriately managed. The cost differences stem from the materials' properties. PLA is cheaper to produce, making it more cost-effective for users focused on aesthetics or non-functional prints. ABS, with its higher strength and heat resistance, comes at a slightly higher cost due to its greater durability and applications in more demanding environments. What Are the Advantages of PLA Compared to ABS? The advantages of PLA compared to ABS are listed below. Biodegradability: PLA is derived from renewable plant-based sources, making it biodegradable. ABS is petroleum-based and non-biodegradable. Printability: PLA is easier to print with and requires lower extrusion temperatures compared to ABS. PLA prints at temperatures ranging from 180°C to 220°C, while ABS needs 210°C to 250°C for optimal results. Environmental Impact: PLA has a lower environmental impact due to its plant-based origin. ABS production relies on non-renewable fossil fuels. Odor: ABS releases unpleasant fumes, requiring proper ventilation. PLA produces less odor during printing Surface Finish: PLA prints have a smoother surface finish and are ideal for detailed models. ABS exhibits a more matte finish and requires additional post-processing. Strength and Durability: ABS offers better strength and impact resistance, making it more suitable for parts that endure higher stress. It is a good alternative when smooth surface finishes are needed and falls under the " What is PLA ?" category. Cost: PLA is less expensive than ABS, making it a more economical choice for everyday printing needs. Does PLA Give Better Detail Resolution Than ABS at the Same Layer Height? Yes, PLA gives better detail resolution than ABS without an enclosure. PLA has a lower melting point (around 180-220°C), which reduces the risk of warping during printing. ABS has a higher melting point and tends to shrink more as it cools, causing warping and less precision when printed without an enclosure. PLA’s ability to maintain stable dimensions at room temperature makes it ideal for precise prints without the need for controlled environments. For example, PLA prints with minimal warping, ensuring better quality for intricate designs or detailed models. The image below shows a few parts that Xometry 3D printed using PLA: Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Interconnected PLA parts 3D printed by Xometry. Does PLA Require Less Bed Adhesion and Print Preparation Than ABS? Yes, PLA requires less bed adhesion and print preparation than ABS. PLA adheres easily to most print beds without the need for a heated surface. It requires minimal preparation (a clean print bed or a light layer of adhesive). ABS, compared to PLA, requires higher temperatures and a heated bed to reduce warping. ABS benefits from an enclosure to maintain temperature consistency during printing. PLA’s ease of use makes it more accessible for quick prints and reduces the likelihood of print failures caused by bed adhesion issues. Is PLA Better Suited Than ABS for Decorative or Non-Functional Prints? Yes, PLA is better suited than ABS for decorative or non-functional prints. PLA provides a smoother surface finish and more vibrant colors, making it ideal for detailed designs or visual projects. It is easier to print with, reducing the likelihood of warping or failure, which is essential for intricate, non-functional items. PLA's low melting point and minimal need for a heated bed make it more convenient for fast prints. ABS is more durable and better suited for functional items, but it is more challenging to work with due to its higher printing requirements compared to PLA. PLA offers superior results and ease of use for decorative objects (figurines or art pieces). Does PLA Maintain Color and Appearance Better Than ABS Over Time? Yes, PLA maintains color and appearance better than ABS over time. PLA is less prone to fading or yellowing when exposed to UV light, making it a more durable choice for items that are displayed or used for long periods. It holds its vibrant colors and glossy finish longer than ABS, which degrades and loses its luster with exposure to sunlight. PLA's superior surface finish makes it more resistant to the effects of aging, while ABS requires additional post-processing to maintain its appearance. For decorative items, PLA provides a longer-lasting, visually appealing result. Need PLA or ABS 3D Printed Parts? Get Your Instant Quote What Are the Advantages of ABS Compared to PLA? The advantages of Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) compared to Polylactic acid (PLA) are listed below. Strength and Durability: ABS is stronger than PLA. The plastic (ABS) withstands higher stress and impact, making it ideal for functional parts such as automotive components or tools. Heat Resistance: ABS has a higher glass transition temperature (around 105°C), allowing it to endure higher temperatures without deforming. It makes it suitable for parts exposed to heat (engine components or household appliances). Post-Processing : ABS is easier to sand, paint, and smooth with acetone, which improves its surface finish. The question, “ what is ABS ?” is answered through the advantages that make it the go-to material for high-quality, polished prints. Flexibility : ABS maintains better flexibility compared to PLA, reducing the likelihood of brittleness in parts subjected to bending or impact. Interconnected ABS parts 3D printed by Xometry. Is ABS Biodegradable, Unlike PLA? No, ABS is not biodegradable like PLA. PLA is derived from renewable resources such as corn starch and is biodegradable under certain conditions. It breaks down naturally in composting environments, making it more environmentally friendly than ABS. ABS, in comparison, is petroleum-based and does not decompose easily in natural environments. It takes hundreds of years to break down, contributing to long-term environmental impact. For eco-conscious applications, PLA is preferred over ABS due to its compostable nature. Is ABS Stronger Compared to PLA? Yes, ABS is stronger compared to PLA. ABS has superior impact resistance and durability, making it suitable for parts that need to withstand physical stress. It performs better under higher temperatures and is less likely to crack or break under impact. PLA is more rigid but tends to be more brittle, making it less suitable for functional parts that endure wear and tear. ABS’s strength and flexibility make it the preferred choice for mechanical applications, while PLA is more commonly used for decorative or low-stress prints. Does ABS Resist Heat Better Compared to PLA? Yes, ABS resists heat better compared to PLA. ABS is able to withstand higher temperatures, with a heat resistance up to ~85–95 °C, while PLA starts to deform around 60°C. It makes ABS more suitable for applications exposed to heat (automotive parts or appliances). PLA is more sensitive to high temperatures and warps or loses its structural integrity when exposed to heat for prolonged periods. ABS’s superior heat resistance makes it a better option for functional parts that need to endure higher thermal conditions. Is ABS More Durable Compared to PLA? Yes, ABS is more durable compared to PLA. ABS has higher impact resistance and withstands more physical stress without cracking. It is more flexible and less brittle than PLA, making it ideal for parts that are subjected to regular handling or mechanical wear. ABS performs better in high-temperature environments, where PLA softens and loses its structural integrity. For example, ABS is commonly used in automotive parts or functional prototypes, while PLA is more suited for decorative items and low-stress applications. The added durability and heat resistance of ABS make it a better choice for long-lasting and functional parts. Does ABS Warp More Easily Compared to PLA? No, ABS does not warp more easily compared to PLA. ABS is more prone to warping due to its higher printing temperature and tendency to shrink during cooling. PLA, with a lower melting point, experiences less shrinkage and is less likely to warp during printing. ABS requires a heated bed and controlled environment to minimize warping for larger prints. PLA is printed without a heated bed and tends to maintain its shape more easily. The difference in temperature sensitivity and shrinkage characteristics makes PLA a better option for prints that need to avoid warping. Is ABS More Flexible Than PLA? Yes, ABS is more flexible than PLA. ABS has better impact resistance and bends without breaking, making it ideal for functional parts that require durability and flexibility. PLA is more rigid and tends to be brittle, which leads to cracking or breaking under stress. ABS’s flexibility allows it to withstand physical stress better than PLA in applications (automotive parts or tools). PLA’s rigidity, while suitable for decorative and low-stress prints, makes it less ideal for parts that need to endure mechanical forces. PLA has dimensional stability, low shrinkage, and is easy to process, allowing accurate prints at lower extrusion temperatures without heated beds or enclosures. However, it suffers from low glass-transition temperature and brittle failure under impact or sustained heat. ABS offers higher impact resistance, superior layer fusion, chemical resistance, and significantly higher heat tolerance due to its higher glass-transition temperature, at the cost of increased warping risk, higher energy input, and the need for controlled thermal environments. Material selection therefore hinges on whether the application favors visual quality, accuracy, and indoor safety (PLA) or functional durability, thermal resilience, and mechanical toughness under real-world loads (ABS). What Are the Main Material Differences Between ABS and PLA for 3D Printing? The main material differences between ABS and PLA for 3D printing are listed below. Printing Temperature : PLA has a lower printing temperature, between 180°C and 220°C, while ABS requires higher temperatures, ranging from 220°C to 250°C. The difference affects the ease of printing, with PLA being easier to print at lower temperatures. Strength and Durability : ABS is stronger and more impact-resistant than PLA. ABS is more flexible and handles higher stress without breaking. PLA is more rigid and brittle, making it less suitable for parts that undergo mechanical stress. Heat Resistance : ABS has better heat resistance, maintaining its shape at higher temperatures (up to 100°C). PLA begins to deform at around 60°C, limiting its use in high-temperature environments. Surface Finish : PLA provides a smoother, shinier finish compared to ABS. ABS is smoothed with acetone to achieve a glossy finish, while PLA’s finish is more consistent. Environmental Impact : PLA is biodegradable and made from renewable resources, making it more environmentally friendly than ABS, which is petroleum-based and not biodegradable. How Do ABS Fumes Compare to PLA Fumes During Printing? ABS fumes are compared to PLA fumes during printing by their chemical compound (styrene). ABS emits styrene, a volatile organic compound that irritates the respiratory system and causes long-term health risks if inhaled in large amounts. PLA produces minimal fumes compared to ABS, mainly consisting of harmless, biodegradable compounds (lactide). ABS requires proper ventilation or an enclosure to minimize exposure to harmful fumes, while PLA is considered safer to print with in non-ventilated spaces. PLA’s fumes pose a much lower health risk compared to the more toxic fumes released by ABS during printing. Using acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and poly-lactic acid (PLA) presents a risk of exposure to respirable particles according to “Particle emissions from fused deposition modeling 3D printers: Evaluation and meta-analysis,” written by P Byrley and BJ George on November 12, 2018. PLA is considered safer to print with in indoor environments, as it poses lower health risks than ABS. Which One Is Better for Temperature (Heat) Resistance, PLA vs ABS? ABS is better for temperature (heat) resistance compared to PLA. ABS withstands temperatures up to 100°C without deforming, making it ideal for parts exposed to heat (automotive or appliance components). PLA begins to soften at around 60°C, making it unsuitable for high-temperature applications. ABS’s higher glass transition temperature allows it to maintain its shape and strength under heat, while PLA’s lower heat resistance leads to warping or failure in hot environments. For heat-resistant applications, ABS is far superior in heat resistance, as it bears temperatures up to 100°C or more without losing structural integrity, according to “PLA vs. ABS – Which Is Better?” written by BigRep, published on June 03, 2025. Which Material, ABS or PLA, Offers Better Impact Resistance? ABS offers better impact resistance compared to PLA because of its molecular structure and material properties. ABS is more flexible and withstands higher forces before breaking or cracking. It is used for parts that require durability (protective covers and automotive components). PLA is more brittle and tends to break under stress, making it less suitable for applications requiring high impact resistance. ABS's superior strength and toughness make it the ideal choice for functional parts exposed to mechanical stress. “PLA shows brittle nature when subjected to out-of-plane loading, i.e., impact,” according to “An Investigation Into Low Velocity Impact Of 3D Printed Thermoplastic Plates” written by Guneet Kaur Mankoo, published on October 08, 2021. Which Material Cools and Solidifies More Predictably, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that cools and solidifies more predictably. PLA has a lower melting point, ranging from 180 to 220°C, and solidifies fast once the print head moves away. Its cooling process is less prone to warping, and the material retains its shape better without the need for additional temperature control. ABS has a higher melting point and tends to shrink and warp as it cools. It makes ABS more challenging to work with for larger prints, as it requires a heated bed and an enclosure to prevent temperature fluctuations that affect the solidification process. Which Material Provides Better Overall Tensile Strength, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that provides better overall tensile strength. ABS has higher impact resistance and endures more stress before breaking or deforming. It is more flexible, allowing it to absorb forces without fracturing. PLA is more rigid and tends to break under stress, offering lower tensile strength. ABS is ideal for applications where durability and mechanical strength are required (automotive parts or functional components). PLA is more suited for decorative items that do not undergo significant mechanical stress. Which Material Shows Less Warping During Printing, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that shows less warping during printing. PLA has a lower melting point and solidifies fast, which reduces the likelihood of warping as it cools. ABS tends to shrink more as it cools, leading to higher stress and warping on larger prints. PLA's lower temperature sensitivity makes it easier to print without the need for a heated bed or enclosure, unlike ABS, which requires both to prevent warping. It makes PLA a more reliable material for precise prints and smaller projects. Which Material Delivers Higher Dimensional Accuracy, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that delivers higher dimensional accuracy. PLA has lower shrinkage during cooling, which results in fewer distortions and better precision in prints. ABS, on the other hand, tends to shrink more as it cools, leading to potential warping and dimensional inaccuracies. PLA's ease of printing without the need for a heated bed ensures that the printed object retains its intended shape and size. ABS requires more careful temperature control to maintain dimensional consistency, making PLA a more reliable material for accurate prints. Which Material Performs Better in Outdoor Environments, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that performs better in outdoor environments. ABS has higher Ultraviolet (UV) resistance and withstands prolonged exposure to sunlight without degrading. PLA, being biodegradable, breaks down faster when exposed to outdoor elements (sunlight and moisture). ABS maintains its strength and color for a longer period, making it suitable for outdoor applications (automotive parts and garden tools). PLA’s sensitivity to environmental factors makes it more appropriate for indoor use or short-term outdoor projects. Which Material Has Superior Layer Adhesion, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that has superior layer adhesion. ABS bonds better between layers due to its higher printing temperature and improved layer fusion. The higher extrusion temperature of ABS allows for better adhesion between layers, reducing the likelihood of delamination or layer separation. PLA, with its lower printing temperature, struggles to bond layers as effectively in prints that require strength and durability. PLA and ABS are two of the commonly used 3D printing filaments, but they differ in key areas (strength, ease of use, and heat resistance). Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) is stronger and more impact-resistant than Polylactic acid (PLA). PLA is more suited for decorative or non-functional items where strength is not a priority in terms of heat resistance. ABS has a higher glass transition temperature, allowing it to withstand higher temperatures without warping. PLA has lower heat resistance and deforms under heat, making it unsuitable for high-temperature applications. PLA is easier to print than ABS because it does not require a heated print bed and is less prone to warping. ABS needs a heated bed and shrink, leading to potential print failures if not appropriately managed. The cost differences stem from the materials' properties. PLA is cheaper to produce, making it more cost-effective for users focused on aesthetics or non-functional prints. ABS, with its higher strength and heat resistance, comes at a slightly higher cost due to its greater durability and applications in more demanding environments. What Are the Advantages of PLA Compared to ABS? The advantages of PLA compared to ABS are listed below. Biodegradability: PLA is derived from renewable plant-based sources, making it biodegradable. ABS is petroleum-based and non-biodegradable. Printability: PLA is easier to print with and requires lower extrusion temperatures compared to ABS. PLA prints at temperatures ranging from 180°C to 220°C, while ABS needs 210°C to 250°C for optimal results. Environmental Impact: PLA has a lower environmental impact due to its plant-based origin. ABS production relies on non-renewable fossil fuels. Odor: ABS releases unpleasant fumes, requiring proper ventilation. ABS exhibits a more matte finish and requires additional post-processing. Strength and Durability: ABS offers better strength and impact resistance, making it more suitable for parts that endure higher stress. PLA’s ability to maintain stable dimensions at room temperature makes it ideal for precise prints without the need for controlled environments. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / How to Smooth 3D Prints: PLA, ABS, and FDM Prints How to Smooth 3D Prints: PLA, ABS, and FDM Prints Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 26 min read Published May 24, 2023 Updated August 26, 2026 Your guide to smoothing options to get 3D printed parts with better aesthetics To smooth 3D prints, achieving a high-quality finish is essential for aesthetic appeal and functionality. A smooth surface increases visual appeal by minimizing visible layer lines and providing a more refined finish. The process makes the print more suitable for subsequent post-processing. Smoothing the surface promotes better adhesion for additional layers or paint, improving the print's durability and functionality. Proper surface preparation is essential to ensure optimal adhesion. Different filament types (such as PLA and ABS) and FDM-printed parts require specific smoothing techniques due to their varying material characteristics. Each filament behaves differently when exposed to heat, solvents, or abrasives. PLA prints can be smoothed using specific solvents such as ethyl acetate or through mechanical methods, while ABS prints are best smoothed with acetone vapor. FDM prints require a combination of sanding and chemical smoothing, depending on the material and finish desired. The guide details methods for how to smooth 3D prints, providing step-by-step instructions and practical tips for smoothing PLA prints, ABS prints, and other FDM prints. The guide ensures that novice and experienced users apply the correct methods. Various techniques (sanding, vapor smoothing, and chemical refinement) are discussed to help achieve a professional-quality finish. Each technique is tailored to the print material and desired results. Each method is explained in precise steps to ensure novice and experienced 3D printers learn how to make 3D prints smooth and improve their print quality through effective 3D print smoothing techniques. The 3D Prints that are smoothed using the proper methods are more appealing and suitable for further post-processing (painting, detailing, or functional use). 3D Print Smoothing Techniques 1. Using Paint and Sanding Material Using paint and sanding material is an effective method for smoothing 3D prints. A filler primer is applied first to fill minor gaps or imperfections, providing a more even surface once it dries. Sanding is used to smooth the surface. Sandpaper with varying grits is employed, starting with medium grit to address flaws and moving to finer grits for a polished finish. The technique helps achieve a smooth, professional appearance on 3D prints for materials (PLA or ABS). The process helps eliminate rough textures and uneven layers, which are common results of 3D printing. The method is beneficial when preparing the print for further painting or post-processing. 2. Using Abrasive Smoothing Methods Using abrasive smoothing methods is a common technique to refine the surface of 3D prints for materials (PLA, ABS, PETG, and nylon). The process involves using abrasive materials (sandpaper, grinding wheels, or abrasive pads) to remove rough spots and imperfections physically. The process starts with a medium grit to address larger imperfections, followed by progressively finer grits to achieve a smoother finish. Abrasive smoothing is done manually with sandpaper or with mechanical tools, depending on the print's size and desired finish. The method is effective for improving the appearance of 3D prints with visible layer lines or surface defects. The process provides control over the amount of smoothing, allowing for a customized finish. Abrasive smoothing is a cost-effective option that does not require specialized equipment, making it accessible for hobbyists and professionals. The primary advantage is its ability to achieve a smooth surface free from defects, improving the print's quality and preparing it for further post-processing (painting or coating). Cost : A few hundred dollars for the equipment, or you can have a service like Xometry do it. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo "Currently Xometry only offers vapor smoothing for SLS and MJF nylon based materials, as the chemical solvent our network uses is compatible with nylons." Christian Tsu-Raun Team Lead, Manual Quoting 3. Finishing with Fine Sandpaper and Micro-Mesh Finishing with fine sandpaper and micro-mesh provides a detailed method for smoothing 3D prints when aiming for a high-quality finish. Fine sandpaper is used to smooth the print further after initial sanding with coarser grades, though it does not entirely remove all roughness. Progressing through medium to fine grits before using micro-mesh yields the best results. Micro-mesh pads are effective for refining the surface, working to smooth out micro-imperfections and providing a polished finish. The method is beneficial for smoothing out minor flaws and improving the appearance of the print. The process is effective for delicate projects or when a high-quality finish is essential. The primer improves the appearance and increases the adhesion of subsequent paint layers, though its effectiveness in promoting adhesion depends on the print material and primer quality. Using Heat Gun Using a heat gun can reduce surface roughness on some 3D prints (including ABS), but it requires careful control to avoid warping. The heat gun works by applying controlled heat to the surface of the print, causing the plastic to soften. The softening allows the material to flow slightly, helping reduce minor imperfections (layer lines and rough spots). The process does not eliminate imperfections. The print is evenly heated by moving the heat gun over the surface, helping to achieve a more uniform finish. Careful control of the temperature and distance from the print is essential to avoid warping or distorting the model. Chemical Smoothing (ABS) Chemical smoothing for ABS involves using solvents (acetone) to smooth the surface of 3D prints. The process works by exposing the print to acetone vapor, which softens the outer layer of the ABS material, allowing the surface to become smoother and more uniform. The process does not eliminate deeper imperfections (visible layer lines) while the softening provides a glossy finish. The print is placed in a sealed chamber with acetone, and the vapor gently softens the outer layers. The process helps smooth out the surface, but additional post-processing is necessary for a polished finish. The method is effective for improving the appearance of ABS prints when a smoother surface is desired. The process is a cost-effective and efficient way to enhance ABS prints while requiring adequate safety precautions. 8. The vapor gently softens the outer layer of the PLA material, causing it to flow and smooth out imperfections like visible layer lines and rough patches. The procedure does not ‘melt’ the material but softens it just enough to achieve a smoother finish. The water temperature must be controlled to avoid melting the print, as water that is too hot causes deformation. The print is placed in hot water, around 60-70°C (140-158°F), and left for a brief period. Selecting the correct filler for the material is essential to ensure proper adhesion and smoothing.
