The different types of viscosity are listed below. Dynamic Viscosity : Dynamic viscosity measures the internal resistance of a fluid to shear under an applied force. The viscosity formula is defined by the equation μ = τ / γ̇, where μ is dynamic viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation between fluid layers). Dynamic viscosity is critical in industries such as lubrication, fluid transport, and hydraulics. Viscosity examples include dynamic viscosity, which ensures the fluid maintains a protective film between moving engine parts to reduce wear and friction in motor oils. Higher-viscosity oils can provide better protection at high temperatures, while lower-viscosity oils improve flow and fuel efficiency. Kinematic Viscosity : Kinematic viscosity is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to fluid density, expressed as ν = μ / ρ, where ν is kinematic viscosity, μ is dynamic viscosity, and ρ is fluid density. The property characterizes a fluid’s resistance to flow under its own weight or inertia, independent of external pressure forces. Kinematic viscosity is significant in industries (pipeline transport and coatings), where gravity and inertia influence fluid movement. For example, oil with a higher kinematic viscosity flows more slowly through pipelines, requiring more energy to pump, while in coatings, appropriate kinematic viscosity ensures uniform film formation without drips or uneven coverage. Apparent Viscosity : Apparent viscosity refers to the effective viscosity of a non-Newtonian fluid measured at a specific shear rate, temperature, or other defined condition. The formula is expressed as ηₐₚₚ = τ / γ̇, where ηₐₚₚ is apparent viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation). Apparent viscosity is used to characterize materials (adhesives, paints, and polymer melts) whose viscosity changes with shear rate during processing. For example, the apparent viscosity of a resin affects how it flows and adheres during layer deposition in 3D printing, influencing print quality and speed. What is Dynamic Viscosity? Dynamic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s internal resistance to shear under an applied force. Dynamic viscosity relates the shear stress exerted on the fluid to the resulting rate of deformation between adjacent layers. Fluid flow becomes sluggish and requires greater energy input to maintain movement when dynamic viscosity is high. Appropriate dynamic viscosity helps maintain a stable thin film of lubricant between moving parts and prevents direct metal-to-metal contact in applications such as engine lubrication, injection molding , and industrial machinery, thereby reducing wear. The lubricant film breaks down and causes damage if the dynamic viscosity is too low. The fluid does not circulate efficiently if the dynamic viscosity is too high, increasing drag, pump load, and energy consumption. What is Kinematic Viscosity? Kinematic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s inherent resistance to flow relative to its density. Kinematic viscosity is calculated by dividing a fluid’s dynamic viscosity by its density (ν = μ / ρ). A fluid's kinematic viscosity indicates how easily it moves under its own mass per unit volume compared with its internal resistance to flow. Fuel flow systems use it for consistent delivery, coolant circulation systems for reliable channel traversal, and manufacturing fluid transport processes where gravity and inertia influence throughput and stability. What is Apparent Viscosity? Apparent viscosity is the effective measure of a fluid’s resistance to shear under specific processing conditions (defined shear rate, temperature, or applied stress). Apparent viscosity describes how a fluid’s internal structure responds when adjacent layers move at different rates. Non-Newtonian fluids have a variable apparent viscosity depending on the shear rate or applied stress. For example, coatings must have a lower apparent viscosity under high shear during spraying for easy application and a higher apparent viscosity at rest to prevent sagging. Sealants require an apparent viscosity that allows them to flow into joints and then stabilize to remain in place. Apparent viscosity determines how readily the material flows under high shear during extrusion and how well it maintains shape after exiting the die in polymer extrusion. Proper control of apparent viscosity ensures uniform products, efficient processing, and minimal defects in manufacturing. How does Viscosity Affect Injection Molding Processes? Viscosity affects the injection molding process by determining how easily the resin flows into the mold, how it cools, and the final part quality. High-viscosity resins flow more slowly, which leads to incomplete filling or short shots in intricate or thin-walled sections. Higher injection pressures are required, which increases overall cycle time. Resins with excessively low viscosity can leak into parting lines, create flash, or reduce dimensional accuracy. Proper viscosity ensures that the mold fills, cools evenly, and produces parts with smooth surfaces, minimal sink marks, and strong weld lines. Expertise in material selection helps balance viscosity for optimal mold filling, cooling, and part quality. How does Viscosity Impact Extrusion Processes? Viscosity impacts polymer extrusion by governing how the melt flows, stabilizes, and forms the final product dimensions. High-viscosity melts resist flow, requiring more force to push material through the screw and die, which reduces production rates. Lower-viscosity melts flow more easily and increase throughput, but lead to unstable flow, uneven wall thickness, or surface defects. Fluctuations in melt viscosity in non-Newtonian polymers cause pressure variations that affect dimensional consistency and product quality. Precise control of viscosity ensures uniform die filling, consistent cross-sections, and proper cooling. Real-time monitoring of melt viscosity allows adjustments to screw speed, temperature, and back-pressure, making viscosity a critical factor for quality control and process optimization in extrusion. What is the Importance of Viscosity in Casting? The importance of viscosity in casting is listed below. Flow into Mold Cavities : Viscosity determines how easily molten metal or ceramic slurry penetrates mold geometry. High viscosity or insufficiently heated metal prevents full filling of thin sections, leading to voids or incomplete castings. Defect Prevention : Maintaining proper viscosity reduces defects such as porosity, surface roughness, and, in investment casting, shell cracking and incomplete shell formation. Stable viscosity ensures uniform shell thickness and reliable strength. Die Casting Relevance : The molten alloy must flow rapidly into the mold before solidification begins in die casting. Lower viscosity improves mold filling, reduces cold shuts, and increases part quality. Investment Casting Relevance : The viscosity of the ceramic slurry affects coating layers on the wax pattern, shell integrity, and final casting accuracy in investment casting. Maintaining optimal viscosity ensures proper coating, mold strength, and dimensional precision. How does Viscosity Influence 3D Printing (Additive Manufacturing)? Viscosity influences 3D printing processes by governing how well the material flows, how each layer adheres, and how the final structure maintains its shape. Stereolithography (SLA) requires low-viscosity resin to refill the tank rapidly between layers, reduce trapped air or voids, and enable fine feature resolution. The viscosity of molten polymer affects flow through the nozzle, filament bonding, and layer consistency, directly impacting print precision, strength, and quality in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). Powder-bed processes such as Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) depend on the flow behavior of the partially melted powder to ensure particles coalesce properly, which affects density, mechanical strength, and dimensional accuracy. Proper control of viscosity across the processes ensures high print precision, strong interlayer adhesion, and superior structural integrity in printed parts. Why is Viscosity Important in Coatings and Paint Formulations? Viscosity is essential in coatings and paint formulations because it controls how the liquid flows onto and adheres to a surface. Proper viscosity improves sprayability, film formation, and drying behavior in industrial paints and powder coatings. Low viscosity increases atomization during spray application, permitting fine mist formation and even coverage. High viscosity supports a thicker film build without sagging on vertical surfaces, provided it remains within the application range. Maintaining optimal viscosity in paint lines ensures a consistent surface finish, accurate film thickness, and defect-free drying. Powder coatings benefit from controlling melt viscosity during curing to ensure proper flow, leveling, and uniform protective layers. Insufficient viscosity control results in uneven coatings, runs, orange peel texture, and reduced durability of the finished product. How does Viscosity Affect the Performance of Adhesives and Sealants? Viscosity affects the performance of adhesives and sealants by controlling how well the material flows, wets the substrate, and forms a strong bond, and how easily it is applied. Proper viscosity ensures the adhesive penetrates surface irregularities and establishes intimate contact between surfaces. Lower viscosity adhesives flow readily, filling micro‑voids on rough or porous surfaces and improving bond strength. Higher viscosity adhesives remain in place under gravity or vertical orientation, preserving joint thickness and preventing sagging or dripping during application. The viscosity of epoxy resins influences mixing, dispensing, and layer uniformity, affecting cohesive strength upon curing. Sealant viscosity determines how well the material extrudes into joints and gaps and how well it resists movement under load after curing. Deviations from the optimal viscosity range reduce bond strength, impair gap-filling, or compromise joint integrity. Why Do Lubricants in Machining Depend on Viscosity? Lubricants in machining depend on viscosity because it determines the thickness of the protective film between moving parts, reducing wear, friction, and heat generation. Correct viscosity ensures the film remains stable under load, preventing metal‑to‑metal contact. The lubricant is unable to form a sufficient film if the viscosity is too low, increasing friction and wear. Excessively high viscosity impedes fluid flow and reduces cooling efficiency, increasing localized heat. Viscosity influences chip removal and tool friction in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining by controlling how well the lubricant or coolant reaches the cutting interface. Proper viscosity ensures adequate lubrication of critical components in automotive engines, increasing performance and prolonging engine life. What are Real-World Applications of Viscosity in Manufacturing? The real-world applications of viscosity in manufacturing are listed below. Automotive : Viscosity determines how lubricants flow in engines, how fuel is injected and sprayed, and how sealants cure on body panels. Proper viscosity ensures reliable component performance, reduces wear, and supports tight tolerances in drivetrain and chassis systems. Xometry’s Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining and 3D printing services allow for precision manufacturing of automotive components where viscosity-controlled fluids or coatings are required. Aerospace : Viscosity affects coatings on airframes and turbines, adhesive bonding in composite assemblies, and hydraulic fluid behavior in flight control systems. Controlling viscosity delivers consistent surface finish, durable bonds, and stable fluid performance under temperature and pressure extremes. Xometry provides aerospace-grade materials and precision machining to meet the exacting standards for aerospace components requiring specific viscosity ranges in fluids and coatings. Medical : Viscosity impacts the formulation of syringes, fluid delivery systems, and biocompatible adhesives. Accurate viscosity control ensures correct flow in micro‑channels, layer printing in implant manufacturing, and consistent material behavior in sterile environments. Xometry’s services (custom injection molding and 3D printing) support the medical industry’s need for high-quality, precise parts where viscosity is important in fluid handling and material consistency. Chemical : Viscosity influences mixing, pumping, and coating of chemical slurries, resins, and polymer melts. Viscosity must remain within range to prevent blockages in process lines, maintain productivity, and ensure uniform product quality across batches. Xometry’s manufacturing processes (injection molding and CNC machining) ensure precision control in producing components that require specific viscosity tolerances for reliable performance in chemical industries. Food : Viscosity shapes how sauces, creams, and liquids flow through filling machines, coat surfaces, and deliver mouthfeel. Controlled viscosity ensures stable processing, predictable production rates, and consistent consumer experience. Xometry’s services (3D printing and injection molding) provide custom solutions for food packaging and dispensing systems, where precise viscosity is essential to maintaining quality and performance. How does Viscosity Affect Fluid Transport Systems? Viscosity influences fluid transport systems by determining flow resistance, pressure drop, energy consumption, and system design regulation. Higher viscosity leads to greater internal friction and slower fluid movement, which demands higher pumping power and increased operational cost. Fluid transport lines carrying viscous liquids require appropriately rated pumps, larger pipe diameters, and accurate temperature control to maintain target flow rates and avoid issues (cavitation or blockages). Effective viscosity management enables consistent flow velocity, stable delivery of process fluids, and precise system performance in manufacturing pipelines and transfer networks. How is Viscosity Used in Food and Beverage Processing? Viscosity plays a critical role in food and beverage processing through the following steps. First, measure the viscosity of ingredients (sauces, creams, or beverages) to determine their flow characteristics and set appropriate processing parameters. Second, adjust temperature and ingredient concentrations to achieve the desired viscosity, ensuring proper flow during manufacturing while maintaining consistent texture and mouthfeel. Third, control viscosity during transportation through pipes and filling systems to prevent clogging, ensure even flow, and minimize splashing or foaming. Lastly, perform regular quality control checks to verify that viscosity remains within the target range, maintaining uniformity and product quality throughout production. Each step helps optimize manufacturing efficiency, improve product consistency, and ensure a high-quality final product. What is the Viscosity of Water? The viscosity of water is 0.001 Pa·s (1.0 mPa·s) at 20 °C under standard atmospheric pressure. Water is used as a reference fluid because its physical properties are well-characterized, stable, and reproducible across laboratories. Water's uniform response to temperature, wide availability in pure form, and consistent flow behavior make it a reliable benchmark for comparing the viscosity of other liquids. Using water as a reference allows researchers and engineers to evaluate whether a fluid flows more easily or more slowly relative to the standard, facilitating consistent measurement and comparison of fluid viscosities. How does Viscosity Relate to Fluid Mechanics? Viscosity relates to fluid mechanics by determining how fluids resist motion and interact under applied forces. Viscosity defines the internal friction that influences whether a flow remains smooth or becomes turbulent. High viscosity reduces flow velocity and stabilizes the motion of fluid layers, promoting laminar flow where energy loss through friction is predictable. Low viscosity encourages faster movement and turbulence, leading to irregular flow patterns and greater energy dissipation. Viscosity determines how much pressure is needed to move a fluid through a pipeline in fluid transport systems. Engineers design pipe diameters, pump capacities, and flow rates based on viscosity to maintain efficient flow while minimizing energy loss. The balance between viscosity, velocity, and pipe geometry governs Reynolds number, an important indicator of whether the flow is laminar or turbulent in fluid mechanics. Proper understanding of viscosity in relation to fluid mechanics ensures efficient pipe design, reduced wear, and improved system performance across industrial applications. What is the Difference Between Viscosity and Density? The difference between viscosity and density lies in how each property characterizes fluid behavior. Viscosity measures a fluid’s internal resistance to flow or deformation under shear stress, determining how easily it moves when force is applied. Density measures the mass of a substance per unit volume, indicating how much matter is contained in a given space. Viscosity affects how fluids flow through pipes, machinery, and lubrication systems, influencing pumping resistance and energy requirements. Density affects fluid weight, hydrostatic pressure, and buoyancy, which are critical in storage, transport, and separation processes. Viscosity governs injection and lubrication performance in fuel systems, while density contributes to overall fuel mass and pressure distribution, influencing combustion efficiency. Viscosity and density are essential in engineering and process design, as the two govern flow behavior, energy efficiency, and system performance across industrial applications. events.before: Resources / Sheet / Understanding Sheet Metal Tolerances Understanding Sheet Metal Tolerances Written by Greg Paulsen 2 min read Published October 6, 2020 Updated August 21, 2026 Check out our list of quick tips and tolerance specifications for designing Sheet Metal countersinks, curls, and hems! A Quick Guide to Countersinks, Curls, and Hems Compared to other machining processes, designing Sheet Metal parts is relatively straight-forward. Sheet metal parts are made from a single metal sheet by punching, cutting, stamping, and/or bending and are known for their end-use durability. But there are still many important design-for-manufacturability issues to consider. Check out our list of quick tips and tolerance specifications for designing Sheet Metal countersinks, curls, and hems! And for even more information, download our free Sheet Metal Design Guide ! Countersinks The maximum depth of a countersink is .6 times the material thickness of the part. Countersinks must be at least 8 times the material thickness from each other, 4 times the material’s thickness from an edge, and 3 times the material’s thickness from a bend. Curls Outside radius of curls must be at least 2 times the material’s thickness. Holes should be placed away from the curl at least a distance of the radius of the curl plus the material’s thickness. Bends should be at least 6 times the material’s thickness plus the radius of the curl. Hems Hems are folds to the edge of a part to create a rounded, safe edge. Hems may be open, flat, or tear-dropped, and tolerances depend on the hem’s radius, material thickness, and features near the hem (Note: flat hems risk fracturing the material at the bend and should be avoided if possible). For open hems, minimum inside diameter is equal to the material thickness (larger diameters tend to lose circular shape), and the return length is at least 4 times the material’s thickness. Tear-dropped hems must maintain an inside diameter of at least one material’s thickness, an opening of at least ¼ the material’s thickness, and return length is also 4 times the material’s thickness. events.before: Resources / Supplier Shop Tips / Tapping Away: Common Problems, Causes, and Corrections for Taps and Tap Sets Tapping Away: Common Problems, Causes, and Corrections for Taps and Tap Sets Written by Team Xometry 7 min read Published September 18, 2020 Updated August 21, 2026 From breakage to loading, and galling to rough threads, we’ve got some answers that could save you some serious frustration and keep broken taps from breaking your bank. Tapping is one of the machining types most prone to issues because it requires careful balance, planning, and research . Especially when you’re using a CNC machine, lack of sensory connection to the tapping operation can mean that you might miss issues until they’re too late to correct. Because tapping is also one of the last operations to be performed on a part, screwing it up can result in a whole lot of scrapped parts and wasted time. From breakage to loading, and galling to rough threads, we’ve got some answers that could save you some serious frustration and keep broken taps from breaking your bank. First Issue: Tap Breakage By far, the most obvious sign of an issue is tap breakage. If your tool is breaking, cracking, or chipping, you need to administer some TLC quickly. First, just double check that you’re using a machine with the correct power output, and tool. If your tool geometry is off, or the tap isn’t the correct hardness for the use case, you’re fighting a losing battle. Also, make sure the tap is sharp. If you’re working with a dull tap, you maybe have one or two sharpens before you should get yourself a replacement . Also, try not to let your tap get too dull before resharpening. Since dull tools can also cause work hardening (also a cause of breakage), you have extra incentive to stay on the up and up with your tool maintenance. Similarly, you can reduce issues by making sure you’ve got the right grind on your tap. A proper cutting angle and chamfer angle ensure good work. Also often overlooked in tapping is the quality of the hole itself. If your drilled hole is too shallow or too small, you’re either going to ruin the tool or the workpiece with shoddy work. Keep in mind that drill size does not always equal hole size. Checking that the entire process is solid — not just the tool — is essential. If your drilled hole is too shallow for the tap you’re using, that’s going to cause issues as well. Either adjust your drilled hole or the length of your chamfer. Similarly, if your drilled hole and your tap are misaligned — even by a frog hair — your tap is at risk of damage. Honestly, this is the number one reason for tap breakage. Misalignment by even a fraction will be magnified the further the process is pushed, and doubly cause screw-ups (see what I did there?) when your tap reverses from the hole. Misalignment-related breakage is also caused by using incorrect holding devices. Check that the holding device you are using is correct for alignment with the hole. Lastly, you might not be applying the right kind of lubrication — and I don’t mean bribe money or bourbon (though we wouldn’t personally refuse either)*. If you’re experiencing breakage, chipping, or fracturing, you may need to reduce the friction on your tap by increasing the amount of lubrication during machining. You may need to switch the type of lubrication you’re using — a purpose-made tapping lubricant is your best bet. Better lubrication also improves chip removal. This is definitely one area where more is more. *I’m joking. Or am I? Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Second Issue: Tap Failure on Reversal When your tap craps out during reversal, it might be because it’s cutting too tightly. Check that your cutting angle isn’t too small, and increase it if necessary. Galling is a possible player here as well. Basically, when your threads gall, the pressure, and friction between material and tap are high enough that some of the material is pulled along as the tap moves. That’s some pretty unfortunate physics. You can reduce pressure by decreasing the thread percentage you’re trying to cut at, and increasing your land(s) width. The face angle on the back of the land is often the main culprit in this case. If your tap is stalling on reversal, the cause is likely chips jamming too tightly in the tap flutes. You should try to avoid this at all costs since it can quickly ruin your work or break your tap. If your chips aren’t forming and evacuating right, it might call for a different type of tap, with more generous chamfers or a cutting angle better suited to the material or project. As usual, also keep an eye on the lubrication type and amount you’re providing. Don’t skimp! Another possibility is that your flutes are ground incorrectly. If your flute geometry is wrong for the workpiece material, chip evacuation is going to be a whole mess. Third Issue: Stripped or Chipped Tap Threads If you’re having issues with stripped or chipped threads, it’s most likely that your tap and hole are not properly aligned. Even a slight misalignment can increase pressure and friction greatly. Check your tap holder and machine are right for the job, and possibly look into chamfering the hole before you try to use a tap on it. Also, make sure to check the tap alignment from several perspectives before you go ahead and start machining. Stripping can also be caused by a dull or worn tap, which is also an issue that might “work harden” your workpiece. Sadly, trying to tap work-hardened material may also cause your tap to chip, which makes this issue a bit of a vicious circle. A poorly sharpened tap might produce similar results, so it’s sometimes better to replace a tool rather than risk ruining your work. Chipping is also a symptom of poor handling. Taps have to be much harder than the materials they are cutting, but this additional hardness also makes them brittle and prone to chipping. Handle with care! If you’re nice to your tools, they’ll be nice to you right back. Your surface treatment can also make a whole world of difference when it comes to tap effectiveness and wear. Different coatings are optimal at different temperatures, and ideal for different workpiece types. Finding the correct combination of coating, tool geometry, and tapping speed is a tricky balance, but a worthwhile line to walk. Shop affordable Taps and Tap Sets at Xometry Supplies Shop Now Fourth Issue: Torn Threads in Tapped Part Torn threads are just about the biggest letdown after stripped threads. If your tap is tearing or pulling the metal as it turns, the issue is most likely that your speed is too low. You may also need to sharpen or replace your tap. Be sure that your tap doesn’t have broken threads itself, as that’s a problem for obvious reasons. The amount and kind of lubricant you’re using is also an important factor. Make sure you’re not being stingy, and are using an ideal lubricant for your use-type. Lastly, check that chips aren’t clogging up your flute and mucking up your machining. Torn threads might also happen if your cutting face angle is too small. The cutting face angle is largely responsible for reducing impact load, as well as managing chip formation and evacuation. Slight differences in the cutting face geometry of your taps can take your part quality up several notches. You also might need to check the size of the hole you’re drilling in comparison to the size of your tap . It could very well be the case that your tap drill is too small. This isn’t an uncommon problem, but it is an important one to get straight. The fight here is thread strength (i.e., enough material) vs. reasonable torque (i.e., bigger hole/tap ratio). If you’re getting pulled and torn threads, you probably need to reevaluate the relationship between your hole and tap, specifically to reduce torque. Depending on your needs, increase your tap drill size to create a larger hole, or possibly reduce your tap size. If you’re working with a dull tap, you maybe have one or two sharpens before you should get yourself a replacement . Also, try not to let your tap get too dull before resharpening. Since dull tools can also cause work hardening (also a cause of breakage), you have extra incentive to stay on the up and up with your tool maintenance. Similarly, you can reduce issues by making sure you’ve got the right grind on your tap. A proper cutting angle and chamfer angle ensure good work. Also often overlooked in tapping is the quality of the hole itself. If your drilled hole is too shallow or too small, you’re either going to ruin the tool or the workpiece with shoddy work. Keep in mind that drill size does not always equal hole size. Checking that the entire process is solid — not just the tool — is essential. If your drilled hole is too shallow for the tap you’re using, that’s going to cause issues as well. Either adjust your drilled hole or the length of your chamfer. Similarly, if your drilled hole and your tap are misaligned — even by a frog hair — your tap is at risk of damage. Honestly, this is the number one reason for tap breakage. Misalignment by even a fraction will be magnified the further the process is pushed, and doubly cause screw-ups (see what I did there?) when your tap reverses from the hole. Misalignment-related breakage is also caused by using incorrect holding devices. Check that the holding device you are using is correct for alignment with the hole. Lastly, you might not be applying the right kind of lubrication — and I don’t mean bribe money or bourbon (though we wouldn’t personally refuse either)*. If you’re experiencing breakage, chipping, or fracturing, you may need to reduce the friction on your tap by increasing the amount of lubrication during machining. You may need to switch the type of lubrication you’re using — a purpose-made tapping lubricant is your best bet. Better lubrication also improves chip removal. This is definitely one area where more is more. *I’m joking. Or am I? Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Second Issue: Tap Failure on Reversal When your tap craps out during reversal, it might be because it’s cutting too tightly. Check that your cutting angle isn’t too small, and increase it if necessary. Galling is a possible player here as well. Basically, when your threads gall, the pressure, and friction between material and tap are high enough that some of the material is pulled along as the tap moves. That’s some pretty unfortunate physics. You can reduce pressure by decreasing the thread percentage you’re trying to cut at, and increasing your land(s) width. The face angle on the back of the land is often the main culprit in this case. If your tap is stalling on reversal, the cause is likely chips jamming too tightly in the tap flutes. You should try to avoid this at all costs since it can quickly ruin your work or break your tap. If your chips aren’t forming and evacuating right, it might call for a different type of tap, with more generous chamfers or a cutting angle better suited to the material or project. As usual, also keep an eye on the lubrication type and amount you’re providing. Don’t skimp! Another possibility is that your flutes are ground incorrectly. If your flute geometry is wrong for the workpiece material, chip evacuation is going to be a whole mess. Third Issue: Stripped or Chipped Tap Threads If you’re having issues with stripped or chipped threads, it’s most likely that your tap and hole are not properly aligned. Even a slight misalignment can increase pressure and friction greatly. Check your tap holder and machine are right for the job, and possibly look into chamfering the hole before you try to use a tap on it. Also, make sure to check the tap alignment from several perspectives before you go ahead and start machining. Stripping can also be caused by a dull or worn tap, which is also an issue that might “work harden” your workpiece. Sadly, trying to tap work-hardened material may also cause your tap to chip, which makes this issue a bit of a vicious circle. A poorly sharpened tap might produce similar results, so it’s sometimes better to replace a tool rather than risk ruining your work. Chipping is also a symptom of poor handling. Taps have to be much harder than the materials they are cutting, but this additional hardness also makes them brittle and prone to chipping. Handle with care! If you’re nice to your tools, they’ll be nice to you right back. Your surface treatment can also make a whole world of difference when it comes to tap effectiveness and wear. Different coatings are optimal at different temperatures, and ideal for different workpiece types. Finding the correct combination of coating, tool geometry, and tapping speed is a tricky balance, but a worthwhile line to walk. Shop affordable Taps and Tap Sets at Xometry Supplies Shop Now Fourth Issue: Torn Threads in Tapped Part Torn threads are just about the biggest letdown after stripped threads. If your tap is tearing or pulling the metal as it turns, the issue is most likely that your speed is too low. You may also need to sharpen or replace your tap. Be sure that your tap doesn’t have broken threads itself, as that’s a problem for obvious reasons. The amount and kind of lubricant you’re using is also an important factor. Make sure you’re not being stingy, and are using an ideal lubricant for your use-type. Lastly, check that chips aren’t clogging up your flute and mucking up your machining. Torn threads might also happen if your cutting face angle is too small. The cutting face angle is largely responsible for reducing impact load, as well as managing chip formation and evacuation. Slight differences in the cutting face geometry of your taps can take your part quality up several notches. You also might need to check the size of the hole you’re drilling in comparison to the size of your tap . It could very well be the case that your tap drill is too small. This isn’t an uncommon problem, but it is an important one to get straight. The fight here is thread strength (i.e., enough material) vs. reasonable torque (i.e., bigger hole/tap ratio). If you’re getting pulled and torn threads, you probably need to reevaluate the relationship between your hole and tap, specifically to reduce torque. Depending on your needs, increase your tap drill size to create a larger hole, or possibly reduce your tap size. events.before: Resources / Supplier Shop Tips / How to Optimize Your Xometry Profile for More Visibility How to Optimize Your Xometry Profile for More Visibility Written by Tricia Contreras 5 min read Published September 2, 2026 A complete, up-to-date shop profile is your most powerful tool for getting access to pre-matched Xometry jobs — it determines which jobs reach your Job Board and how much of your capacity gets put to work. Xometry helps its manufacturing Partners turn open capacity into revenue by matching shops’ capabilities and certifications to the best-fit jobs, from rapid prototypes to mass production. Your shop’s profile is the key that unlocks all of your potential jobs. Read on to learn how your profile determines which jobs you see on your Job Board, how to complete your profile, and how certain elements can boost your visibility to Xometry’s internal matching algorithm and high-value RFQ opportunities. Why Your Profile Determines Job Matching Access to a consistent flow of pre-matched jobs is one of the top reasons to be a Xometry Manufacturing Partner . After a Xometry customer places an order, that job appears on the Job Board for Partners that meet the manufacturing, certification, and inspection requirements. An incomplete or outdated profile directly limits which jobs a Partner is eligible for, and what they see on their Job Board. “Having an incomplete profile reduces the potential number of job offers a Partner can receive,” said Kacey Bennett, partner engagement manager at Xometry. “Adding all of their certifications and processes to their profile allows Partners to receive more specialized offers that maximize their shop capacity. If they don’t list a capability on their profile, they won’t get matched with a job that requires it.” Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Complete Your Shop Capabilities Profile To complete or update your shop profile, log in to Workcenter and click the gear icon in the upper-right corner. Select Shop Capabilities, and from there you can add or update the following capabilities. Processes: Which processes is your shop equipped to handle? Xometry offers customers more than 21 processes —the more capabilities your shop has, the more jobs you’ll be eligible for. Subprocesses: Make sure you go into as much detail as possible when adding processes to your profile. Don’t forget to add subprocesses such as roll forming for sheet metal and grinding for CNC machining. Materials: Xometry customers can choose from more than 200+ materials when ordering custom parts. Listing all the materials your shop can process makes your profile better reflect your capabilities, but you’ll still be able to view jobs that might include materials that aren’t listed on your profile. Machines: Machines are the heart of your shop — make sure you add them to your shop profile! Updating your profile when you add a new machine to your shop ensures that you can get a return on your investment by filling open capacity and putting that machine to work. Adding your certifications to your profile is simple — just upload your certificates, and a member of the Xometry Partner team will validate and approve them. Certifications Certifications give customers confidence that Xometry Partners can handle the demands of their specific industries, from aerospace and defense to automotive and medical. Having in-demand certifications can elevate your shop to a higher tier in the Xometry Manufacturing Partner Network, making you eligible for higher-value jobs. On average, certified shops earn 6x more than shops without certifications. Certified Partners experience a significant increase in both the number of job offers and average job value. Adding your certifications to your profile is simple — just upload your certificates, and a member of the Xometry Partner team will validate and approve them. You’ll get a reminder to update your certifications before they need to be renewed, so you don’t lose out on any jobs because of an expired certification. First/Formal Inspection Training Completing a First Article Inspection Report or a Formal Inspection Report is another way to build customer confidence and make your shop eligible for more high-level jobs. These forms will be available on your Job Board if a job requires them. If you need any guidance for filling them out, check out this article or join Xometry’s Quality Support Hour , hosted Monday through Friday from 3:00–4:00 pm ET. QMS in a Box QMS certifications are the gold standard for documenting security and compliance, but if your shop doesn’t have a certain certification, you can still qualify for Xometry jobs. To support our Partners who are not third-party accredited and wish to align with Xometry’s requirements for accessing more complex work, Xometry offers comprehensive quality management system (QMS) guidance and templates — a starter “QMS in a box.” This guide can help you establish a QMS foundation or enhance your existing QMS to meet Xometry’s expectations. Based on the level completed, you may qualify for a higher tier and will become eligible for higher-value jobs. Partner Success Score and Outsourcing Tier Eligibility When you log in to Workcenter, your dashboard automatically displays your up-to-date Partner Success Score (PSS). Your PSS is based on all activities in the last 90 days or the last 20 jobs, whichever represents the most job volume. The quality and timeliness of your work determine your score, and a higher score opens you up to a higher volume of Xometry jobs. Maintaining a high PSS makes you eligible for a higher job volume, so if something looks off with your score, you can request a review in Workcenter through the Scorecard page by clicking “Request Review” next to any of the jobs impacting your score. Learn more about your PSS score here . A complete, up-to-date shop profile is your most powerful tool for getting access to pre-matched Xometry jobs — it determines which jobs reach your Job Board and how much of your capacity gets put to work. Take a few minutes today to review your processes, materials, machines, and certifications in Workcenter, and start seeing the results on your Job Board. events.before: Resources / Supplier Shop Tips / When to Invest in New Manufacturing Equipment When to Invest in New Manufacturing Equipment Written by Joel Schadegg 3 min read Published October 6, 2026 Considering a new machine for your shop? Learn the signals to watch for and what to weigh before you move forward. Knowing when to buy a machine rarely comes down to a single factor. The better indicator is what your shop is already telling you: how often machines go down, repair costs, how booked your shop is, and whether you can get the right work to pay off your investment. This article covers the signals to look for and considerations to keep in mind when you're thinking about adding a new piece of equipment to your shop. Signs It's Time to Invest in New Equipment First off, you'll want to look at patterns over the year. Don't let one bad month convince you it's time to sink money into brand-new gear. These are the four signs to be most aware of: Rising Downtime and Breakdowns Look at the last 12 months of downtime. If the same machine keeps stopping and the same components keep failing, repairs are buying time, not reliability. Continued repeat failures on a machine you already fixed are your cue to start looking for a replacement. Climbing Maintenance Costs Add up those repairs, service calls, and replacement parts for each machine. Annual maintenance commonly benchmarks at 2-5% of replacement value. A machine well above that and still climbing, or a rebuild quote nearing over half the replacement cost, is hard to justify. Utilization Above a Healthy Range Many job shops run at 60-65% spindle utilization, and strong shops aim for 80%. If a machine stays loaded at the top of that range and you're still running overtime or passing on work, it's a sign you've outgrown it. Spare Parts Becoming Hard to Source Past 15 years or so, controls and drives get harder to find. Age alone isn't the test; plenty of 20+ year-old machines run fine. If the only source for a board is the secondary market and lead times keep stretching, that's a signal. Looking for A Steady Work Stream? Become A Supplier Weigh Utilization and ROI Before You Buy Before you cut a PO, check whether the capacity is already on your floor. Idle time from changeovers, tool prep, and first-article approvals hides more spindle hours than most shops expect, and recovering them costs far less than a machine. If the purchase still holds up, run a payback calculation: total investment (machine, installation, tooling, training) divided by the annual net benefit. Being under three to four years is generally considered strong. Be honest about run hours, since an inflated estimate makes your hourly cost look better than it is. Many owners also ask how many hours a month the machine needs to cover its payment. Buy to fix a problem you can name, not the biggest machine you can finance. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo It was always drilled into me that you don't buy more equipment until what you have is paid for or a contract comes your way that pays for the equipment up front. Jason McClure VP, Manufacturing Operations Work in hand is what makes the math safe. If you need work to keep new iron busy, the Xometry Partner Network matches jobs to your capabilities, skips the bidding process, and lets you pick what fits your capacity and expertise. Update Your Shop Capabilities Profile When You Invest If you're a Xometry supplier, don't forget to keep your shop machinery and capabilities up-to-date in Workcenter. Our job board shows work that matches your Shop Capabilities profile, so if the right type of machine isn't listed on your Machines Page, jobs that require it won't reach you. As far as job matching goes, an unlisted machine doesn't exist. Add it the week it's running, along with any subprocesses it opens up, such as grinding on the machining side or roll forming for sheet metal. Certifications and registrations work the same way. If you become ITAR-registered or obtain a new certification, such as AS9100 or ISO 9001, adding them to your profile opens access to higher-value jobs that go to qualified shops. That's a bigger subject, so see how to optimize your Xometry profile for the full walkthrough. In summary, good timing comes from your own numbers: downtime, upkeep, loading, and parts. Make the case on those, buy what the work needs, and make investments when it makes sense. When you're ready to put your capacity to work, apply to the Xometry Partner Network if you're not already a supplier, and keep your shop's capabilities up to date. events.before: Resources / Supply Chain / How to Handle Supply Chain Disruption How to Handle Supply Chain Disruption Written by Tricia Contreras 2 min read Published April 30, 2025 Updated August 26, 2026 Having a resilient supply chain is essential to staying competitive. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). F 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. F 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. F 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. If your PCB Assembly demands are beyond these capabilities, please contact us at Service@pcbway.com , we will respond if we can do or not within 24 hours. Item # Item Name PCBA Capability 1. Lead Time Our assembly time ranges from 24 Hours to a few weeks. Please choose appropriate time option to fit your schedule and budget. Due to the complexity of how to determine the turn time of PCBA services, our policy is that turn-time begins immediately after all the parts are ready and all the PCB files (Gerber files/other PCB files, etc.,) , Centroid (Pick & Place PNP file, or XY Data or files in other formats), BOM, and all other necessary data or documents/images/photos are complete for our assembly work. 2. Parts Source Consigned/kitted We prefer you supply all the parts for the PCBA services. In this case, please send us all the components with BOM file and detailed packing list indicating item number, customer or manufacturer’s part number and quantity in kit. Turn-key With our wide and powerful network of parts sourcing, we offer Turn-key PCBA service. We do not mark up on the parts cost. Considering the big price gap between different suppliers, we only source from reliable suppliers who may have no price advantages. We will always ask for your approval before making any decisions. Partial Turn-key/Combo This is our regular practice which you offer the main devices and components, while we source the rest for you. Just like the Turn-key service, we will ask for your approval on every details of the parts concerning price, quality and availability. 3. Assembly Options We offer Surface Mount (SMT), Thru-Hole (THT) and hybrid of both. We also offer single or double-sided placement. 4. Types of Solder We offer both leaded and lead-free (RoHS Compliant) assembly services for our customers. Please choose one to best fit your PCB and the parts on the PCB. 5. Stencils We use laser cut stainless steel stencils to ensure high reliability for fine pitch and BGA components. Nano coating is available upon request. 6. Minimum Order Our minimum is as low as 5 pieces. We do not want you to pay for what you do not need indeed to save you money. 7. Component Size Passive Component: we can accept components as small as 01005, 0201,0402. BGA: We have the ability to handle BGA of 0.3mm pitch for rigid PCBs and 0.4mm for flex boards with X-ray testing. (The details can be confirmed according to the board design.) Fine Pitch Parts: we can assemble 0.25mm fine pitch parts. 8. Component Package We accept parts in Reels, Cut Tape, Tube & Tray, Loose Parts and Bulk. 9. Board Dimension Min Board Size: 10mm x 10mm (Boards smaller than this size need to be panelized) Max Board Size: 250mm x 500mm 10. Board Shape We can assemble boards in Rectangular, Circular and any Odd Shapes. (For shapes other than rectangle, you need to panelize the boards in an array, and add break-away rails at the two longer paralleled edges of the panelized boards to ensure that the boards can be assembled by the machine.) 11. Board Type Currently we handles Rigid boards mostly. As we have the ability to handle flex and rigid-flex boards, please contact Service@pcbway.com if your boards are of flex or rigid-flex. 12. Repair & Rework Repair and rework can be difficult, but we do. Our BGA reballing service with which we can safely remove the misplaced BGA, reball it and put it back on the PCB correctly. It is cost-effective. Testing Procedures Various testing method will be applied to the assembled boards before the final shipment:: Visual inspection: general quality check. X-ray Inspection: checks for BGAs, QFN and bare circuit boards. AOI Testing: checks for solder paste, 0201 components, missing components and polarity. ICT (In-Circuit Test). Functional test (Following your test procedures). ISO Certification PCBWay’s production facilities are ISO9001 certified to ensure we go beyond your expectations.
